well-anatomy.title: Human body: how it works & how to care for it
well-anatomy.description: Human anatomy and physiology system by system, with nutrition, hygiene, sleep and body care — school-health style, medically accurate and practical.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Cells, tissues & organ systems
courses.summary: How a human body is built from cells up to organ systems, and how it keeps its inside steady (homeostasis). The foundation for every other unit.
outcomes: Learners can name the main parts of a human cell and their jobs
Learners can tell apart the four basic tissue types with examples
Learners can list the organ systems and what each does
Learners can explain homeostasis and negative feedback with body-temperature and blood-sugar examples

lessons.title: The cell: the body's building block

scenes.text: In the school lab Kabir scrapes the inside of his cheek with a clean ice-cream stick and stains it blue.
Under the microscope he sees flat cells with a dark dot in each. 'That dot is me?' he laughs.
Ma'am Iyer: 'That dot is the nucleus — it holds the instructions for making all of you.'

steps.title: What a cell is
steps.body: A **cell** is the smallest unit that can carry out life processes on its own. An adult body has roughly **30–37 trillion** cells (scientists' estimates vary). They come in about 200 broad types — nerve cells, muscle cells, blood cells, skin cells — but most share the same basic parts.

steps.title: Parts of an animal cell
steps.body:
- **Cell (plasma) membrane** – thin flexible boundary; controls what enters and leaves (selectively permeable).
- **Cytoplasm** – jelly-like fluid where most chemical reactions happen.
- **Nucleus** – holds DNA in chromosomes (46 in most human cells); controls the cell.
- **Mitochondria** – release energy from food by **cellular respiration** (the 'powerhouse').
- **Ribosomes** – make proteins.
- **Endoplasmic reticulum & Golgi body** – make, pack and ship materials.
- **Lysosomes** – break down waste and worn-out parts.

Human cells have **no cell wall and no chloroplasts** — those are plant features.

steps.title: Solved example: how small is a red blood cell?
steps.body:
A red blood cell is about **8 micrometres (µm)** across. How many would fit side by side across 1 mm?

- Step 1: 1 mm = 1000 µm.
- Step 2: 1000 ÷ 8 = **125 cells**.

Second example: a typical cheek cell is ~60 µm. How many fit in 1 cm? 1 cm = 10 000 µm → 10 000 ÷ 60 ≈ **167 cells**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'all cells have a nucleus' – mature human **red blood cells have no nucleus** (more room for haemoglobin).
- Drawing a cell wall around an animal cell.
- Mixing up *cell membrane* (all cells) and *cell wall* (plants, fungi, bacteria).
- Thinking mitochondria 'make' energy – they **release** energy stored in glucose.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Look at the back of your hand. Every bit of it is made of cells that are constantly replaced — the outer skin layer renews roughly every few weeks.

activity.prompt: Match the cell part to its job
pairs: Holds DNA and controls the cell

quiz.q: Which part of a human cell holds the chromosomes?
quiz.why: The nucleus holds the cell's DNA, which is packaged as chromosomes.

quiz.q: Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT human cells?
quiz.why: Plant cells have a cell wall outside the membrane, for support. Human (animal) cells have only a cell membrane.

quiz.q: Mature human red blood cells lack…
quiz.why: Mature red blood cells lose their nucleus, which leaves more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen.

quiz.q: Cellular respiration mainly happens in the…
quiz.why: Cellular respiration, which releases energy from glucose using oxygen, mainly happens in the mitochondria, the 'powerhouses' of the cell.

quiz.q: How many 10 µm cells fit side by side across 1 mm?
quiz.why: 1 mm = 1000 µm. If each cell is 10 µm wide, then 1000 ÷ 10 = 100 cells fit across 1 mm.

lessons.title: Tissues: teams of similar cells

scenes.text: Sara gets a paper cut while turning a page.
It stings (nerve tissue), bleeds (blood, a connective tissue) and later heals over with new skin (epithelial tissue).
'One tiny cut and I met three tissue types,' she writes in her notebook.

steps.title: What a tissue is
steps.body: A **tissue** is a group of similar cells working together on one job. Humans have **four basic tissue types**.

steps.title: The four tissue types
steps.body:
- **Epithelial** – covers and lines: skin surface, lining of the gut and mouth, glands.
- **Connective** – supports and connects: bone, cartilage, tendons, ligaments, fat, **blood** (yes, blood is a fluid connective tissue).
- **Muscular** – contracts to move: **skeletal** (voluntary, striped), **smooth** (involuntary, gut and blood vessels), **cardiac** (heart only, never tires).
- **Nervous** – carries electrical signals: neurons in brain, spinal cord and nerves.

steps.title: Solved example: classify these
steps.body:
Classify: (a) tendon, (b) stomach lining, (c) heart wall, (d) spinal cord.

- (a) Tendon joins muscle to bone → **connective**.
- (b) Stomach lining covers an inner surface → **epithelial**.
- (c) Heart wall contracts all life → **cardiac muscle**.
- (d) Spinal cord carries signals → **nervous**.

Second: ligament vs tendon. Ligament joins **bone to bone**; tendon joins **muscle to bone**. Both connective.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that **blood** and **bone** are connective tissues.
- Swapping tendon and ligament.
- Calling the heart 'skeletal muscle' — it is its own type, cardiac muscle.

activity.prompt: Sort each example into its tissue type

quiz.q: Blood is classed as which tissue?
quiz.why: Blood is a connective tissue. Its cells are spread in a liquid matrix (plasma), and it links the parts of the body together by carrying substances.
A ligament joins bone to bone at a joint. A tendon joins muscle to bone.

quiz.q: Which muscle type is involuntary and found in the gut wall?
quiz.why: Smooth muscle is involuntary, which means we do not control it. It is found in the gut wall and moves food along.

quiz.q: The lining of the stomach is mainly…
quiz.why: The lining of the stomach is epithelial tissue. Epithelial tissue forms the coverings and linings of the body.
Nervous tissue is made of neurons (nerve cells), which carry electrical signals (impulses).

lessons.title: Organs and organ systems

scenes.text: Arjun sprints for a quick single.
His heart beats faster, lungs breathe harder, muscles pull on bones, his brain judges the run.
'Every system is batting for you at once,' says his coach.

steps.title: Levels of organisation
steps.body:
**Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.**

An **organ** is made of several tissues working together (the stomach has epithelial lining, smooth muscle, nerves and blood). An **organ system** is a group of organs doing one big job.

steps.title: The main human organ systems
steps.body:
- **Skeletal** – support, protection, blood-cell making.
- **Muscular** – movement, posture, heat.
- **Digestive** – break down food, absorb nutrients.
- **Circulatory (cardiovascular)** – transport blood.
- **Respiratory** – gas exchange.
- **Excretory (urinary)** – remove wastes, balance water.
- **Nervous** – fast control by signals.
- **Endocrine** – slower control by hormones.
- **Immune & lymphatic** – defence, fluid return.
- **Integumentary** – skin, hair, nails.
- **Reproductive** – making offspring; matures at puberty.

steps.title: Solved example: which systems are involved?
steps.body:
*Eating a banana before a run.*

- Step 1: Chewing and swallowing → **digestive** (plus muscular).
- Step 2: Glucose absorbed into blood → **circulatory**.
- Step 3: Oxygen taken in → **respiratory**.
- Step 4: Insulin from the pancreas helps cells take up glucose → **endocrine**.
- Step 5: CO₂ breathed out; urea later removed by kidneys → **respiratory, excretory**.

Second: *touching a hot pan* → nervous (reflex), muscular (pull away), integumentary (skin may burn), immune (heals).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 'organ' when you mean 'tissue' (muscle tissue vs the biceps muscle organ).
- Thinking systems work alone — almost every action uses several.
- Forgetting the skin is an organ (the largest one by area).

activity.prompt: Match the system to its main organ

quiz.q: The correct order of organisation is…
quiz.why: The levels of organisation go from small to large: cell → tissue → organ → organ system.

quiz.q: Which system controls the body using hormones?
quiz.why: The endocrine system controls body functions using hormones, which glands release into the blood.

quiz.q: The largest organ by surface area is the…
quiz.why: Skin is the largest organ by surface area, covering about 1.5–2 m² in an adult.

quiz.q: Bone marrow making blood cells is a job of the…
quiz.why: Red bone marrow inside bones makes blood cells, so the skeletal system does this job as well as support and protection.
The reproductive system matures at puberty, under the influence of hormones. This is a normal part of growing up.

lessons.title: Homeostasis: keeping the inside steady

scenes.text: Meher, 13, shivers under two blankets though the room is warm.
The thermometer reads 38.6 °C. Her mother gives water and calls the doctor for advice.
Later the fever breaks and Meher sweats a lot. 'Your body turned the thermostat back down,' the doctor explains.

steps.title: What homeostasis means
steps.body: **Homeostasis** is keeping internal conditions (temperature, water, blood sugar, pH, oxygen) within a narrow, healthy range even when the outside changes. Normal core body temperature is about **37 °C** (roughly 36.1–37.2 °C; it varies across the day). A temperature of **38 °C (100.4 °F) or higher** is usually counted as a fever.

steps.title: Negative feedback in 4 parts
steps.body:
1. **Stimulus** – a change (body heats up).
2. **Receptor** – detects it (temperature sensors in skin and the hypothalamus).
3. **Control centre** – the **hypothalamus** in the brain compares it to the set point.
4. **Effector** – responds to reverse the change (sweat glands make sweat; skin blood vessels widen).

When too cold: shivering (muscles make heat), vessels narrow, 'goosebumps'.

steps.title: Solved example: blood sugar
steps.body:
After a meal, blood glucose rises.
- Step 1: Pancreas detects the rise.
- Step 2: It releases **insulin**.
- Step 3: Liver and muscles take up glucose and store it as **glycogen**.
- Step 4: Glucose falls back to normal.

If glucose falls (long gap without food), the pancreas releases **glucagon**, and the liver releases glucose. In **type 1 diabetes** the body makes little or no insulin; in **type 2** cells respond poorly to insulin. Both need medical care.

steps.title: Common mistakes and when to see a doctor
steps.body:
- Saying 'sweat cools you by being cold' — it cools by **evaporating**, which takes heat from the skin.
- Mixing **glucagon** (raises sugar) with **glycogen** (stored sugar).

See a doctor for fever above 39 °C, fever lasting over 2–3 days, a stiff neck, rash, confusion, trouble breathing, or any fever in a baby under 3 months. Emergency: **112**.

activity.prompt: Put the cooling response in order
items: Hypothalamus compares with the set point
Sweat glands release sweat and skin vessels widen
Sweat evaporates and temperature falls to normal

quiz.why: The hypothalamus, at the base of the brain, acts as the body's thermostat. It also controls many hormones.
Insulin lowers blood glucose by helping cells take up glucose, and the liver store it. Glucagon does the opposite.
Shivering is rapid muscle contraction. Working muscles produce heat, which warms the body when it is cold.
In negative feedback, the response reverses the change and brings the body back to its normal level, like a thermostat switching a heater off.

questions.q: The basic unit of life is the…
questions.why: The cell is the basic unit of life. Atoms are smaller and are not alive, and tissues and organs are made of cells.

questions.q: Which tissue type is bone?
questions.why: Bone is a connective tissue. It is hard because it has minerals like calcium in its matrix.

questions.q: The control centre for body temperature is the…
questions.why: The hypothalamus in the brain is the control centre for body temperature.

questions.q: Which organelle makes proteins?
questions.why: Ribosomes make proteins in the cell.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle is found in the…
questions.why: Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart. It contracts on its own, without tiring.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: A tendon joins muscle to bone, and a ligament joins bone to bone. So only 'Tendon – muscle to bone' is right.

questions.q: Most human body cells contain how many chromosomes?
questions.why: Most human body cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes, which makes 46. Egg and sperm cells have 23.

questions.q: Assertion: Red blood cells cannot divide. Reason: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Cell division needs DNA, and mature red blood cells have no nucleus, so they cannot divide. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is the correct negative-feedback order?
questions.why: In negative feedback, a stimulus is detected by a receptor, the control centre compares it with the normal level, and an effector acts to bring it back to normal.

questions.q: Glucagon causes the liver to…
questions.why: Glucagon tells the liver to break down stored glycogen and release glucose into the blood, so it raises blood glucose.

questions.q: Case: After lunch Riya's blood glucose rises. Which hormone and which organ respond first?
questions.why: After a meal, blood glucose rises, and the pancreas releases insulin. Insulin helps cells take up glucose and lowers the level.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an organ system?
questions.why: Epithelial is a type of tissue, not an organ system. Lymphatic, endocrine and integumentary (skin) are organ systems.

questions.q: A cell is 25 µm wide. How many fit across 1 mm?
questions.why: 1 mm = 1000 µm. 1000 ÷ 25 = 40 cells fit across 1 mm.

questions.q: Convert a body temperature of 39 °C to °F.
Sweating cools the body mainly because…
questions.why: Sweat cools the body because when it evaporates, it takes heat from the skin (evaporation needs heat energy).

questions.q: Assertion: The stomach is an organ. Reason: It is made of only one tissue type.
questions.why: The assertion is true: the stomach is an organ. The reason is false, as organs are made of several tissues (muscle, epithelial, nervous and connective in the stomach).

questions.q: In type 1 diabetes, the main problem is…
questions.why: In type 1 diabetes, the body's immune system destroys the insulin-making cells in the pancreas, so little or no insulin is made and glucose stays high in the blood.

questions.q: Case: In very hot, humid weather sweating cools you less. Why?
questions.why: In hot, humid weather, the air is already full of water vapour, so sweat evaporates slowly. Less heat is taken away, and cooling is weaker.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Bones, joints, muscles & movement
courses.summary: The skeleton, the types of joints, how muscles pull in antagonistic pairs, and how to keep bones and posture healthy for life.
outcomes: Learners can state the functions of the skeleton and name major bones
Learners can classify joints and give examples
Learners can explain antagonistic muscle pairs
Learners can apply bone-health and posture habits, and recognise injuries that need a doctor

lessons.title: The skeleton: 206 bones with five jobs

scenes.text: Dadi slipped in the bathroom and the doctor shows the family her wrist X-ray.
'This is the radius — the forearm bone on the thumb side. A small crack,' she says.
Grandson Ishaan counts bones on a chart: 'A baby has more bones than Dadi?!'

steps.title: Numbers that surprise
steps.body: An adult skeleton has **206 bones**. A newborn has around **270–300** bony pieces; many fuse as we grow (for example, the skull plates and the bones of the base of the spine). Bone is living tissue with blood vessels and nerves — it repairs itself.

steps.title: Five functions
steps.body:
1. **Support** – the frame that holds us up.
2. **Protection** – skull protects brain; ribs protect heart and lungs; vertebrae protect the spinal cord.
3. **Movement** – muscles pull on bones as levers.
4. **Blood-cell production** – red bone marrow.
5. **Mineral store** – calcium and phosphate.

steps.title: Major bones to know
steps.body: Skull (cranium), mandible (lower jaw), clavicle (collarbone), scapula (shoulder blade), sternum (breastbone), ribs (12 pairs), vertebral column (33 vertebrae in a child; several fuse so adults are often counted as 26 bones), humerus (upper arm), radius & ulna (forearm), pelvis (hip), femur (thigh — the longest and strongest bone), patella (kneecap), tibia & fibula (lower leg). Smallest bone: the **stapes** in the middle ear.

steps.title: Solved example: proportion
steps.body:
An adult is 170 cm tall. The femur is roughly a quarter of height. Estimate femur length.
- 170 ÷ 4 = **42.5 cm** (real values ~40–50 cm).

Second: if 12 pairs of ribs, how many ribs? 12 × 2 = **24**. (Men and women have the same number — a common myth says otherwise.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Bones are dead' – they are living and remodel all life.
- 'Men have one fewer rib' – false; both sexes usually have 24.
- Calling the patella part of the femur.

activity.prompt: Match the bone to where it is

quiz.q: How many bones in a typical adult?
quiz.why: A typical adult has 206 bones. Babies are born with more (about 300), as some fuse during growth.
The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone in the body.

quiz.q: Which bones protect the heart and lungs?
quiz.why: The ribs and sternum form the rib cage, which protects the heart and lungs.
Blood cells are made in red bone marrow, found inside some bones.
Both men and women usually have 12 pairs of ribs (24 in all). Sex does not change the number.

lessons.title: Joints: where bones meet

scenes.text: Tanvi practises a Bharatanatyam pose: knees bent, arms circling.
Her shoulder turns in a full circle, but her elbow only bends one way.
'Why can't my elbow spin like my shoulder?' — different joints, different designs.

steps.title: Three classes of joints
steps.body:
- **Fixed (fibrous)** – no movement: sutures of the skull.
- **Slightly movable (cartilaginous)** – between vertebrae (discs), where ribs meet the sternum.
- **Freely movable (synovial)** – most limb joints; a capsule with lubricating **synovial fluid** and smooth **cartilage** on the bone ends.

steps.title: Types of synovial joint
steps.body:
- **Ball-and-socket** – shoulder, hip: movement in all directions.
- **Hinge** – elbow, knee, fingers: one plane, like a door.
- **Pivot** – top of neck (atlas–axis) lets you shake your head 'no'; also radius–ulna for turning the palm.
- **Gliding** – wrist and ankle small bones slide past each other.
- **Saddle** – base of the thumb.

steps.title: Solved example: identify the joint
steps.body:
(a) Nodding 'yes' vs shaking 'no'. Shaking 'no' = **pivot** joint between the first two neck vertebrae.
(b) Bowling a cricket ball overarm = **ball-and-socket** (shoulder) + **hinge** (elbow) + gliding (wrist).
(c) Kicking a football = ball-and-socket (hip) + hinge (knee).

steps.title: Common mistakes & injuries
steps.body:
- Knee is a hinge (mainly), not ball-and-socket.
- **Sprain** = ligament injury; **strain** = muscle/tendon injury; **fracture** = broken bone; **dislocation** = bone pushed out of the joint.

See a doctor if you cannot bear weight, there is deformity, numbness, severe swelling or the pain is not improving in 2–3 days. Never try to push a dislocated joint back yourself.

activity.prompt: Sort each joint

quiz.q: Which joint allows the widest range of movement?
quiz.why: A ball-and-socket joint (shoulder, hip) allows movement in all directions, so it has the widest range.
Synovial fluid lubricates joints, which reduces friction between bone ends.
The skull bones are joined by sutures, which are fixed joints that hardly move. This protects the brain.
A sprain is an injury to a ligament, which joins bone to bone. A strain is an injury to a muscle or tendon.

quiz.q: Turning your head side to side uses a…
quiz.why: Turning the head from side to side uses a pivot joint between the first two neck bones (the atlas rotates on the axis).

lessons.title: Muscles: pulling in pairs

scenes.text: At the gym Vikram curls a dumbbell. His upper arm bulges at the front.
Lowering it, the back of his arm works instead.
His trainer: 'Muscles only pull. They work in teams of two.'

steps.title: Antagonistic pairs
steps.body:
Muscles can only **contract (pull)**; they cannot push. So they work in **antagonistic pairs**:
- **Biceps** contracts → elbow bends (flexion); triceps relaxes.
- **Triceps** contracts → arm straightens (extension); biceps relaxes.
- Hamstrings and quadriceps do the same for the knee.

steps.title: How a contraction happens
steps.body: A nerve signal reaches the muscle → muscle fibres shorten using **ATP** energy (from respiration in mitochondria) → the tendon pulls the bone, which acts as a **lever** with the joint as the pivot. The body has **600+ skeletal muscles**; the largest is the **gluteus maximus** (buttock).

steps.title: Solved example: which muscle?
steps.body:
(a) Standing on tiptoe – calf muscle (**gastrocnemius**) contracts, pulling the heel via the **Achilles tendon**.
(b) Straightening the knee to kick – **quadriceps** contracts, hamstrings relax.
(c) Lowering a dumbbell slowly – the biceps still works while lengthening (controlled 'eccentric' action).

steps.title: Healthy muscles
steps.body: Warm up 5–10 minutes, stretch after exercise, build strength gradually, drink water, eat enough protein, sleep. Muscle **cramps** are sudden painful contractions — gentle stretching usually helps; frequent cramps need a doctor's check.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'The triceps pushes the arm straight' — it **pulls** on the forearm from behind the elbow.
- Mixing **tendon** (muscle–bone) with **ligament** (bone–bone).
- Lifting heavy weights without supervision while still growing — technique first.

statements.s: Muscles can push as well as pull.
When the biceps contracts, the triceps relaxes.
Cardiac muscle gets tired quickly like skeletal muscle.
The Achilles tendon joins the calf muscle to the heel bone.
statements.why: It lets you rise on tiptoe.

statements.s: The quadriceps straighten the knee.

quiz.q: Bending the elbow is done by the…
quiz.why: The biceps contracts to bend (flex) the elbow, while the triceps straightens it.

quiz.q: The energy molecule for contraction is…
quiz.why: Muscle contraction uses ATP as its energy source. Cells make ATP from glucose in respiration.
The gluteus maximus (the buttock muscle) is the largest muscle in the body, as it holds the body upright and powers walking and climbing.

quiz.q: The antagonist of the hamstrings is the…
quiz.why: The hamstrings (back of the thigh) bend the knee, and the quadriceps (front of the thigh) straighten it, so they work as an antagonistic pair.

quiz.q: In the lever system of the arm, the pivot is the…
quiz.why: In the arm as a lever, the joint (elbow) is the pivot, called the fulcrum. The muscle supplies the effort and the hand carries the load.

lessons.title: Healthy bones and posture for life

scenes.text: Rohan's school bag weighs 7 kg. He weighs 35 kg and slouches to one side.
His back aches by evening.
His PE teacher weighs the bag, removes extra books and shows him how to wear both straps.

steps.title: Building bone
steps.body:
Most bone mass is built by your **late teens to mid-20s**. Help it with:
- **Calcium** – milk, curd, paneer, ragi, sesame (til), green leafy vegetables, tofu.
- **Vitamin D** – sunlight on skin (short regular exposure), eggs, fortified foods; deficiency is common in India.
- **Weight-bearing exercise** – running, skipping, dancing, sports.
- Avoid smoking and excess cola/soft drinks.

steps.title: Solved example: the 10% bag rule
steps.body:
Many guidelines suggest a school bag should be **no more than about 10% of body weight**.
- Rohan: 35 kg × 0.10 = **3.5 kg** maximum; his 7 kg bag is double.
- Priya weighs 48 kg → limit ≈ 4.8 kg.

steps.title: Posture basics
steps.body: Screen at eye level, feet flat, back supported, shoulders relaxed. Every 30–45 minutes stand, stretch and move. Phone held at eye level reduces 'text neck'.

steps.title: Myths and when to see a doctor
steps.body:
- 'Cracking knuckles causes arthritis' — studies have not found that it does.
- Rickets (soft bones in children) comes from lack of vitamin D/calcium.
- See a doctor for back pain with fever, numbness, weakness, night pain, or a visibly curved spine (possible scoliosis).

activity.prompt: Using the 10% guideline, what is the maximum bag weight for a 42 kg student (in kg)?

quiz.q: Peak bone mass is mostly reached by…
quiz.why: Peak bone mass is mostly reached between the late teens and mid-20s, so young people should 'bank' bone with calcium, vitamin D and exercise.
Ragi (finger millet) is rich in calcium. Sugar, chips and cola have little or none.

quiz.q: Vitamin D is made in skin with…
quiz.why: The skin makes vitamin D when exposed to sunlight (UVB rays).

quiz.q: Rickets is linked to lack of…
quiz.why: Rickets, in which bones are soft and bend, is linked to a lack of vitamin D (and calcium).

quiz.q: A 50 kg student's bag limit (10% rule) is…
quiz.why: The 10% rule says a school bag should weigh no more than about 10% of body weight: 50 × 0.1 = 5 kg.

questions.q: Number of bones in an adult skeleton:
questions.why: An adult human skeleton has 206 bones.

questions.q: The kneecap is the…
questions.why: The kneecap is the patella, a small bone that protects the knee joint.

questions.q: Muscles move bones by…
questions.why: Muscles move bones by pulling, because they can only shorten (contract). They cannot push.

questions.q: A hinge joint is found at the…
questions.why: The elbow is a hinge joint, which moves back and forth like a door hinge.

questions.q: Which supplies calcium?
questions.why: Curd (dairy) supplies calcium. Coffee, cola and candy do not.

questions.q: Which joint is fixed?
questions.why: Skull sutures are fixed joints that do not move. The knee is a hinge joint, the wrist is gliding, and the neck pivot is a rotating joint.

questions.q: A strain affects…
questions.why: A strain is an injury to a muscle or tendon. A sprain affects a ligament.

questions.q: When straightening the arm, which is the effector muscle?
questions.why: To straighten the arm, the triceps contracts, as it extends the elbow. The biceps relaxes at the same time.

questions.q: Assertion: Muscles work in antagonistic pairs. Reason: Muscles can only contract.
options: Both true; reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Muscles can only contract (pull), so they need a partner to pull the bone back the other way. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is the smallest bone?
questions.why: The stapes in the middle ear is the smallest bone in the body.

questions.q: Red bone marrow's job:
questions.why: Red bone marrow makes blood cells (red cells, white cells and platelets).

questions.q: Case: Aman twists his ankle; ligaments are overstretched; he can walk with pain. This is most likely a…
questions.why: Overstretched ligaments after a twisted ankle, where the person can still walk with pain, point to a sprain. A fracture or dislocation usually makes walking very difficult.

questions.q: A 60 kg student's bag weighs 9 kg. By how many kg does it exceed the 10% guideline?
questions.why: 10% of 60 kg is 6 kg. The bag is 9 kg, so it exceeds the guideline by 9 − 6 = 3 kg.

questions.q: Which describes a synovial joint correctly?
options: Capsule with lubricating fluid and cartilage-covered bone ends
questions.why: A synovial joint has a capsule filled with lubricating synovial fluid, and its bone ends are covered with smooth cartilage. It allows free movement.

questions.q: Bone mass built in youth matters later because…
options: higher peak bone mass lowers later osteoporosis risk
questions.why: Bones keep gaining mass until the mid-20s. A higher peak bone mass means more is left in old age, so the risk of osteoporosis (weak bones) is lower. It does not prevent all fractures.

questions.q: Case: A girl stays indoors all day, avoids dairy, and has aching bones. The two most likely deficiencies are…
questions.why: Staying indoors means little sunlight (less vitamin D) and avoiding dairy means little calcium. Both are needed for strong bones, and low levels can cause aching bones.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Digestion, nutrients & a balanced plate
courses.summary: The journey of food through the digestive system, what each nutrient does, deficiency diseases, building a balanced Indian plate, reading food labels and staying hydrated.
outcomes: Learners can trace food through the alimentary canal and name the role of each organ
Learners can match enzymes to the foods they digest
Learners can name the seven nutrient groups and deficiency diseases
Learners can plan a balanced plate and read a nutrition label

lessons.title: The food's journey: mouth to large intestine

scenes.text: Zoya bites into an aloo paratha at breakfast.
Over the next 24–48 hours it will travel about 8–9 metres through her body.
Her biology teacher draws the route on the board like a metro map.

steps.title: The alimentary canal in order
steps.body:
**Mouth → pharynx → oesophagus (food pipe) → stomach → small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) → large intestine (caecum, colon, rectum) → anus.**

Helper organs (food does not pass through them): **salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, pancreas**.

steps.title: What happens where
steps.body:
- **Mouth** – teeth chew (mechanical digestion); saliva's **amylase** starts breaking starch.
- **Oesophagus** – waves of muscle (**peristalsis**) push food down; takes seconds.
- **Stomach** – churns food with **hydrochloric acid** (kills germs) and **pepsin** (starts protein digestion); 2–4 hours.
- **Small intestine** – most digestion and **absorption**; bile (from liver, stored in gallbladder) breaks fat into droplets; pancreatic juice adds enzymes. Inner surface has millions of finger-like **villi**.
- **Large intestine** – absorbs water and salts; gut bacteria live here; forms faeces.

steps.title: Solved example: why are villi useful?
steps.body:
Imagine a 3 m small intestine as a smooth tube vs one folded with villi and microvilli. Folding multiplies surface area many times (estimates often quote tens of square metres), so more nutrients can be absorbed per minute. **Bigger surface area → faster absorption.**

Second: *Why do we chew well?* Smaller pieces = more surface for enzymes → faster digestion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the liver 'digests' food — it makes **bile**, which **emulsifies** fat (no enzymes in bile).
- Thinking most absorption happens in the stomach — it happens in the **small intestine**.
- Mixing up oesophagus (food) with trachea (air). The **epiglottis** flap stops food entering the windpipe.

activity.prompt: Put the organs in the order food passes through

quiz.q: Most nutrient absorption happens in the…
quiz.why: Most nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine, which has villi that give a large surface area.
The liver makes bile. The gallbladder only stores it.
Peristalsis is a wave of muscle contractions that pushes food along the digestive tract.
The large intestine mainly absorbs water and salts from the leftover material, which forms faeces.

quiz.q: The flap that stops food entering the windpipe:
quiz.why: The epiglottis is a flap that closes the windpipe when you swallow, so food goes down the food pipe.

lessons.title: Enzymes: the chemical scissors

scenes.text: Dev chews plain bread for two minutes without swallowing.
It starts tasting slightly sweet.
'Your saliva is turning starch into sugar,' his teacher says.

steps.title: What enzymes do
steps.body: **Enzymes** are proteins that speed up chemical reactions without being used up. Digestive enzymes break large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed. Each enzyme fits a particular food molecule (**specificity**), and works best at a certain temperature (~37 °C) and pH.

steps.title: Enzyme table
steps.body:
- **Amylase** (saliva, pancreas): starch → maltose/sugars.
- **Pepsin** (stomach, acidic): proteins → smaller peptides.
- **Trypsin** (pancreas): proteins → peptides.
- **Lipase** (pancreas): fats → fatty acids + glycerol.
- Intestinal enzymes finish the job: sugars → **glucose**, peptides → **amino acids**.

End products absorbed: glucose, amino acids, fatty acids & glycerol, vitamins, minerals, water.

steps.title: Solved example: pH
steps.body:
Stomach pH is about **1.5–3.5** (strongly acidic); small intestine is near neutral to slightly alkaline (~7–8). Question: why does pepsin stop working in the small intestine? → Pepsin needs acid; in alkaline conditions its shape changes and it stops working.

Second: why does boiling saliva stop starch digestion? → High heat **denatures** amylase (changes its shape permanently).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that enzymes are 'alive' – they are molecules (proteins).
- 'Bile is an enzyme' – no; it emulsifies fat.
- Saying proteins break into glucose – proteins → **amino acids**.

activity.prompt: Match enzyme to the food it digests

quiz.why: Proteins are digested into amino acids, which the body uses to build its own proteins.
Pepsin works best in acidic conditions, such as in the stomach, where hydrochloric acid keeps the pH low.
Lipase digests fats (lipids) into fatty acids and glycerol.

quiz.q: Why does chewed bread taste sweet?
quiz.why: Chewed bread tastes sweet because salivary amylase, an enzyme in saliva, breaks starch into sugars.
Very high heat denatures enzymes, which means their shape is lost and they stop working.

lessons.title: The seven nutrient groups and deficiency diseases

scenes.text: Tara, 15, feels tired, breathless on stairs and looks pale.
A blood test shows low haemoglobin — iron-deficiency anaemia, common in Indian teenage girls.
The doctor advises iron tablets as prescribed, plus foods like dal, green leafy vegetables, jaggery, eggs/meat if she eats them, with vitamin C (amla, lemon) to help absorption.

steps.title: Seven groups
steps.body:
- **Carbohydrates** – main energy (rice, roti, millets, potatoes). 1 g ≈ 4 kcal.
- **Proteins** – growth and repair (dal, beans, milk, eggs, fish, soy, paneer). 1 g ≈ 4 kcal.
- **Fats** – concentrated energy, cell membranes, absorb vitamins A, D, E, K (oils, ghee, nuts). 1 g ≈ 9 kcal.
- **Vitamins** – small amounts for many reactions.
- **Minerals** – iron, calcium, iodine, zinc etc.
- **Fibre** – keeps bowels regular (whole grains, fruit, vegetables).
- **Water** – about 60% of adult body mass.

steps.title: Deficiency diseases
steps.body:
- Vitamin A → **night blindness**
- Vitamin B1 → **beriberi**
- Vitamin C → **scurvy** (bleeding gums)
- Vitamin D → **rickets** (children)
- Iron → **anaemia**
- Iodine → **goitre** (enlarged thyroid) — why salt in India is iodised
- Severe protein-energy lack → **kwashiorkor** / **marasmus**

steps.title: Solved example: calories
steps.body:
A snack has 20 g carbohydrate, 5 g protein and 10 g fat. Energy?
- Carbs: 20 × 4 = 80 kcal
- Protein: 5 × 4 = 20 kcal
- Fat: 10 × 9 = 90 kcal
- **Total = 190 kcal**

Second: which macronutrient gives most energy per gram? **Fat (9 kcal/g)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Fat is always bad' – some fat is essential; limit trans fats and excess saturated fat.
- Taking vitamin/iron pills without advice – too much iron or vitamin A/D can be harmful. Ask a doctor.
- Thinking fibre is 'useless' because it isn't digested.

activity.prompt: Match deficiency to disease

quiz.why: Fat gives 9 kcal per gram. Carbohydrate and protein give about 4 kcal per gram.

quiz.q: Scurvy is due to lack of…
quiz.why: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C, which causes bleeding gums and slow healing.
Iodised salt gives the iodine needed by the thyroid, so it prevents goitre (swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck).

quiz.q: Vitamin C helps the body absorb…
quiz.why: Vitamin C helps the body absorb iron, especially iron from plant foods. So lemon with dal or greens helps.

quiz.q: Energy in 10 g protein + 10 g fat:
quiz.why: Protein gives 4 kcal/g, so 10 g gives 40 kcal. Fat gives 9 kcal/g, so 10 g gives 90 kcal. Total = 130 kcal.

lessons.title: Building a balanced Indian plate

scenes.text: At the school canteen the class compares lunches.
Ravi has only rice and pickle; Neha has rice, dal, sabzi, curd and a fruit.
'Neha's thali has every group — that's what balanced looks like,' says the nutrition club leader.

steps.title: The 'my plate' idea
steps.body: A simple guide used in Indian nutrition advice: about **half the plate vegetables and fruits**, a quarter **whole grains / millets**, a quarter **protein** (dal, pulses, eggs, fish, chicken, paneer, soy), plus some **milk/curd**, a little oil, nuts or seeds. Vary colours over the week.

steps.title: Limits that matter
steps.body:
- **Salt**: WHO suggests under **5 g a day** for adults (about one level teaspoon) — pickles, papad, chips and instant noodles hide a lot.
- **Added sugar**: WHO advises keeping free sugars under 10% of energy, ideally under 5%.
- Choose water, lassi or nimbu-pani over sugary soft drinks.

steps.title: Solved example: improve the meal
steps.body:
Ravi's lunch: rice + pickle.
- Missing protein → add dal or rajma.
- Missing vegetables → add sabzi or salad.
- Missing calcium → add curd.
- Reduce pickle (high salt).

Second: breakfast of biscuits + sweet tea → swap for poha with peanuts and vegetables, or an egg/besan chilla, plus a fruit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping breakfast before school (hurts concentration).
- 'Diet' = starving. Growing teens need regular meals.
- Believing one 'superfood' fixes everything – variety matters more.

activity.prompt: Sort the foods into their main group

quiz.q: WHO's adult daily salt limit is about…
quiz.why: WHO advises adults to eat less than 5 g of salt a day (about one teaspoon).
A balanced plate has about half vegetables and fruits, with the rest for grains and protein.

quiz.q: Which is a good plant protein?
quiz.why: Rajma (kidney beans) is a pulse, a good plant source of protein. Butter, sugar and cornflour are not.
Water is the best drink with a meal. Cola, energy drinks and syrups add sugar (and caffeine).

quiz.q: Pickles and papad are high in…
quiz.why: Pickles and papad are high in salt (sodium), so they should be eaten in small amounts.

lessons.title: Food labels, hydration & junk-food smarts

scenes.text: Kunal reads the back of a 'baked, healthy!' chips packet.
Per 100 g: 520 kcal, 30 g fat, 1.6 g sodium.
'Healthy on the front, salty on the back,' he says.

steps.title: How to read a label
steps.body: Look at: **serving size**, **energy (kcal)**, **total fat & saturated/trans fat**, **sugar**, **sodium**, **fibre**, ingredient list (listed from most to least by weight). Indian packs also show a **green dot (vegetarian)** or **brown/red dot (non-vegetarian)**.

steps.title: Solved example: sodium to salt
steps.body:
Salt (sodium chloride) ≈ sodium × 2.5.
- 1.6 g sodium per 100 g → 1.6 × 2.5 = **4 g salt** per 100 g.
- If you eat a 50 g pack → **2 g salt**, already ~40% of the 5 g daily limit.

Second: a drink has 35 g sugar in 330 ml. 1 teaspoon ≈ 4 g sugar → 35 ÷ 4 ≈ **9 teaspoons**.

steps.title: Water
steps.body: Needs vary with heat, activity and size; a common guide is 6–8 glasses a day for teens, more in summer and sport. Pale-yellow urine is a simple sign you're drinking enough. Signs of dehydration: dark urine, headache, dizziness, dry mouth. Heat stroke (hot dry skin, confusion) is an emergency — call **112**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trusting front-of-pack words like 'natural' or 'multigrain' without checking the back.
- Energy drinks ≠ sports drinks; energy drinks contain caffeine and are not advised for children and teens.
- Comparing labels with different serving sizes — compare **per 100 g**.

activity.prompt: A packet lists 0.8 g sodium per serving. Roughly how many grams of salt is that? (salt ≈ sodium × 2.5)

options: from most to least by weight
quiz.why: On a food label, ingredients are listed from most to least by weight, so the first ingredient is the largest part.
Salt (sodium chloride) is about 40% sodium, so 1 g of sodium is about 2.5 g of salt.
Pale-yellow urine is a sign of good hydration. Dark urine, headache and dry lips can mean you need more water.

quiz.q: A green dot on an Indian food pack means…
quiz.why: On Indian food packs, a green dot inside a square means the product is vegetarian. A brown dot means non-vegetarian.
Energy drinks have a lot of caffeine and sugar, so they are not advised for teenagers. Water is better.

questions.q: Digestion of starch begins in the…
questions.why: Starch digestion begins in the mouth, where salivary amylase starts to break it into sugars.

questions.q: Iodine deficiency causes…
questions.why: Lack of iodine causes goitre, a swollen thyroid gland. Rickets is vitamin D, beriberi vitamin B1, scurvy vitamin C.

questions.q: Which organ makes bile?
questions.why: The liver makes bile, which is stored in the gallbladder.

questions.q: The end product of fat digestion:
questions.why: Fats are digested into fatty acids and glycerol by lipase.

questions.q: Villi are found in the…
questions.why: Villi, tiny finger-like folds that absorb nutrients, are found in the small intestine.

questions.q: Which is a protective food?
questions.why: Guava is a protective food, rich in vitamin C and other protective nutrients. Sugar and white bread give mostly energy.

questions.q: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach helps by…
questions.why: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills germs in food and gives the acidic pH in which pepsin works.

questions.q: Assertion: Bile helps digest fats. Reason: Bile contains lipase.
questions.why: The assertion is true: bile helps digest fats by breaking them into small droplets (emulsifying). The reason is false: bile has no enzymes such as lipase.

questions.q: Night blindness is linked to lack of…
questions.why: Night blindness is caused by a lack of vitamin A, which is needed for seeing in dim light.

questions.q: Case: A girl with heavy periods feels tired and breathless. Most likely nutritional issue:
questions.why: Heavy periods cause blood (and iron) loss. With low iron, the body makes less haemoglobin, which causes tiredness and breathlessness. This is iron-deficiency anaemia, and it is common and treatable.

questions.q: Energy in 30 g carbohydrate + 10 g protein + 5 g fat:
questions.why: Carbohydrate: 30 × 4 = 120, protein: 10 × 4 = 40, fat: 5 × 9 = 45. Total = 120 + 40 + 45 = 205 kcal.

questions.q: A 40 g snack has 1.2 g sodium per 100 g. Salt in the whole snack ≈
questions.why: 40 g contains 1.2 × 0.4 = 0.48 g sodium. Salt ≈ sodium × 2.5, so 0.48 × 2.5 = 1.2 g salt.

questions.q: Pepsin stops working in the small intestine because…
questions.why: Pepsin works in acid. In the small intestine, bile and pancreatic juice make the pH alkaline, so pepsin stops working.

questions.q: Why are villi thin-walled with many capillaries?
options: For short diffusion distance and transport of absorbed food
questions.why: Villi have thin walls, so substances have only a short distance to diffuse. Many capillaries then carry the absorbed food away in the blood.

questions.q: A 330 ml drink contains 40 g sugar. Using 4 g per teaspoon, how many teaspoons?
questions.why: 40 g of sugar ÷ 4 g per teaspoon = 10 teaspoons, which is far more than a teen should have in a whole day.

questions.q: Case: Boiled saliva + starch shows no sugar after 10 min; unboiled saliva + starch does. The best conclusion:
questions.why: Boiling destroys enzymes (denatures them). Boiled saliva made no sugar, so its amylase stopped working. The unboiled saliva still had working amylase, which turned starch into sugar.

questions.q: Which statement about fats is MOST accurate?
options: Fats have no role in cells
Fats are needed to absorb vitamins A, D, E, K; limit trans fats
questions.why: Fats are needed to absorb the vitamins A, D, E and K, and they are part of cell membranes. But trans fats should be limited. Fat gives 9 kcal/g, not 4.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Heart, blood & circulation
courses.summary: How the four-chambered heart pumps blood through double circulation, what blood is made of, blood groups, blood pressure and pulse, and heart-healthy habits.
outcomes: Learners can trace blood through the heart and double circulation
Learners can name blood components and their functions
Learners can compare arteries, veins and capillaries
Learners can measure pulse and interpret blood pressure in broad terms
Learners can recognise heart-attack and stroke warning signs and know CPR basics exist

lessons.title: The heart: a four-chambered pump

scenes.text: At a school health camp Dr. Bose lets Anika listen to her own heart.
'Lub-dub, lub-dub.' 'Those are your valves closing,' the doctor smiles.
'Your heart is about the size of your fist and has beaten every second since before you were born.'

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: The heart sits in the chest, slightly left of centre, protected by the ribs. It has **four chambers**: two upper **atria** (receive blood) and two lower **ventricles** (pump blood out). A wall called the **septum** keeps the right side (deoxygenated blood) separate from the left (oxygenated). The **left ventricle has the thickest wall** because it pumps blood to the whole body.

steps.title: The route
steps.body:
**Body → vena cava → right atrium → (tricuspid valve) → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs** (pick up O₂, drop CO₂) **→ pulmonary veins → left atrium → (bicuspid/mitral valve) → left ventricle → aorta → body.**

Blood passes through the heart **twice** per full circuit: **double circulation**. Valves stop backflow; their closing makes the 'lub-dub'.

steps.title: Solved example: odd vessels
steps.body:
Q: Which artery carries deoxygenated blood? → **Pulmonary artery** (heart → lungs).
Q: Which vein carries oxygenated blood? → **Pulmonary vein** (lungs → heart).

Rule: **arteries carry blood Away from the heart; veins carry it back** — oxygen level does not define them.

steps.title: Solved example: cardiac output
steps.body: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. At rest, 70 beats/min × 70 ml/beat = 4900 ml ≈ **4.9 L per minute** — roughly the whole blood volume (about 5 L in an adult) every minute.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'All arteries carry oxygenated blood' — not the pulmonary artery.
- Drawing the heart from your own view: diagrams show the patient's left on **your right**.
- Saying the right ventricle is thicker — the **left** is.

activity.prompt: Trace one drop of blood starting from the body

quiz.q: Which chamber has the thickest wall?
quiz.why: The left ventricle has the thickest wall, since it pumps blood to the whole body at high pressure.
The pulmonary vein is the exception among veins: it carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart (left atrium).
Heart valves keep blood flowing in one direction, preventing backflow.

quiz.q: Double circulation means blood passes through the heart…
quiz.why: In double circulation, blood passes through the heart twice in each full circuit: once on the way to the lungs and once on the way to the body.

quiz.q: HR 80, stroke volume 60 ml. Cardiac output?
quiz.why: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 80 × 60 = 4800 ml/min = 4.8 L/min.

sources: NCERT (Life processes; Body fluids and circulation)

lessons.title: Blood: what it is made of

scenes.text: Nikhil's father donates blood at a college camp.
The bag is later separated into red cells, plasma and platelets — one donation can help several patients.
'Donating is safe for healthy adults 18–65 and takes about 10 minutes,' the nurse explains.

steps.title: Components
steps.body:
- **Plasma** (~55%) – yellowish liquid, mostly water; carries dissolved food, hormones, CO₂, urea, proteins.
- **Red blood cells (RBCs)** – carry oxygen using **haemoglobin** (contains iron); live ~120 days; no nucleus.
- **White blood cells (WBCs)** – fight infection (some engulf germs, some make **antibodies**).
- **Platelets** – cell fragments that help **clotting**.

Adults have about **5 litres** of blood.

steps.title: Blood groups
steps.body:
ABO groups: **A, B, AB, O**, plus **Rh** positive/negative.
- **O negative** – often called the universal *donor* for red cells.
- **AB positive** – universal *recipient* for red cells.
- Transfusions are always cross-matched in the lab before use.

steps.title: Solved example: who can receive?
steps.body:
Rahul is **A+**. Can he receive red cells from: O−? yes · A−? yes · B+? **no** (anti-B antibodies) · AB+? **no**.

Second: haemoglobin normal ranges (approx.): adult women ~12–15.5 g/dL, men ~13.5–17.5 g/dL; values below suggest anaemia — a doctor interprets results.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Blood is blue in veins' – it is always red (darker when low in oxygen); veins look bluish through skin due to how light scatters.
- Forgetting platelets are fragments, not full cells.
- Thinking blood group can be changed by diet.

activity.prompt: Match the component to its job

quiz.q: Which blood cell has no nucleus?
quiz.why: Mature red blood cells (RBCs) have no nucleus. White blood cells all have a nucleus.
Platelets help blood clot, which stops bleeding after an injury.
O negative red cells have no A, B or Rh antigens, so they can be given to almost anyone. That makes O− the universal red-cell donor.
Red blood cells live for about 120 days before being broken down and replaced.
Haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying pigment in red blood cells, contains iron.

lessons.title: Arteries, veins, capillaries — and your pulse

scenes.text: In PE class everyone places two fingers on the inside of their wrist.
Resting pulse: 76. After 20 jumping jacks: 128.
Two minutes later it's back to 84 — the fitter you are, the faster it recovers.

steps.title: Three kinds of vessel
steps.body:
- **Arteries** – carry blood away from heart; thick, elastic, muscular walls; high pressure; you feel their pulse.
- **Veins** – return blood; thinner walls; wider space inside; have **valves** to stop backflow; low pressure.
- **Capillaries** – one cell thick; where oxygen, food and waste are exchanged with tissues.

steps.title: Solved example: measuring pulse
steps.body:
Count beats for 15 s and multiply by 4.
- 19 beats in 15 s → 19 × 4 = **76 beats per minute (bpm)**.

Second: 30 beats in 20 s → 30 × 3 = **90 bpm**. Normal resting heart rate for teens and adults: roughly **60–100 bpm** (athletes may be lower).

steps.title: Blood pressure
steps.body: Written as **systolic/diastolic** in mmHg, e.g. **120/80**. Systolic = pressure when ventricles contract; diastolic = when the heart relaxes. Adults with readings repeatedly at or above about **140/90** (some guidelines use 130/80) have high blood pressure (**hypertension**) — often no symptoms, so regular checks matter. Children's BP ranges depend on age and height.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using your thumb to take a pulse — the thumb has its own pulse; use index + middle fingers.
- Thinking capillaries carry blood straight back to the heart — they connect arteries to veins.
- 'High BP always causes headaches' — usually silent.

activity.prompt: You count 22 beats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?

quiz.why: Veins have valves to stop blood flowing backwards, since the pressure in them is low.
Exchange of materials with tissues takes place in capillaries, which have very thin walls.
In a reading of 120/80, 120 is the systolic pressure, when the heart contracts. 80 is the diastolic pressure, when it relaxes.

quiz.q: A normal resting heart rate is about…
quiz.why: A normal resting heart rate for adults is about 60–100 beats per minute.
25 beats in 15 seconds: 15 s is a quarter of a minute, so multiply by 4: 25 × 4 = 100 bpm.

lessons.title: A healthy heart, and recognising emergencies

scenes.text: At a wedding, 55-year-old Uncle Suresh feels crushing chest pain spreading to his left arm, and is sweating.
His niece Pooja, 17, recognises the signs, calls **112** and keeps him seated and calm.
Doctors later say fast action saved heart muscle. 'Time is muscle.'

steps.title: Heart-healthy habits
steps.body:
- At least **60 minutes of activity daily** for children and teens (WHO); 150 minutes a week of moderate activity for adults.
- Eat plenty of vegetables, fruit, whole grains, pulses; limit salt, sugary drinks, fried and ultra-processed foods.
- Never start smoking or vaping; avoid alcohol.
- Sleep well; manage stress; regular BP checks for adults.

steps.title: Heart attack warning signs
steps.body: Chest pain, pressure or tightness (can spread to arm, jaw, back), breathlessness, cold sweat, nausea, light-headedness. Women and people with diabetes may have milder or unusual symptoms. **Call 112 immediately.** Do not drive the person yourself if an ambulance can come.

steps.title: Stroke: think FAST
steps.body: **F**ace drooping · **A**rm weakness · **S**peech difficulty · **T**ime to call 112. Note the time symptoms began — treatment is time-critical.

steps.title: Solved example: what to do
steps.body:
Case: a 60-year-old collapses, does not respond and is not breathing normally.
- Step 1: Check the scene is safe; shout for help.
- Step 2: Call **112** (put the phone on speaker).
- Step 3: Start **hands-only CPR**: push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about **100–120 per minute**, ~5–6 cm deep for adults.
- Step 4: Use an **AED** if one is available; follow its voice prompts.

Trained first-aid courses are the best way to learn this properly.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This lesson is general education, not medical advice. For any worrying symptom, see a doctor.

a.text: Your grandfather says his chest feels tight and heavy, and his left arm aches. He's sweating. What do you do first?

choices.label: Call 112 and keep him resting
Give him a big meal
choices.feedback: Food doesn't help and wastes time.

choices.label: Tell him to sleep it off
choices.feedback: Never wait out possible heart-attack symptoms.

x.text: Time is passing and symptoms are getting worse. Try again: what now?

choices.label: Call 112 now

b.text: Help is coming. He suddenly collapses and isn't breathing normally.

choices.label: Start hands-only CPR, 100–120 pushes/min, and ask someone to find an AED
Pour water on his face and wait

b2.text: He still isn't breathing. The dispatcher tells you to push on the chest.

choices.label: Start CPR now

end1.text: Paramedics arrive and take over. Your fast action gave him the best chance.

quiz.why: FAST (Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call for help) is used to recognise stroke.
Hands-only CPR uses chest compressions at about 100–120 per minute.
WHO advises young people (5–17 years) to be active for an average of at least 60 minutes a day.
The all-in-one emergency number in India is 112.

options: a device that can shock a heart back to rhythm
quiz.why: An AED (automated external defibrillator) is a device that can deliver a shock to restore a normal heart rhythm in cardiac arrest.

questions.q: The heart has how many chambers?
questions.why: The human heart has four chambers: two atria (upper) and two ventricles (lower).

questions.q: Blood cells that fight germs:
questions.why: White blood cells (WBCs) fight germs. Platelets help clotting and red cells carry oxygen.

questions.q: Arteries carry blood…
questions.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the body (and lungs).

questions.q: Which vessel carries blood from the heart to the lungs?
questions.why: The pulmonary artery carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. The aorta goes to the body.

questions.q: Normal BP example for a healthy adult:
questions.why: A normal blood pressure for a healthy adult is about 120/80 mmHg.

questions.q: Clotting needs…
questions.why: Platelets are needed for blood clotting. They clump at a wound and help form a clot.

questions.q: Assertion: The left ventricle wall is thicker than the right. Reason: It pumps blood around the whole body at higher pressure.
questions.why: Both are true. The left ventricle pumps blood around the whole body at higher pressure, so it needs a thicker muscular wall than the right, which pumps only to the lungs.

questions.q: Veins have valves because…
options: pressure is low and blood could flow backwards
questions.why: Veins have valves because the pressure in them is low, so blood could flow backwards. The valves keep it flowing towards the heart.

questions.q: A person with blood group B+ can receive red cells from…
questions.why: O negative red cells carry no A, B or Rh antigens, so a person with B+ blood can safely receive them. A+ and AB blood carry A antigen, which anti-A antibodies in B+ would attack.

questions.q: Which is NOT a heart-attack warning sign?
questions.why: Chest pressure, cold sweat and pain spreading to the jaw are warning signs of a heart attack. Sneezing is unrelated.

questions.q: 17 beats in 10 seconds =
questions.why: 17 beats in 10 seconds: there are 6 ten-second periods in a minute, so 17 × 6 = 102 bpm.

questions.q: HR 90 bpm, stroke volume 80 ml. Cardiac output?
questions.why: Cardiac output = 90 × 80 = 7200 ml/min = 7.2 L/min.

questions.q: Case: A man's face droops on one side and he slurs words. Best action?
options: Call 112 immediately and note the time
questions.why: Face drooping and slurred speech are signs of a stroke. Call 112 immediately, as treatment works best if given quickly, and note the time the signs began. Do not give food or drink, and do not wait.

questions.q: Why are capillary walls one cell thick?
options: To allow quick exchange by diffusion
questions.why: Capillary walls are one cell thick, so oxygen, food and waste can diffuse across quickly over a very short distance.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
options: The vena cava returns blood to the right atrium
The aorta carries blood to the lungs
The pulmonary vein carries deoxygenated blood
questions.why: The vena cava brings deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium. Capillaries do not have valves, the aorta goes to the body, and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

questions.q: Case: Hypertension often goes undetected because…
questions.why: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is called the 'silent' condition, since it usually has no symptoms. Regular blood pressure checks are the way to find it.

questions.q: Why is O negative called a universal red-cell donor?
options: Its red cells lack A, B and Rh(D) antigens
questions.why: O negative red cells have no A, B or Rh(D) antigens on them, so there is nothing for the recipient's antibodies to attack. That is why they can be given to most people.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Breathing, lungs & respiration
courses.summary: The respiratory tract, how breathing works, gas exchange in alveoli, aerobic vs anaerobic respiration, and protecting lungs from smoke, vaping, pollution and asthma triggers.
outcomes: Learners can name the parts of the respiratory system in order
Learners can explain inhalation and exhalation using the diaphragm and ribs
Learners can distinguish breathing from cellular respiration and write the word equations
Learners can describe the effects of smoking, vaping and air pollution and basic asthma care

lessons.title: The airway: nose to alveoli

scenes.text: The AQI app shows 'Severe'. Aarav's throat feels scratchy.
His mother hands him a well-fitted N95 mask for the walk to school.
In class they learn how the nose, hairs and mucus try to filter what we breathe.

steps.title: The pathway
steps.body:
**Nose/nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx (voice box) → trachea (windpipe) → two bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli (air sacs).**

The trachea is held open by **C-shaped rings of cartilage**. The lungs sit in the chest cavity surrounded by **pleural membranes**; the **diaphragm** (dome-shaped muscle) lies beneath.

steps.title: Built-in cleaning
steps.body:
- Nose hairs and **mucus** trap dust and germs; air is warmed and moistened.
- **Cilia** (tiny hairs) on airway cells sweep mucus up to the throat to be swallowed or coughed out.
- Smoking paralyses and damages cilia — one reason smokers cough.

steps.title: Alveoli
steps.body: About **300–500 million** alveoli give a huge surface (roughly tennis-court-sized, often quoted ~50–100 m²). Each is **one cell thick**, moist, and wrapped in capillaries. Oxygen diffuses into blood; CO₂ diffuses out — from high to low concentration.

steps.title: Solved example: why breathe through the nose?
steps.body:
Compare nose vs mouth breathing in cold dusty air:
- Nose: filters (hairs/mucus), warms, moistens → less irritation.
- Mouth: none of that.
**Answer:** nose breathing protects the lower airways better.

Second: why does the trachea have cartilage rings? → To stop it collapsing when air pressure falls during inhalation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Lungs are muscles' — lungs have no skeletal muscle; the **diaphragm and intercostal muscles** move air.
- Mixing up larynx (voice box) and pharynx (throat).
- Saying oxygen is 'pumped' into blood — it **diffuses**.

activity.prompt: Order the air's path

quiz.why: Gas exchange happens in the alveoli, tiny air sacs in the lungs with thin walls and many capillaries.
Rings of cartilage keep the trachea (windpipe) open, so that it does not collapse when we breathe in.
Cilia are tiny hairs that sweep mucus, with trapped dust and germs, upward and out of the airways.
The larynx is the voice box. It holds the vocal cords, which vibrate to make sound.
Oxygen moves from the air in the alveoli into the blood by diffusion, from a place of higher concentration to lower.

lessons.title: How breathing works

scenes.text: Ms. Thomas builds a model: a bottle with balloons inside and a rubber sheet stretched over the bottom.
Pulling the sheet down inflates the balloons.
'The sheet is your diaphragm,' she says. 'Lower pressure inside — air rushes in.'

steps.title: Inhalation (active)
steps.body:
- **Diaphragm contracts** and flattens (moves down).
- **External intercostal muscles** contract → ribs move **up and out**.
- Chest volume **increases** → pressure inside lungs **falls** below atmospheric → **air flows in**.

steps.title: Exhalation (mostly passive at rest)
steps.body:
- Diaphragm **relaxes** (domes up); ribs move down and in.
- Volume **decreases** → pressure **rises** → **air flows out**.
- During exercise or coughing, internal intercostals and abdominal muscles push air out forcefully.

steps.title: Solved example: breathing rate & volume
steps.body:
Resting adult: ~12–20 breaths/min, ~500 ml per breath (tidal volume).
- 15 breaths × 0.5 L = **7.5 L of air per minute**.

Second: inhaled air ~21% O₂, exhaled ~16% O₂ — so we use only part of the oxygen; that is why rescue breaths still contain useful oxygen.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'air comes in, so the chest expands' — it is the **other way round**: the chest expands first, then air enters.
- Saying exhaled air has no oxygen.
- Forgetting that pressure difference drives airflow.

statements.s: When the diaphragm contracts, it moves downward.
Air pressure in the lungs rises during inhalation.
Exhaled air contains about 16% oxygen.
Quiet exhalation needs strong muscle effort.

quiz.why: During inhalation, the rib muscles lift the ribs up and out while the diaphragm moves down. This makes the chest bigger, so air rushes in.

quiz.q: Inhaling happens because lung pressure becomes…
quiz.why: We inhale when the pressure inside the lungs falls below the pressure of the air outside. Air always moves from high pressure to low pressure, so it flows into the lungs.

quiz.q: Tidal volume at rest is about…
quiz.why: At rest, a person breathes in and out about 500 ml (0.5 L) of air with each normal breath. This is called the tidal volume.
Minute ventilation = breaths per minute × volume per breath = 12 × 0.5 L = 6 L per minute.
The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs, is the main muscle of breathing. It flattens to draw air in.

lessons.title: Respiration in cells: aerobic and anaerobic

scenes.text: Saanvi sprints the 400 m at sports day.
Her thighs burn in the last 100 m and she gasps for breath afterwards.
'Your muscles briefly made energy without enough oxygen — that's anaerobic respiration,' her coach explains.

steps.title: Breathing ≠ respiration
steps.body: **Breathing** moves air in and out of lungs. **Respiration** is the chemical process in every cell (in mitochondria) that releases energy from glucose.

steps.title: Two types
steps.body:
**Aerobic** (with oxygen):
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + **lots of energy**
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (ATP)

**Anaerobic in muscles** (short of oxygen):
glucose → **lactic acid** + a little energy

**In yeast** (fermentation): glucose → ethanol + CO₂ + a little energy (used for bread and idli batter rising).

steps.title: Solved example: oxygen debt
steps.body:
After a sprint you keep breathing hard. Why?
- Step 1: Muscles made lactic acid when oxygen was short.
- Step 2: Extra oxygen is now needed to deal with the lactic acid and restore energy stores — sometimes called **oxygen debt** (EPOC).
- Step 3: So breathing and heart rate stay high for a while.

Second: why is aerobic better for long races? → It releases far more energy per glucose and no lactic-acid build-up.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Plants don't respire' — all living cells respire, plants too.
- Writing 'energy is made' — energy is **released**.
- Saying anaerobic respiration in humans makes alcohol — that's yeast; humans make **lactic acid**.

activity.prompt: Complete the aerobic respiration word equation

quiz.why: Cellular respiration takes place in the mitochondria of every cell, where energy is released from glucose. The lungs only bring in the oxygen.
When muscles work hard without enough oxygen, they respire anaerobically and make lactic acid. Ethanol is made in yeast, not in muscle.

quiz.q: Which releases more energy per glucose?
quiz.why: Aerobic respiration (with oxygen) releases much more energy from each glucose molecule than anaerobic respiration.

quiz.q: Idli batter rises because yeast/bacteria release…
quiz.why: The yeast or bacteria in idli batter respire (ferment) and release carbon dioxide gas. The gas bubbles make the batter rise and become fluffy.
Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.

lessons.title: Protecting your lungs: smoke, vapes, pollution & asthma

story.title: The vape at the bus stop

scenes.text: An older boy offers Yash a fruity-smelling vape: 'It's just water vapour, bro.'
Yash remembers: e-cigarettes are banned in India, and the aerosol usually contains nicotine and other chemicals.
'Nah, I'm good,' he says and walks to his friends.

steps.title: Tobacco & vaping facts
steps.body:
- Tobacco smoke contains thousands of chemicals, many harmful and some causing cancer; smoking damages cilia and alveoli (leading to **COPD**, lung cancer, heart disease).
- Smokeless tobacco (gutkha, khaini) causes mouth cancers — common in India.
- **E-cigarettes** are prohibited in India under the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act, 2019. Vapes are not 'just water': they usually contain **nicotine** (highly addictive, harms the developing brain) and other chemicals.
- Selling tobacco to under-18s is prohibited (COTPA).

steps.title: Air pollution
steps.body: **PM2.5** particles are small enough to go deep into lungs and blood. On high-AQI days: limit outdoor exercise, keep windows closed during peak hours, use a well-fitting N95 if you must go out, avoid burning waste.

steps.title: Asthma
steps.body: Asthma narrows and inflames airways → wheezing, cough, tight chest. Triggers: dust, smoke, pollen, cold air, infections, exercise for some. Treatment uses **inhalers** prescribed by a doctor — 'reliever' (fast) and 'preventer' (daily). Inhalers are safe and not addictive. **Emergency:** can't speak in full sentences, lips bluish, reliever not working → **112**.

steps.title: Solved example: help a friend with an asthma attack
steps.body:
- Step 1: Sit them upright; stay calm.
- Step 2: Help them use their **own reliever inhaler** as their plan says (often with a spacer).
- Step 3: If no improvement within minutes or they get worse, call **112**.
- Step 4: Don't lie them flat; don't crowd them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Hookah is safer than cigarettes' — it still delivers smoke, carbon monoxide and nicotine.
- 'Inhalers make asthma worse/addictive' — myth.
- This is general education, not medical advice.

a.text: At a party a friend passes you a vape: 'Everyone's trying it.'

choices.label: 'No thanks, I don't want nicotine.' Change the topic.
Take one puff so you don't look awkward
choices.feedback: Nicotine is highly addictive, especially for teens.

b.text: You feel dizzy and your chest feels odd. Your friend wants you to try again.

choices.label: Stop, sit down in fresh air, tell a trusted adult if you feel unwell
Have more to 'get used to it'
choices.feedback: Getting used to it is how dependence begins. Try again.

end1.text: Nobody really minded. Saying no was easier than you thought.

end2.text: You feel better. Next time you know how you'll answer.

quiz.why: E-cigarettes are prohibited in India under the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act, 2019, because they deliver nicotine and are harmful, especially to the young.

options: tiny particles reach deep lungs and blood
quiz.why: PM2.5 particles are extremely small (under 2.5 micrometres), so they travel deep into the lungs and can even pass into the blood, causing harm.

options: a fast-acting medicine that opens airways
quiz.why: A reliever inhaler holds a fast-acting medicine (a bronchodilator) that relaxes the airway muscles, so the airways open and breathing becomes easier during an asthma attack. It is not addictive.

options: mucus isn't cleared and cough develops
quiz.why: Smoking damages cilia, so the lungs cannot sweep out mucus and dirt. The mucus builds up, and the person develops a smoker's cough.

quiz.q: Smokeless tobacco mainly increases risk of…
quiz.why: Smokeless tobacco (such as gutka or khaini) mainly raises the risk of mouth (oral) cancer, as the chemicals stay in contact with the mouth lining.

questions.q: Air sacs in lungs are called…
questions.why: The tiny air sacs in the lungs, where gases are exchanged, are called alveoli.

questions.q: The muscle under the lungs:
questions.why: The diaphragm is the dome-shaped muscle below the lungs that helps in breathing.

questions.q: Respiration releases energy from…
questions.why: Respiration releases energy from glucose (food). Oxygen is needed to do this, but it is not the source of energy.

questions.q: During exhalation, the diaphragm…
questions.why: During exhalation, the diaphragm relaxes and bulges up like a dome. The chest space becomes smaller, so air is pushed out.

questions.q: Lactic acid is made during…
questions.why: Lactic acid is made in muscles during anaerobic respiration, such as in a hard sprint when oxygen runs short.

questions.q: Vapes usually contain…
questions.why: Vapes usually contain nicotine, which is addictive, and other chemicals. They are not just water vapour.

questions.q: Assertion: Alveoli are efficient for gas exchange. Reason: They are thin, moist, numerous and surrounded by capillaries.
questions.why: Both are true. Alveoli are thin, moist, numerous and surrounded by capillaries, which gives a large surface area and a short path for gases. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is the correct order?
questions.why: Air goes from the pharynx (throat) to the larynx (voice box) and then down the trachea. After that it enters the bronchi and alveoli.

questions.q: Yeast fermentation produces…
questions.why: When yeast ferments sugar without oxygen, it makes ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide. Lactic acid is made in muscles.

questions.q: Case: A classmate wheezes, can't finish sentences after PE, and has an inhaler. First step?
options: Help her sit up and use her reliever inhaler
questions.why: Help her sit upright and use her reliever inhaler, which opens the airways. Lying flat makes breathing harder. If she does not improve, call 112.

questions.q: 16 breaths/min with 0.5 L each =
questions.why: Minute ventilation = 16 × 0.5 L = 8 L per minute.

questions.q: Why does breathing stay fast after a sprint?
options: To repay oxygen debt and clear lactic acid
questions.why: After a sprint, muscles built up an oxygen debt and lactic acid. Fast breathing brings in extra oxygen to pay back the debt and clear the lactic acid.

questions.q: Inhalation occurs because…
options: chest volume increases and pressure drops
air enters first then chest expands
questions.why: We inhale when the chest volume increases, since this makes the pressure inside drop below the outside air pressure, so air flows in. This follows Boyle's law.

questions.q: If inhaled air is 21% O₂ and exhaled 16% O₂, what % of air volume is O₂ taken up?
questions.why: The air breathed in has 21% oxygen and breathed out 16%, so the body takes up the difference: 21 − 16 = 5% of the air volume.

questions.q: Case: On a 'severe' AQI day, which plan is best for a school football match?
options: Move indoors or postpone; masks for travel
questions.why: On a 'severe' AQI day, the air is very polluted. It is best to move the match indoors or postpone it, and to wear masks when travelling, so that students are exposed less.

questions.q: Which pair is mismatched?
questions.why: The diaphragm moves air in and out. Gas exchange happens in the alveoli, so 'Diaphragm – gas exchange' is the mismatched pair.

questions.q: Why is smoking linked to heart disease as well as lung disease?
options: Smoke chemicals and carbon monoxide damage blood vessels and reduce oxygen carrying
questions.why: Smoke chemicals and carbon monoxide damage blood vessels and reduce the blood's ability to carry oxygen. This raises the risk of heart disease as well as lung disease.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Kidneys, excretion & skin
courses.summary: How kidneys filter blood and make urine, the other excretory organs, staying hydrated, kidney health, and the skin as an organ: structure, sun safety, acne and everyday skin care.
outcomes: Learners can describe the urinary system and the nephron's role
Learners can explain how kidneys balance water
Learners can describe the skin's layers and functions
Learners can apply evidence-based skin care and know when to see a doctor

lessons.title: The urinary system and the nephron

scenes.text: On a 6-hour school trip Ritu avoids drinking water so she won't need the toilet.
By evening she has a headache and her urine is dark yellow.
Her teacher explains why kidneys need water to do their job — and why holding urine for too long is not a good idea.

steps.title: The system
steps.body: **Two kidneys** (bean-shaped, either side of the spine, lower back) → **ureters** → **urinary bladder** (stores urine) → **urethra** (to the outside). Kidneys filter around **180 litres** of blood plasma a day but make only about **1–2 litres** of urine — the rest is reabsorbed.

steps.title: The nephron (filter unit)
steps.body:
Each kidney has about **a million nephrons**.
1. **Filtration** – in the **glomerulus** (a knot of capillaries) inside **Bowman's capsule**, pressure pushes water, salts, glucose and urea out of blood; cells and big proteins stay in.
2. **Selective reabsorption** – along the tubule, all glucose and most water and useful salts go back to blood.
3. **What's left** – urea, excess salts and water = **urine** → collecting duct → ureter.

steps.title: Solved example: what % is reabsorbed?
steps.body:
Filtered: 180 L/day. Urine: 1.8 L/day.
- Reabsorbed = 180 − 1.8 = 178.2 L.
- % = 178.2 ÷ 180 × 100 = **99%**.

Second: glucose in urine is a warning sign — it can mean blood sugar is so high that the tubules can't reabsorb it all (as in uncontrolled diabetes).

steps.title: Other excretory organs
steps.body: Lungs (CO₂), skin (sweat: water, salts, a little urea), liver (makes urea from excess amino acids; breaks down old RBCs into bile pigments).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing **ureter** (kidney → bladder) with **urethra** (bladder → outside).
- 'Excretion = egestion' — egestion is removing undigested food (faeces); excretion removes **metabolic waste**.
- Thinking urea is made in the kidney — it's made in the **liver**.

activity.prompt: Put urine's path in order

quiz.q: The filtering knot of capillaries is the…
quiz.why: The glomerulus is the knot of capillaries in the nephron where blood is filtered.
Urea is made in the liver, from the breakdown of amino acids. The kidneys remove it from the blood.
Urine is stored in the bladder until we pass it out.

quiz.q: Normally glucose in the filtrate is…
quiz.why: In a healthy kidney, all the glucose filtered is reabsorbed back into the blood, so there is no glucose in normal urine.
Reabsorbed = 150 − 1.5 = 148.5 L. As a percentage: 148.5/150 × 100 = 99%.

lessons.title: Water balance and kidney health

scenes.text: During exams Sameer drinks only tea and cola, and feels foggy.
He switches to water bottles on his desk.
Concentration improves; his urine goes from dark to pale.

steps.title: Kidneys control water
steps.body: When you're short of water, the brain (hypothalamus, via the pituitary) releases **ADH (antidiuretic hormone)** → kidneys reabsorb more water → small amount of **dark, concentrated urine**. When you drink a lot, less ADH → lots of **pale, dilute urine**.

steps.title: Kidney-friendly habits
steps.body: Drink enough water; don't hold urine for very long; limit salt; avoid unnecessary painkillers (frequent use of some, like NSAIDs, can harm kidneys — use only as advised); control blood pressure and diabetes as an adult.

steps.title: Solved example: interpret the colour
steps.body: Morning urine dark yellow after a hot day of cricket with little water → mild **dehydration**; drink water. Pale straw colour → well hydrated. Red/brown urine, pain or burning → **see a doctor** (possible infection, stones or other causes).

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: Burning when passing urine, needing to go very often, fever with back pain, blood in urine, swelling of face/feet, very little urine. **UTIs (urinary tract infections)** are common, especially in girls and women, and are treatable — wiping front to back and not holding urine help prevent them.

bands.text: Darker yellow — drink some water soon.
Dark amber — likely dehydrated; drink water now and rest in shade.
Brown/red tints are not about water — see a doctor.

quiz.why: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) makes the kidneys reabsorb more water, so less water is lost in urine.

quiz.q: Dark urine after a hot day suggests…
