quiz.why: Dark urine after a hot day means it is concentrated, since the body lost water in sweat. It is a sign of dehydration, so drink more water.
Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are more common in girls and women because the urethra is shorter, so germs reach the bladder more easily.
Wiping front to back keeps germs from the anus away from the urethra, which helps prevent UTIs. Holding urine for long and drinking too little water raise the risk.

quiz.q: Frequent painkiller use without advice can harm the…
quiz.why: Using painkillers often without medical advice can damage the kidneys, as the kidneys have to filter these drugs.

lessons.title: Skin: the body's largest organ

scenes.text: After a summer camp Arjun has a 'sock tan' and peeling shoulders.
His sister, a pharmacist, says: 'Sunburn is skin damage, even in brown skin.'
Next camp he takes a cap, long sleeves and sunscreen.

steps.title: Layers
steps.body:
- **Epidermis** – outer layer; dead cells on top flake off; **melanin** (pigment) protects from UV.
- **Dermis** – blood vessels, nerves (touch, pain, heat), sweat glands, hair follicles, **sebaceous (oil) glands**.
- **Subcutaneous fat** – insulation and cushioning.

steps.title: Functions
steps.body: Barrier against germs and water loss · temperature control (sweat, blood vessels) · sensation · makes **vitamin D** with sunlight · excretes a little waste in sweat.

steps.title: Sun safety for all skin tones
steps.body: Shade between 11 am and 3 pm, caps and loose long sleeves, sunglasses, broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30+) on exposed skin for long outdoor time, reapplied every ~2 hours and after swimming/sweating. Darker skin has more melanin but can still burn and get skin damage.

steps.title: Solved example: fair-skin creams
steps.body:
Q: An ad says a cream will make you 'fair and successful'. What should you think?
- Skin colour comes mainly from genes (melanin) — every shade is normal and healthy.
- Some unregulated creams have contained harmful substances like **mercury** or **steroids** that damage skin.
- Self-worth doesn't depend on skin colour. **Conclusion:** skip it; protect skin from sun and eat well instead.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Dark skin doesn't need sun protection.'
- Popping boils yourself.
- Using steroid creams from the chemist without a prescription — they can cause thinning, acne and stretch marks.

activity.prompt: Match the skin part to its job

quiz.q: The outer layer of skin is the…
quiz.why: The epidermis is the outer layer of the skin. The dermis lies below it.

quiz.q: Skin makes which vitamin with sunlight?
quiz.why: Skin makes vitamin D when sunlight (UVB) falls on it.
Sebaceous glands in the skin make oil (sebum), which keeps skin and hair soft and waterproof.
Yes. Dark skin has more melanin and burns less easily, but it can still get sunburnt and damaged by the sun.
Steroid creams used without a prescription can thin the skin and cause other side effects. They should be used only as a doctor advises.

lessons.title: Everyday skin, hair & body care (incl. acne)

scenes.text: Two days before the annual function, Mira finds a big pimple on her chin.
She wants to squeeze it. Her mother says: 'Hands off — wash gently, it'll settle faster.'
On stage nobody notices; Mira learns most acne is normal in teens.

steps.title: Acne explained
steps.body: At puberty, hormones (androgens) make oil glands more active. Oil + dead skin cells block pores → **blackheads/whiteheads**; bacteria and inflammation → red pimples. Acne affects most teens to some degree. It is **not caused by dirt** and not a sign of being 'unclean'.

steps.title: What helps
steps.body:
- Wash face twice a day with a mild cleanser and lukewarm water; pat dry.
- **Don't squeeze** (spreads infection, causes scars and dark marks).
- Use oil-free 'non-comedogenic' products.
- Over-the-counter **benzoyl peroxide** or **salicylic acid** may help mild acne (follow pack directions; patch test).
- Change pillowcases; clean phone screens.
- See a doctor/dermatologist for painful deep lumps, scarring, or acne affecting your mood.

steps.title: Body hygiene basics
steps.body: Daily bath (especially in heat and after sport), clean underwear daily, dry well between toes and skin folds (prevents fungal infections), trim nails, wash hair 2–3 times a week or as needed, brush teeth twice daily with fluoride toothpaste and clean the tongue.

steps.title: Solved example: ringworm myth
steps.body:
Itchy round red patch in the groin after sports. Is it a 'worm'?
- No — **ringworm (tinea)** is a fungal infection.
- Keep the area dry, wear clean cotton underwear, don't share towels.
- See a doctor for the right antifungal; avoid steroid-combination creams sold over the counter, which can make it worse.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Scrubbing hard or washing face 6–8 times a day — irritates skin and worsens acne.
- Toothpaste on pimples (irritates skin).
- Believing chocolate alone causes acne — diet's role is modest and individual.

activity.prompt: My daily hygiene routine
items: Brush teeth morning and night (2 minutes)
Bath or shower, especially after sport
Clean underwear and socks every day
Dry between toes and skin folds
Wash face gently twice — no squeezing
Wash hands before eating and after the toilet

options: hormone-driven oil, blocked pores and inflammation
quiz.why: Acne is mainly caused by hormones (at puberty) that make skin oil, pores that get blocked, and inflammation. It is not caused by dirt or food like rice.

options: can cause scars and spread infection
quiz.why: Squeezing pimples can push germs deeper, spread infection and leave scars, so it is best not to.
Ringworm is caused by a fungus, not a worm. It makes a ring-shaped patch on the skin.

quiz.q: Washing your face 8 times a day…
quiz.why: Washing the face too often (8 times a day) can dry and irritate the skin. Washing twice a day with a mild cleanser is enough.

quiz.q: When should you see a dermatologist for acne?
options: Painful deep lumps, scarring or acne affecting mood
quiz.why: See a dermatologist (skin doctor) for painful deep lumps, scarring, or if acne is affecting your mood or confidence. Good treatments are available.

questions.q: Kidneys remove mainly…
questions.why: The kidneys remove urea (a waste made from protein breakdown) and extra water and salts from the blood.

questions.q: Urine leaves the body through the…
questions.why: Urine leaves the body through the urethra. The ureter carries it from the kidney to the bladder.

questions.q: Melanin is a…
questions.why: Melanin is a pigment that gives colour to the skin, hair and eyes.

questions.q: The functional unit of the kidney:
questions.why: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney, where blood is filtered and urine is made.

questions.q: Acne is NOT caused by…
questions.why: Acne is not caused by dirt alone. Oil glands, hormones and blocked pores all play a part.

questions.q: Ringworm treatment needs…
questions.why: Ringworm is a fungal infection, so it needs antifungal medicine. Antibiotics and deworming tablets do not work on it.

questions.q: Assertion: Urea is found in urine. Reason: Urea is produced in the kidneys.
questions.why: Urea is found in urine, which makes the assertion true. But urea is made in the liver, not the kidneys, so the reason is false.

questions.q: When dehydrated, ADH levels…
questions.why: When the body is dehydrated, ADH levels rise, so the kidneys reabsorb more water and make less, darker urine.

questions.q: Which is an excretory organ besides kidneys?
questions.why: The lungs are also excretory organs, since they remove carbon dioxide (a waste of respiration). The skin also removes some wastes in sweat.

questions.q: Case: Priya feels burning when passing urine and needs to go often. Best step?
questions.why: Burning when passing urine, and needing to go often, may be a urinary tract infection (UTI). She should see a doctor, as it is treatable. Holding urine or drinking less water makes it worse.

questions.q: Filtered 170 L; urine 1.7 L. Percentage reabsorbed:
questions.why: Reabsorbed = 170 − 1.7 = 168.3 L. As a percentage: 168.3/170 = 99%.

questions.q: Glucose in urine most likely indicates…
options: very high blood sugar (e.g. uncontrolled diabetes)
questions.why: Normally, all glucose is reabsorbed. Glucose in urine means blood sugar is so high that the kidneys cannot reabsorb it all, as in uncontrolled diabetes.

questions.q: Which sunscreen advice is right?
options: Once in the morning lasts all day
Reapply about every 2 hours and after sweating/swimming
questions.why: Sunscreen wears off, so it should be reapplied about every 2 hours, and after sweating or swimming. All skin colours need sun protection.

questions.q: Excretion differs from egestion because excretion removes…
options: metabolic wastes like urea and CO₂
questions.why: Excretion removes metabolic wastes made by cells, like urea and carbon dioxide. Egestion removes undigested food (faeces), which was never absorbed into the body.

questions.q: Case: A cream sold as 'whitening' gives quick results but skin becomes thin and red. Most likely cause?
questions.why: A 'whitening' cream that gives fast results but leaves skin thin and red probably contains a hidden steroid. Such creams harm the skin and should be avoided.

questions.q: Why does urine become pale and plentiful after drinking lots of water?
options: ADH falls so less water is reabsorbed
questions.why: After drinking a lot of water, ADH falls, so the kidneys reabsorb less water. This gives plenty of pale urine, which keeps the body's water balanced (negative feedback).

questions.q: In the nephron, which is NOT normally filtered into Bowman's capsule?
questions.why: Red blood cells are too big to pass through the filter in the glomerulus, so they normally stay in the blood. Water, glucose and urea are small and are filtered.

courses.title: Unit 7 · Brain, nerves, senses & hormones
courses.summary: How the nervous system and endocrine system control the body: neurons, brain regions, reflex arcs, eyes and ears (with screen and noise safety), and the major hormones including those of puberty.
outcomes: Learners can describe a neuron and how signals travel across synapses
Learners can name brain regions and their roles
Learners can draw and explain a reflex arc in words
Learners can explain how eyes and ears work and protect them
Learners can match endocrine glands to hormones and effects

lessons.title: Neurons and the brain

scenes.text: Kartik rides pillion on his cousin's scooter without a helmet 'just for 2 minutes'.
In biology class next day they learn the brain is soft, about 1.3–1.4 kg, floating in fluid inside the skull.
He decides: helmet every time. Brain injuries can be permanent.

steps.title: The neuron
steps.body: A **neuron** has **dendrites** (receive signals), a **cell body** (with nucleus), and a long **axon** (sends signals), often wrapped in a fatty **myelin sheath** that speeds signals. Signals travel as **electrical impulses** along the axon and cross the tiny gap (**synapse**) to the next cell using chemicals called **neurotransmitters**.

steps.title: Main brain parts
steps.body:
- **Cerebrum** (largest; left & right hemispheres): thinking, memory, language, voluntary movement, senses.
- **Cerebellum** (back, below): balance, coordination, posture.
- **Brainstem / medulla**: automatic functions — breathing, heart rate, swallowing, coughing.
- **Hypothalamus**: temperature, hunger, thirst, controls the pituitary.

**Central nervous system (CNS)** = brain + spinal cord; **peripheral** = nerves to the rest of the body.

steps.title: Solved example: which part?
steps.body:
(a) Riding a cycle without wobbling → **cerebellum**.
(b) Solving a maths problem → **cerebrum**.
(c) Breathing while asleep → **medulla**.
(d) Feeling thirsty on a hot day → **hypothalamus**.

steps.title: Protect your brain
steps.body: Helmets on two-wheelers and cycles (the law requires them for riders and pillion in India), seat belts, no diving into shallow water, report any head injury. After a head knock watch for: worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, drowsiness, unequal pupils → **see a doctor / 112**. Never 'play through' a concussion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'We use only 10% of our brain' — myth; brain scans show activity across all regions.
- Mixing cerebrum and cerebellum.
- Saying signals cross synapses electrically — mostly **chemical**.

activity.prompt: Match the brain part to its role
pairs: Carries signals between brain and body; reflexes

quiz.why: The cerebellum controls balance and coordinates movement.

quiz.q: The gap between neurons is the…
quiz.why: The tiny gap between two neurons, where the signal passes across, is the synapse.
Myelin is a fatty layer that insulates the axon, so nerve signals travel much faster.
The central nervous system (CNS) is made of the brain and the spinal cord.

quiz.q: 'We use only 10% of our brain' is…
quiz.why: 'We use only 10% of our brain' is a myth. Brain scans show we use nearly all of it, and different parts are active at different times.

lessons.title: Reflexes and the spinal cord

scenes.text: Sneha touches the hot tawa while making rotis.
Her hand jerks away before she even feels the pain.
'How did my hand know before I did?' — a reflex arc.

steps.title: Reflex actions
steps.body: A **reflex** is a fast, automatic, protective response that doesn't wait for the brain to decide. Examples: pulling away from heat, blinking, knee-jerk, sneezing, coughing, pupil shrinking in bright light.

steps.title: The reflex arc
steps.body: **Stimulus → receptor (skin) → sensory neuron → relay neuron in spinal cord → motor neuron → effector (muscle) → response.** The message also travels up to the brain, so you feel pain a split second **after** you've moved.

steps.title: Solved example: speed
steps.body:
Nerve signals in fast myelinated fibres can travel ~100 m/s. Distance hand → spinal cord → hand ≈ 2 m round trip.
- Time = distance ÷ speed = 2 ÷ 100 = **0.02 s (20 ms)** for conduction — very fast. (Real reflex times include synapse delays too.)

Second: why is a reflex faster than a voluntary action? → fewer synapses, no conscious decision-making in the cerebrum.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the brain initiates a reflex — the **spinal cord** does (for spinal reflexes).
- Missing the relay neuron in the arc.
- Confusing receptor (detects) with effector (responds).

activity.prompt: Order the reflex arc

quiz.q: A reflex is coordinated mainly by the…
quiz.why: A reflex is coordinated mainly by the spinal cord, which gives a fast response without waiting for the brain to decide.
Blinking at a flying insect is a reflex: it is automatic and fast. Writing, reading and choosing a song are voluntary.

quiz.q: The effector in pulling away is the…
quiz.why: In a reflex like pulling a hand away, the muscle does the action, so the muscle is the effector.

quiz.q: Signal from receptor to spinal cord travels in the…
quiz.why: A sensory neuron carries the signal from the receptor to the spinal cord. A motor neuron carries it from the cord to the muscle.
In a reflex, the hand moves first. The pain signal reaches the brain slightly later, so we feel the pain just after the reflex.

lessons.title: Eyes and ears — and protecting them

scenes.text: Rhea listens to music at full volume for hours on her commute.
One evening she hears ringing in her ears that lasts till bedtime.
Her doctor explains noise can permanently damage tiny hair cells in the inner ear.

steps.title: The eye
steps.body: Light passes through the **cornea** (clear front) → **pupil** (hole in coloured **iris**) → **lens** (focuses) → **retina** (light-sensitive cells: **rods** for dim light, **cones** for colour) → **optic nerve** → brain. Short-sightedness (**myopia**) — distant things blurry — corrected with **concave** lenses; long-sightedness (**hypermetropia**) — near things blurry — **convex** lenses.

steps.title: The ear
steps.body: Outer ear funnels sound → **eardrum** vibrates → three tiny bones (**malleus, incus, stapes**) amplify → **cochlea** (inner ear, hair cells turn vibrations into nerve signals) → auditory nerve. **Semicircular canals** help balance.

steps.title: Protect them
steps.body:
- **20-20-20 rule**: every 20 minutes of screen use, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Outdoor time in daylight is linked to lower myopia risk in children.
- **60/60 guide** for headphones: about 60% volume for no more than 60 minutes at a time. Over-the-ear noise-cancelling helps you keep volume lower.
- Never put cotton buds deep in the ear; earwax is normally self-cleaning.
- Get eyes tested if you squint at the board or get headaches.

steps.title: Solved example: decibels
steps.body: Sound levels: normal talk ~60 dB, heavy traffic ~85 dB, firecrackers can exceed 120–140 dB at close range. Every +10 dB is about **10× more sound intensity**. So 90 dB is 10× the intensity of 80 dB, and 100 dB is 100×. Long exposure above ~85 dB risks hearing damage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concave vs convex mix-up for myopia.
- 'Reading in dim light permanently damages eyes' — it causes strain, not permanent damage.
- Ignoring ringing ears (tinnitus) after loud events — a warning to turn it down.

bands.text: Comfortable for up to about an hour — take breaks.
Loud — limit time; someone near you can probably hear it.
Risky — long listening at this level can permanently damage hearing.

quiz.why: Myopia (short-sightedness) is corrected with a concave (diverging) lens, which moves the focus back onto the retina.
Cones in the retina detect colour and work in bright light. Rods work in dim light.

quiz.q: Sound is converted to nerve signals in the…
quiz.why: The cochlea, a snail-shaped part of the inner ear, turns sound vibrations into nerve signals for the brain.
Every 10 dB is a 10-fold change in intensity. 100 dB is 20 dB more than 80 dB, so it is 10 × 10 = 100 times more intense.
The 20-20-20 rule is for the eyes: every 20 minutes of screen time, look at something 20 feet (6 m) away for 20 seconds, to reduce eye strain.

lessons.title: Hormones and the endocrine glands

scenes.text: Before her speech Ayesha's heart pounds and palms sweat.
'That's adrenaline,' her teacher says, 'your body getting ready for action.'
Slow breathing helps her settle, and she delivers the speech well.

steps.title: What hormones are
steps.body: **Hormones** are chemical messengers made by **endocrine glands** and carried by blood to target organs. They act more slowly than nerves but often last longer.

steps.title: Gland → hormone → effect
steps.body:
- **Pituitary** ('master gland'): growth hormone; signals other glands (incl. FSH and LH for puberty).
- **Hypothalamus**: controls the pituitary.
- **Thyroid** (neck): **thyroxine** — metabolism; needs **iodine**.
- **Pancreas**: **insulin** & **glucagon** — blood sugar.
- **Adrenal glands** (on kidneys): **adrenaline** — 'fight or flight'; **cortisol** — stress response.
- **Ovaries**: **oestrogen, progesterone** — female puberty, menstrual cycle.
- **Testes**: **testosterone** — male puberty, sperm production.
- **Pineal**: **melatonin** — sleep–wake rhythm.

steps.title: Solved example: diagnosis thinking
steps.body:
(a) Swelling in neck + iodine-poor diet → **goitre** (thyroid).
(b) Very short stature from early childhood with low growth hormone → pituitary issue; doctors can treat with growth hormone.
(c) Fast heartbeat, dry mouth before an exam → **adrenaline**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the pancreas only digestive — it is also endocrine.
- 'Hormones travel along nerves' — they travel in **blood**.
- Taking 'hormone boosters' or steroids for muscles — can damage health; never without a doctor.

activity.prompt: Match the gland to its hormone

quiz.why: The pituitary gland is called the 'master gland' because it makes hormones that control other glands.
The thyroid gland needs iodine to make thyroxine.
Hormones travel in the blood to reach their target organs. Nerve signals travel along nerves.
Adrenaline is the 'fight-or-flight' hormone, made by the adrenal glands. It raises heart rate and prepares the body for action.
Melatonin is a hormone linked to the sleep–wake rhythm. It rises in the dark and makes us sleepy.

questions.q: A neuron's long fibre that sends signals is the…
questions.why: The axon is the long fibre of a neuron that carries signals away from the cell body. Dendrites receive signals.

questions.q: Insulin is made by the…
questions.why: Insulin is made by the pancreas, in special cells in its islets.

questions.q: Rods in the retina help with…
questions.why: Rods in the retina work in dim light, but do not see colour. Cones see colour.

questions.q: Which part controls breathing automatically?
questions.why: The medulla (in the brainstem) controls automatic actions like breathing and heartbeat.

questions.q: Knee-jerk is an example of a…
questions.why: A knee-jerk is a reflex. It is a quick, automatic response that does not need conscious thought.

questions.q: Long-sightedness is corrected by…
questions.why: Long-sightedness (hypermetropia) is corrected with a convex (converging) lens, which helps focus light onto the retina.

questions.q: Assertion: Reflexes are faster than voluntary actions. Reason: They are processed in the spinal cord without conscious thought.
questions.why: Both are true. A reflex is processed in the spinal cord, without conscious thought, so the path is short and fast. That is why reflexes are faster than voluntary actions.

questions.q: Goitre is linked to which gland?
questions.why: Goitre is a swelling of the thyroid gland, often caused by a lack of iodine.

questions.q: Hormones differ from nerve impulses because they…
options: travel in blood and usually act more slowly
questions.why: Hormones travel in the blood and usually act more slowly, but for longer. Nerve impulses are fast and short-lived.

questions.q: Case: After a fall from a cycle without a helmet, Ravi vomits twice and is drowsy. What should happen?
questions.why: Vomiting and drowsiness after a fall with a head hit may mean a head injury. He needs urgent medical help, so check with a doctor or call 112. Sleeping it off is not safe.

questions.q: A signal travels 1.5 m at 75 m/s. Time taken:
questions.why: Time = distance ÷ speed = 1.5 m ÷ 75 m/s = 0.02 s.

questions.q: A sound at 95 dB compared with 75 dB has about how many times the intensity?
questions.why: A 20 dB difference means 10² = 100 times the intensity. So 95 dB is about 100 times as intense as 75 dB.

questions.q: Which is the correct reflex sequence?
questions.why: A reflex arc goes receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron (in the spinal cord) → motor neuron → effector (muscle).

questions.q: FSH and LH are released by the…
questions.why: FSH and LH are released by the pituitary gland, and they act on the ovaries or testes during puberty and in reproduction.

questions.q: Case: A 9-year-old spends 6 hours daily on screens and rarely goes outdoors; he now squints at the board. Best advice?
options: Eye test; more outdoor time; 20-20-20 breaks
questions.why: Long screen time and little outdoor time are linked to short-sightedness (myopia), so squinting at the board needs an eye test. More time outdoors and 20-20-20 breaks help.

questions.q: Why is the pancreas called a mixed gland?
options: It has digestive (exocrine) and hormonal (endocrine) functions
questions.why: The pancreas is a mixed gland: it releases digestive enzymes through a duct (exocrine) and makes hormones like insulin and glucagon into the blood (endocrine).

questions.q: Why is 'just one puff' or 'just one pill' of anabolic steroids risky for teens?
options: They disturb natural hormones and can cause lasting harm
questions.why: Anabolic steroids disturb the body's natural hormones, which can cause lasting harm to growth, the heart, the liver and mood. Even 'just once' is not safe for teens.

courses.title: Unit 8 · Germs, immunity, vaccines & hygiene
courses.summary: How germs spread, how the immune system and vaccines protect us, practical hygiene (hands, food, water, oral, toilet), common Indian infections like dengue, malaria, TB and typhoid, and using antibiotics wisely.
outcomes: Learners can name types of pathogens and how they spread
Learners can explain innate and adaptive immunity and how vaccines work
Learners can apply handwashing, food and water safety and oral hygiene
Learners can recognise warning signs of common infections and explain antibiotic resistance

lessons.title: Germs and how they spread

scenes.text: Twelve students in a hostel get stomach upsets after the same street-side pani puri.
Health officials suspect contaminated water.
The warden sets up handwashing stations and boiled drinking water.

steps.title: Types of pathogens
steps.body:
- **Bacteria** – single cells; cause typhoid, cholera, TB, strep throat. Antibiotics can treat many.
- **Viruses** – much smaller; need living cells to multiply; cause colds, flu, COVID-19, measles, dengue, HIV. **Antibiotics do not work on viruses.**
- **Fungi** – ringworm, thrush.
- **Protozoa** – malaria (Plasmodium), amoebic dysentery.
- **Worms** – roundworm, hookworm.

steps.title: Routes of spread
steps.body:
- **Air/droplets**: coughs, sneezes (flu, TB, COVID-19).
- **Food & water** (faecal–oral): cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A & E, diarrhoea.
- **Vectors**: mosquitoes (malaria — *Anopheles*; dengue/chikungunya — *Aedes*).
- **Direct contact**: skin infections, conjunctivitis.
- **Blood & body fluids**: hepatitis B & C, HIV.

steps.title: Solved example: break the chain
steps.body:
Disease: dengue.
- Step 1: Vector? *Aedes* mosquito, bites mostly in **daytime**, breeds in **clean standing water** (coolers, pots, tyres).
- Step 2: Break: empty/clean water containers weekly, cover tanks, full sleeves, repellents, nets.

Second: typhoid → spread by contaminated food/water → boiled or filtered water, handwashing, vaccine available.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Asking for antibiotics for a cold or flu.
- 'Clear water is safe water' — clear water can still carry germs.
- Thinking dengue mosquitoes breed in dirty drains — *Aedes* prefers **clean** stagnant water.

activity.prompt: Sort each disease by how it mainly spreads

quiz.why: Antibiotics work against many kinds of bacteria. They do not work against viruses, such as those causing colds.
Dengue is spread by the Aedes mosquito. Anopheles spreads malaria.
Malaria is caused by a protozoan parasite called Plasmodium, which the Anopheles mosquito carries.
Cholera spreads mainly through water (and food) contaminated with faeces that carry the bacteria.
Aedes mosquitoes breed in clean standing water, such as in coolers, pots, tyres and buckets. Removing standing water cuts breeding.

lessons.title: Your immune system and vaccines

scenes.text: Arnav's mother finds his old vaccination card while cleaning.
BCG, polio drops, MMR, DPT boosters — dozens of entries.
'Each one taught your body to fight a disease before it ever met it,' she says.

steps.title: Lines of defence
steps.body:
1. **Barriers**: skin, mucus, cilia, stomach acid, tears (enzymes).
2. **Innate response**: white blood cells (phagocytes) engulf germs; inflammation; fever.
3. **Adaptive response**: **lymphocytes** — B cells make **antibodies** that fit specific **antigens**; T cells kill infected cells. **Memory cells** remember the germ, so a second infection is fought off faster.

steps.title: How vaccines work
steps.body: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version or part of a germ (weakened, inactivated, a protein, or instructions to make one). The body makes antibodies and **memory cells** without getting the disease. When many are vaccinated, spread falls and even those who can't be vaccinated are protected (**herd immunity**). India's Universal Immunization Programme gives many vaccines free; the HPV vaccine protects against the virus that causes most cervical cancers.

steps.title: Solved example: primary vs secondary response
steps.body:
First exposure: antibodies rise slowly (~1–2 weeks), low peak → person may fall ill.
Second exposure: memory cells → antibodies rise within days, much higher peak → usually no illness.
**Conclusion:** vaccines create that 'first exposure' safely.

steps.title: Myths
steps.body:
- 'Vaccines cause autism' — large studies have found no link.
- 'Natural infection is better' — it can cause severe disease or death.
- Mild fever or a sore arm after a vaccine is common and short-lived. Report rare serious reactions to a doctor.

statements.s: Antibodies are made by B lymphocytes.
Vaccines work by giving you the full disease.
Memory cells make a second response faster.
Fever is always harmful and must be stopped immediately.
statements.why: Fever is part of defence; treat if uncomfortable or very high, and see a doctor when needed.

statements.s: Herd immunity protects people who can't be vaccinated.

quiz.why: Antibodies are proteins that bind to specific antigens (markers on germs) and help destroy them.
Phagocytes are white blood cells that engulf and digest germs. This is called phagocytosis.
A vaccine trains the immune system and makes memory cells, so the body can respond fast if the real germ arrives later.
The HPV vaccine helps prevent cervical cancer (and other cancers caused by the human papillomavirus).
Skin is a physical barrier that keeps germs out. Antibodies, T cells and vaccines are parts of the immune response, not barriers.

lessons.title: Hygiene that actually works

scenes.text: Class 6 learns to hum 'Happy Birthday' twice while washing hands.
They test with glitter-gel 'germs' — quick rinsers still have glitter between fingers.
Proper washing removes nearly all of it.

steps.title: Handwashing (with soap, ≥20 seconds)
steps.body: Wet → soap → rub palms → backs of hands → between fingers → backs of fingers → thumbs → fingertips into palms → wrists → rinse → dry on clean towel. **When:** before eating or cooking, after toilet, after touching animals or garbage, after coughing/sneezing, after coming home. Sanitiser (≥60% alcohol) helps when soap isn't available but doesn't work well on visibly dirty hands.

steps.title: Food & water safety
steps.body: Boil, filter or use treated water. Wash fruit and vegetables. Keep raw meat separate. Cook thoroughly; eat hot food hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Avoid cut fruit and uncovered food from street stalls in monsoon.

steps.title: Oral & toilet hygiene
steps.body: Brush twice a day for 2 minutes with fluoride toothpaste, clean the tongue, limit sugary snacks between meals, dentist visit about once a year. Use toilets (not open defecation), flush, wash hands. For diarrhoea: **ORS** (oral rehydration solution) and zinc for children as advised; see a doctor if blood in stool, high fever, or signs of dehydration.

steps.title: Solved example: make ORS correctly
steps.body: Use a **WHO-ORS packet** dissolved in the exact volume on the pack (often 1 litre) of clean water. If no packet: health guidance has used about **6 level teaspoons of sugar + ½ level teaspoon of salt in 1 litre** of clean water. Too much salt can be harmful — measure carefully, and prefer packets.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rinsing hands with water only for 3 seconds.
- Using a shared towel when someone has conjunctivitis.
- Thinking antibacterial soap is needed — ordinary soap works.

activity.prompt: Order the handwashing steps
items: Scrub backs of hands and between fingers

quiz.q: Hands should be washed for at least…
quiz.why: Wash hands with soap for at least 20 seconds to remove germs.
For diarrhoea, give ORS (oral rehydration solution) to replace the fluid and salts lost. Cola and stopping fluids do not help.
Leftovers should be put in a refrigerator within 2 hours, as germs multiply fast at room temperature.
Fluoride toothpaste strengthens enamel and helps prevent tooth decay.

quiz.q: Sanitiser works poorly when hands are…
quiz.why: Hand sanitiser works poorly on hands that are visibly dirty or greasy. In that case, wash with soap and water.

lessons.title: Common infections in India & using antibiotics wisely

scenes.text: Neel's cough improves after 2 days of antibiotics, so he stops and keeps the rest for 'next time'.
A week later the infection is back, harder to treat.
His doctor explains resistance and asks him to always finish courses as prescribed.

steps.title: Know the warning signs
steps.body:
- **Dengue**: high fever, severe body/eye pain, rash. Danger signs: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums, extreme tiredness → hospital. Use **paracetamol** for fever as advised; avoid aspirin/ibuprofen unless a doctor says so.
- **Malaria**: fever with chills, often in cycles — needs a blood test and full treatment.
- **Typhoid**: prolonged rising fever, stomach pain.
- **TB**: cough over 2 weeks, weight loss, night sweats, fever — **free testing and treatment** under India's national TB programme; it's curable if the full course (usually 6 months+) is completed.

steps.title: Antibiotic resistance
steps.body: Bacteria that survive a short or wrong course can multiply and become **resistant**. WHO calls antimicrobial resistance one of the top global health threats. Rules: take antibiotics **only when prescribed**, the **dose and duration as directed**, never share or save them, and don't demand them for viral illness.

steps.title: Solved example: selection of resistance
steps.body:
Start: 1,000,000 bacteria, 10 are naturally resistant.
- Full course kills nearly all sensitive bacteria; immune system clears the rest.
- Short course kills most sensitive ones but leaves survivors; resistant ones face less competition and multiply.
- **Result:** next infection is dominated by resistant bacteria.

steps.title: Common mistakes & when to see a doctor
steps.body:
- Self-medicating with antibiotics from a chemist.
- Waiting days with high fever in monsoon — get tested early.
- General education, not medical advice: see a doctor for fever over 3 days, breathing difficulty, confusion, dehydration, or any danger sign. Emergency **112**.

a.text: It's monsoon. You've had a 102 °F fever for 2 days with body ache and pain behind the eyes.

choices.label: See a doctor and get a blood test
choices.feedback: Right — dengue and malaria need testing.

choices.label: Take leftover antibiotics from last year
choices.feedback: Antibiotics don't treat dengue and may be the wrong drug.

x.text: No improvement, and now your gums are bleeding a little.

choices.label: Go to hospital immediately

b.text: The test shows dengue. The doctor advises rest, fluids and paracetamol. A friend suggests ibuprofen for the pain.

choices.label: Stick to the doctor's advice and report danger signs
choices.feedback: Ibuprofen/aspirin can raise bleeding risk in dengue.

choices.label: Take ibuprofen too
choices.feedback: Not without the doctor — bleeding risk.

b2.text: You call the doctor first. She says no ibuprofen.

choices.label: Follow advice

end1.text: With rest and monitoring you recover in about a week.

quiz.q: TB in India can be tested and treated…
quiz.why: In India, TB testing and treatment are free under the National TB Elimination Programme.

quiz.q: For dengue fever, the usual safe fever medicine is…
quiz.why: For dengue fever, paracetamol is the usual safe fever medicine when a doctor advises. Aspirin and ibuprofen can raise the risk of bleeding.
Antibiotic resistance grows when people stop courses early, take antibiotics when not needed, or share them. The bacteria that survive become resistant.

quiz.q: A cough over 2 weeks with weight loss could be…
quiz.why: A cough that lasts more than 2 weeks with weight loss could be TB, so the person should be tested. TB is curable with treatment.
Malaria is diagnosed with a blood test, such as a blood smear or a rapid test, which finds the parasite.

questions.q: Viruses are treated by antibiotics.
questions.why: False. Antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses. Viral infections like flu are not treated with antibiotics.

questions.q: Malaria spreads through…
questions.why: Malaria spreads through the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito. Aedes spreads dengue.

questions.q: Handwashing time:
questions.why: Hands should be washed with soap for about 20 seconds.

questions.q: Antibodies are made by…
questions.why: Antibodies are made by B lymphocytes (B cells), a kind of white blood cell.

questions.q: ORS is used for…
questions.why: ORS is used to treat dehydration caused by diarrhoea, as it replaces water and salts.

questions.q: Which is a vector-borne disease?
questions.why: Dengue is a vector-borne disease, as it is carried by a mosquito. Typhoid, TB and hepatitis A spread in other ways (food and water, air).

questions.q: Assertion: Vaccines provide immunity. Reason: They produce memory cells without causing disease.
questions.why: Both are true. A vaccine gives immunity because it makes memory cells without causing the disease. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Herd immunity means…
options: enough people immune that spread is reduced
questions.why: Herd immunity means enough people in a community are immune that the germ spreads less, and this also protects people who cannot be vaccinated.

questions.q: Aedes mosquitoes mainly bite…
questions.why: Aedes mosquitoes mainly bite during the day, so protection like repellents and covered clothing is needed in the daytime.

questions.q: Case: A boy has diarrhoea for a day but is drinking and alert. First step?
options: ORS and fluids; see doctor if danger signs
questions.why: If he is drinking and alert, give ORS and fluids and watch for danger signs, such as blood in stool, not drinking or being very sleepy. Then see a doctor. Antibiotics are not usually needed.

questions.q: Why does a second infection by the same germ often go unnoticed?
options: Memory cells produce a faster, larger antibody response
questions.why: After a first infection, memory cells remember the germ. On the second infection, they make a faster and bigger antibody response, so we often do not even notice the infection.

questions.q: Which helps antibiotic resistance spread?
questions.why: Sharing leftover antibiotics means incomplete or wrong use, which helps resistant bacteria survive and spread. Finishing courses as prescribed, vaccination and handwashing help.

questions.q: Case: A hostel has 30 cases of typhoid. Most likely source and action?
options: Contaminated food/water; check water supply and kitchen hygiene
questions.why: Typhoid spreads by contaminated food and water (the faecal–oral route). So check the water supply and kitchen hygiene, and use clean water and handwashing.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: TB is caused by a bacterium. Malaria is caused by a protozoan, flu by a virus and ringworm by a fungus.

questions.q: Why avoid ibuprofen/aspirin in suspected dengue unless a doctor advises?
questions.why: In dengue, platelets fall and bleeding is a risk. Aspirin and ibuprofen can increase bleeding, so only use a medicine such as paracetamol that a doctor advises.

questions.q: A population of 1,000,000 bacteria includes 10 resistant ones. After repeated short courses, what happens to the proportion resistant?
questions.why: Repeated short courses kill the non-resistant bacteria, but the resistant ones survive and multiply, so the proportion that is resistant increases. This is natural selection.

questions.q: Which is the BEST evidence-based response to a vaccine-autism rumour?
options: Large studies have found no link; vaccines prevent serious disease
questions.why: Large studies in many countries have found no link between vaccines and autism, and vaccines prevent serious disease. So that is the evidence-based response.

courses.title: Unit 9 · Sleep & the body clock
courses.summary: Why sleep matters for growth, memory and mood, how much each age needs, sleep stages and the circadian rhythm, screens and caffeine, a practical sleep plan for exam season, and when sleep problems need a doctor.
outcomes: Learners can state recommended sleep hours by age
Learners can describe sleep stages and the circadian rhythm
Learners can explain how light, screens and caffeine affect sleep
Learners can build a personal sleep plan and spot problems needing medical help

lessons.title: Why we sleep and how much we need

scenes.text: Before her chemistry exam, Ishita studies till 4 am.
In the exam she blanks on equations she knew well.
Her teacher explains: memories are consolidated during sleep. Sleep is part of studying.

steps.title: How much? (approx., from paediatric and sleep-medicine guidance)
steps.body:
- Infants (4–12 months): 12–16 h incl. naps
- Toddlers (1–2 y): 11–14 h
- Pre-school (3–5 y): 10–13 h
- Children (6–12 y): **9–12 h**
- Teens (13–18 y): **8–10 h**
- Adults: **7–9 h** (at least 7)

steps.title: What sleep does
steps.body: Consolidates memory and learning · releases growth hormone (mostly in deep sleep) · repairs tissues · supports immunity · regulates appetite hormones · steadies mood and attention · clears waste from the brain.

steps.title: Solved example: sleep debt
steps.body:
Ravi needs 9 h but sleeps 6.5 h on 5 school nights.
- Daily shortfall = 9 − 6.5 = 2.5 h.
- Weekly = 2.5 × 5 = **12.5 h of sleep debt**.
Long weekend lie-ins only partly fix it and shift the body clock — steady bedtimes work better.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'I'll sleep after exams' — memory and focus need sleep now.
- 'Teens are lazy for sleeping late' — puberty genuinely shifts the body clock later.
- Drowsy driving/riding is dangerous — never ride when very sleepy.

activity.label: Hours you slept last night (for a 13–18-year-old)

bands.text: Seriously short — memory, mood and safety suffer.
A bit short for a teen — aim for 8–10 hours.
Right in the healthy range for teens.
Long — fine occasionally; if you always need this much and still feel tired, check with a doctor.

quiz.why: Teenagers need about 8–10 hours of sleep each night for growth, learning and mood.

quiz.q: Growth hormone is released mostly during…
quiz.why: Growth hormone is released mostly during deep sleep, which is one reason sleep matters for growing children.
Adults need at least 7 hours of sleep a night.

quiz.q: Need 9, sleep 7 for 5 days: sleep debt?
quiz.why: Sleep debt = (9 − 7) × 5 days = 2 × 5 = 10 hours.
At puberty, the body clock shifts later, so teenagers feel sleepy later at night and want to wake later. This is natural.

lessons.title: Sleep stages and the circadian rhythm

scenes.text: Aditya keeps a notebook by his bed to write dreams.
He remembers dreams best when his alarm wakes him in the early morning.
That's because early-morning sleep is rich in REM — the dreaming stage.

steps.title: Sleep cycles
steps.body: A night has **4–6 cycles of ~90 minutes**. Each has **non-REM** stages (light sleep → **deep slow-wave sleep**) and **REM** sleep (rapid eye movement: vivid dreams, brain active, most muscles relaxed). Deep sleep dominates early in the night; REM increases towards morning.

steps.title: The body clock
steps.body: The **circadian rhythm** (~24 h) is set by a 'master clock' in the hypothalamus (the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**). **Morning light** resets it; **darkness** triggers **melatonin** from the pineal gland, making you sleepy. Blue-rich light from screens at night can delay melatonin.

steps.title: Solved example: plan wake-up by cycles
steps.body:
Want to wake at 6:00 am, need ~5 cycles of 90 min = 7.5 h, plus ~15 min to fall asleep.
- 6:00 − 7 h 30 min = 10:30 pm; minus 15 min → **lights out about 10:15 pm**.

Second: for 6 cycles (9 h) → 6:00 − 9 h 15 min = **8:45 pm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Dreams only happen in REM' — mostly, but some dreaming occurs in non-REM too.
- Thinking melatonin is a harmless sweet — melatonin supplements are medicines; ask a doctor before use, especially for children.

activity.prompt: You must wake at 6:30 am and want 5 sleep cycles of 90 minutes plus 15 minutes to fall asleep. How many hours before 6:30 should you be in bed? (decimal hours)

quiz.why: One sleep cycle lasts about 90 minutes, and a night has several cycles.
Most vivid dreams happen in REM (rapid eye movement) sleep.
Morning sunlight helps reset the body clock, which makes it easier to feel sleepy at night.
Melatonin, the sleep hormone, is released mainly when it is dark.
Deep sleep is most common early in the night, in the first sleep cycles. REM sleep is longer towards morning.

lessons.title: Screens, caffeine and a sleep plan that works

scenes.text: At 11:45 pm Kiara is still scrolling. 'Just one more.'
Suddenly it's 1:30 am.
She tries a new rule: phone charges outside the bedroom from 10 pm. In two weeks she falls asleep faster and wakes easier.

steps.title: Screen rules
steps.body: Stop screens **30–60 minutes before bed**; keep phones out of the bedroom or on silent face-down across the room; turn off notifications at night; use night mode if you must. Scrolling feeds are designed to keep you going — set a stopping point before you start.

steps.title: Caffeine
steps.body: Found in tea, coffee, cola, energy drinks and chocolate. Its effect lasts **several hours** (half-life often ~5 h in adults). Avoid caffeine in the afternoon and evening. Energy drinks are not advised for children or teens.

steps.title: Solved example: caffeine half-life
steps.body:
A cola at 6 pm with 40 mg caffeine; half-life 5 h.
- 11 pm: 20 mg left
- 4 am: 10 mg left
So at bedtime half the caffeine is still in your body.

steps.title: The sleep plan
steps.body:
- Same bedtime and wake time daily (within ~1 h on weekends).
- Bright light and activity in the morning; exercise daily (not intensely right before bed).
- Wind-down routine: shower, reading, light stretches, breathing.
- Cool, dark, quiet room.
- Can't sleep after ~20 minutes? Get up, do something calm in dim light, return when sleepy.
- Short naps (≤20–30 min) before 4 pm only.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Weekend catch-up' with 4-hour lie-ins → Monday jet lag.
- Studying in bed → bed becomes linked with being alert.

activity.prompt: My sleep plan for this week
items: Phone out of the bedroom 30–60 min before sleep
Bed only for sleep, not studying

quiz.q: Stop screens before bed by about…
quiz.why: Stop using screens 30–60 minutes before bed, as bright screen light and exciting content keep the brain awake.

quiz.q: 40 mg caffeine, 5 h half-life: after 10 h?
quiz.why: With a half-life of 5 h, 10 h is two half-lives: 40 → 20 → 10 mg. So 10 mg remains.

quiz.q: Can't sleep after 20 min — best move?
options: Get up and do something calm, then return
quiz.why: If you cannot sleep after about 20 minutes, get up and do something calm (like reading in dim light), then return to bed when sleepy. Scrolling, coffee or hard exercise make it worse.
A good nap is short, 20–30 minutes at most, and early in the afternoon, so it does not spoil night sleep.
Energy drinks have a lot of caffeine and sugar, so they are not advised for teenagers. They can disturb sleep and heart rhythm.

lessons.title: Sleep problems and when to see a doctor

scenes.text: Twelve-year-old Om snores loudly, sometimes pauses breathing, and falls asleep in class.
His parents mention it to a doctor.
Enlarged tonsils/adenoids are found; after treatment he sleeps better and his marks improve.

steps.title: Common problems
steps.body:
- **Insomnia** – trouble falling or staying asleep for weeks; often linked to stress, screens, irregular schedule, anxiety or depression.
- **Obstructive sleep apnoea** – loud snoring with breathing pauses; daytime sleepiness. In children often due to large tonsils/adenoids.
- **Nightmares and night terrors** – common in children; usually outgrown.
- **Sleepwalking** – keep the area safe; usually harmless in children.
- **Restless legs**, **narcolepsy** (sudden sleep attacks) — need a doctor.

steps.title: Solved example: spot the issue
steps.body:
(a) Teen sleeps 5 h on school nights, 12 h on weekends, tired in class → **insufficient sleep + irregular schedule**: fix routine first.
(b) Adult snores loudly, gasps at night, dozes while driving → possible **sleep apnoea**: see a doctor promptly.
(c) Child screams in sleep, doesn't remember in morning → likely **night terror**: stay calm, keep safe; mention to a doctor if frequent.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: Snoring with breathing pauses · falling asleep in class or while riding · insomnia over 3 weeks despite good habits · low mood or worry stopping sleep · sleepwalking with injuries. If low mood includes thoughts of not wanting to live, talk to someone today: **14416 (Tele-MANAS)** or **112**.

steps.title: Calm the busy mind
steps.body: Write tomorrow's worries and a to-do list on paper before bed ('parking the thoughts'), then try slow breathing — e.g. 4 seconds in, 6 seconds out.

activity.label: Bedtime breathing: in for 4, out for 6

quiz.q: Snoring with breathing pauses may indicate…
quiz.why: Loud snoring with pauses in breathing may be sleep apnoea, and the person should see a doctor.

quiz.q: Insomnia lasting weeks despite good habits →
quiz.why: If insomnia lasts for weeks despite good habits, see a doctor. Do not take sleeping pills from a friend.

options: common in children and usually outgrown
quiz.why: Night terrors are common in children and are usually outgrown. They look scary but are not dangerous, and the child does not remember them.

quiz.q: A worry list before bed helps by…
quiz.why: Writing a worry list before bed 'parks' your thoughts on paper, so your mind can relax and you can sleep.
Tele-MANAS, India's free tele-mental-health helpline, is 14416.

questions.q: Teens need about…
questions.why: Teenagers need about 8–10 hours of sleep.

questions.q: Melatonin comes from the…
questions.why: Melatonin is made by the pineal gland in the brain.

questions.q: Caffeine is found in…
questions.why: Caffeine is found in cola, tea, coffee and energy drinks. Water, rice and milk have none.

questions.q: REM sleep is linked to…
questions.why: REM sleep is the stage linked to vivid dreaming. The brain is very active then, though the body is mostly still.

questions.q: A sleep cycle is about…
questions.why: A full sleep cycle lasts about 90 minutes.

questions.q: Best place for a phone at night:
questions.why: The best place for a phone at night is outside the bedroom, so that light, buzzes and the temptation to scroll do not disturb sleep.

questions.q: Assertion: Teenagers often feel sleepy later at night. Reason: Puberty shifts the circadian rhythm later.
questions.why: Both are true. Puberty shifts the circadian (body clock) rhythm later, so teens naturally feel sleepy later at night. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which helps reset the body clock?
questions.why: Morning daylight helps reset the body clock. Late-night screens, evening coffee and irregular naps push it the wrong way.

questions.q: Deep sleep is mainly in…
options: the first half of the night
questions.why: Deep sleep mainly happens in the first half of the night, during the early sleep cycles.

questions.q: Case: Arun dozes in class, snores loudly and stops breathing for seconds at night. Best advice?
options: See a doctor for possible sleep apnoea
questions.why: Dozing in class, loud snoring and pauses in breathing at night may mean sleep apnoea. He should see a doctor, as it is treatable. Energy drinks do not fix it.

questions.q: Sleep debt: need 8.5 h, get 6 h on 6 days. Total?
questions.why: Sleep debt = (8.5 − 6) × 6 = 2.5 × 6 = 15 hours.

questions.q: 100 mg caffeine at 4 pm, half-life 5 h. Amount at 9 pm?
questions.why: 4 pm to 9 pm is 5 hours, which is one half-life, so 100 mg falls to 50 mg.

questions.q: Wake at 7:00, want 5 × 90-min cycles + 15 min to fall asleep. Bedtime?
questions.why: 5 cycles × 90 min = 450 min = 7 h 30 min, plus 15 min to fall asleep = 7 h 45 min. Counting back from 7:00 am gives a bedtime of 11:15 pm.

questions.q: Why is 'catching up' with long weekend lie-ins not ideal?
options: It shifts the body clock and causes Monday tiredness
questions.why: Sleeping very late on weekends shifts the body clock (social jet lag), so you feel tired on Monday. It is better to keep wake-up times fairly regular.

questions.q: Case: A student can't sleep for 4 weeks, feels hopeless and says 'what's the point'. Most important step?
options: Talk to a trusted adult/doctor today; Tele-MANAS 14416
questions.why: Not sleeping for four weeks with feelings of hopelessness can be a sign of depression. Talk to a trusted adult or doctor today, or call Tele-MANAS (14416). Help is available, and it is okay to ask for it.

questions.q: Which is the best explanation for why screens at night delay sleep?
options: Blue-rich light suppresses melatonin and content keeps the brain alert
questions.why: Blue-rich light from screens suppresses melatonin, the sleep hormone. Exciting content also keeps the brain alert. Both delay falling asleep.

questions.q: Which statement about melatonin supplements is correct?
options: Medicines — ask a doctor before use
questions.why: Melatonin supplements are medicines, not vitamins or sweets. Ask a doctor before use, and they do not cure insomnia permanently.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Human body
courses.summary: One-stop revision: key facts sheet for every system, all the numbers and calculations in one place, answer-writing tips, and a 20-question mock paper.
outcomes: Learners can recall key facts for all body systems
Learners can solve standard calculations (pulse, cardiac output, calories, reabsorption, sleep debt)
Learners can attempt assertion–reason and case-based questions confidently

lessons.title: Key facts sheet: every system on one page

scenes.text: Tanya has one evening before her biology test and nine units to revise.
She uses a one-page sheet per system and tests herself with flashcards.
Short, active recall beats rereading the whole book.

steps.title: Cells & tissues
steps.body: Cell → tissue → organ → system. 4 tissues: epithelial, connective (incl. blood, bone), muscular (skeletal, smooth, cardiac), nervous. Homeostasis by negative feedback; hypothalamus = thermostat; insulin lowers, glucagon raises glucose.

steps.title: Bones & muscles
steps.body: 206 bones; femur longest; stapes smallest. Joints: fixed, cartilaginous, synovial (ball-and-socket, hinge, pivot, gliding, saddle). Tendon: muscle→bone; ligament: bone→bone. Antagonistic pairs (biceps/triceps).

steps.title: Digestion
steps.body: Mouth (amylase) → oesophagus (peristalsis) → stomach (HCl, pepsin) → small intestine (bile emulsifies, pancreatic enzymes, villi absorb) → large intestine (water). Deficiencies: A–night blindness, B1–beriberi, C–scurvy, D–rickets, iron–anaemia, iodine–goitre.

steps.title: Circulation & breathing
steps.body: RA→RV→pulmonary artery→lungs→pulmonary vein→LA→LV→aorta. Arteries away; veins back (valves); capillaries exchange. RBC (O₂, haemoglobin), WBC (defence), platelets (clotting). Airway: nose→pharynx→larynx→trachea→bronchi→bronchioles→alveoli. Inhale: diaphragm contracts, ribs up/out. Aerobic: glucose + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + energy; anaerobic (muscle): lactic acid.

steps.title: Kidneys, nerves, hormones, immunity, sleep
steps.body: Nephron: glomerulus filters, tubule reabsorbs (~99% water); ADH ↑ = less urine. Brain: cerebrum (thought), cerebellum (balance), medulla (automatic). Reflex arc: receptor→sensory→relay→motor→effector. Glands: pituitary (master), thyroid (thyroxine, iodine), pancreas, adrenal (adrenaline), ovaries, testes, pineal (melatonin). Vaccines → memory cells. Teens 8–10 h sleep; cycles ~90 min.

quiz.why: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs. It is the exception among arteries.
Blood is a connective tissue. The gut lining and skin surface are epithelial, and neurons are nervous tissue.
In children, a lack of vitamin D causes rickets, in which bones become soft and bend.
A knee-jerk is a reflex coordinated by the spinal cord, so the response is quick.
Lactic acid is made by anaerobic respiration in muscles when they work without enough oxygen.

lessons.title: All the numbers and calculations

scenes.text: Harsh keeps losing marks on easy calculations.
He makes a card: pulse, cardiac output, calories, salt, reabsorption, °F.
Next test: full marks on numericals.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- Pulse (bpm) = beats in 15 s × 4
- Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume
- Minute ventilation = breaths/min × tidal volume
- Energy: carbs 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal/g
- Salt ≈ sodium × 2.5
- °F = °C × 9/5 + 32
- % reabsorbed = (filtered − urine) ÷ filtered × 100
- Sleep debt = (need − got) × nights
- Caffeine left = start × (½)^(time ÷ half-life)

steps.title: Worked set
steps.body:
1. 21 beats in 15 s → **84 bpm**.
2. HR 75, SV 70 ml → 5250 ml = **5.25 L/min**.
3. 25 g carbs + 8 g protein + 12 g fat → 100 + 32 + 108 = **240 kcal**.
4. 2 g sodium → **5 g salt** (the full adult daily limit!).
5. 38 °C → 38 × 1.8 + 32 = **100.4 °F**.
6. Filtered 180 L, urine 1.5 L → 178.5/180 = **99.2%**.

steps.title: Common slips
steps.body:
- Multiplying 15-second counts by 6 instead of 4 (that's for 10 s).
- Forgetting to convert ml to L.
- Using 4 kcal/g for fat.
- Adding 32 before multiplying in °F conversions.

activity.prompt: A snack has 15 g carbohydrate, 6 g protein and 8 g fat. How many kcal?

quiz.why: Count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4: 18 × 4 = 72 bpm.
Cardiac output = 60 × 80 = 4800 ml/min = 4.8 L/min.
Fat gives 9 kcal per gram, so 12 g gives 12 × 9 = 108 kcal.
Salt ≈ sodium × 2.5, so 1.2 g sodium ≈ 1.2 × 2.5 = 3 g salt.

lessons.title: Answer-writing: assertion–reason & case questions

scenes.text: Assertion–reason questions confuse Zara: both statements look true!
Her tutor gives a 3-step method.
She now gets them right nearly every time.

steps.title: 3-step method for A–R
steps.body:
1. Is the **Assertion** true on its own?
2. Is the **Reason** true on its own?
3. If both are true, does R **explain why** A is true? Read it as 'A **because** R'.

steps.title: Worked A–R
steps.body:
A: Veins have valves. R: Blood in veins is under low pressure.
- A true. R true. 'Veins have valves because blood is under low pressure (and could flow back)' — makes sense → **both true, R explains A**.

A: The liver digests fat. R: The liver produces bile.
- A false (bile emulsifies; lipase digests). R true → **A false, R true**.

steps.title: Case-based questions
steps.body: Underline the key facts in the case (age, symptom, timing). Ask: which system? what's normal? what's the danger sign? Then match to the option that is both **accurate** and **safe** (for health cases, the safe answer usually involves a trusted adult, doctor or 112).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing 'R explains A' just because both are true.
- Ignoring words like 'NOT', 'always', 'only'.

statements.s: In A–R, if both are true, R always explains A.
'Always' and 'only' are warning words in options.
In health cases, the safest accurate option is usually right.

quiz.q: A: Sweating cools the body. R: Evaporation absorbs heat.
quiz.why: Both are true. Sweat takes heat from the skin when it evaporates, which cools the body. The reason explains the assertion.

quiz.q: A: Arteries carry oxygenated blood always. R: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
quiz.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, which makes the reason true. But they do not always carry oxygenated blood, since the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood. So the assertion is false.

quiz.q: A: Insulin raises blood sugar. R: Insulin is made by the pancreas.
quiz.why: Insulin lowers blood sugar, so the assertion is false. The reason is true, since the pancreas makes insulin.

quiz.q: First step in a case question:
quiz.why: In a case question, first underline the key facts. This helps you pick the right information and reach the correct answer.

questions.q: Smallest bone:
questions.why: The stapes, in the middle ear, is the smallest bone in the body.

questions.q: Insulin is from the…
questions.why: Insulin is made by the pancreas.

questions.q: Air sacs:
questions.why: The air sacs of the lungs are the alveoli. Villi are in the small intestine and nephrons in the kidneys.

questions.q: Teens' sleep need:
questions.why: Teens need about 8–10 hours of sleep a night.

questions.q: Bile is stored in the…
questions.why: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gallbladder.

questions.q: Malaria is caused by…
questions.why: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan parasite. Aedes is the mosquito for dengue.

questions.q: Hinge joint:
questions.why: The knee is a hinge joint. The hip and shoulder are ball-and-socket joints, and the neck rotates on a pivot joint.

questions.q: Effector in a reflex:
questions.why: In a reflex, the muscle is the effector, as it carries out the response.

questions.q: A: RBCs lack a nucleus. R: This gives more space for haemoglobin.
questions.why: Both are true. Red blood cells lose their nucleus, which gives more space for haemoglobin to carry oxygen. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: ADH increases when…
questions.why: When the body is dehydrated, ADH rises, so the kidneys save water by reabsorbing more of it.

questions.q: Which is NOT a function of the skeleton?
questions.why: The skeleton supports, protects, stores minerals and makes blood cells. It does not produce insulin, which is made by the pancreas.

questions.q: Case: Child with goitre in a hilly area. Likely cause?
questions.why: Goitre in a hilly area is likely from iodine deficiency, as the soil and water there often lack iodine. Iodised salt prevents it.

questions.q: 22 beats in 15 s:
questions.why: 22 beats in 15 seconds × 4 = 88 bpm.

questions.q: 20 g carbs + 10 g protein + 10 g fat:
questions.why: Carbohydrate: 20 × 4 = 80, protein: 10 × 4 = 40, fat: 10 × 9 = 90. Total = 210 kcal.

questions.q: 12 breaths × 0.6 L =
questions.why: Minute ventilation = 12 × 0.6 L = 7.2 L/min.

questions.q: Case: After a short antibiotic course, infection returns and the drug no longer works. Best explanation:
questions.why: If the course was too short, some bacteria that were more resistant survived and multiplied. The next infection is then caused by resistant bacteria, so the drug no longer works.

questions.q: Why does the left ventricle need a thicker wall than the right?
options: It pumps blood through the whole systemic circuit at higher pressure
questions.why: The left ventricle pumps blood through the whole body (systemic circuit), which needs higher pressure. So its wall is thicker. The right ventricle pumps only to the lungs.

questions.q: Which is TRUE?
options: Lungs contain skeletal muscle that inflates them
Pressure drop in chest causes air to enter
questions.why: When the chest expands, the pressure inside drops below the outside pressure, so air enters. The trachea has cartilage rings, lungs have no muscle of their own, and exhaled air still has about 16% oxygen.

questions.q: A cola with 60 mg caffeine at 5 pm (half-life 5 h). At 3 am about how much remains?
questions.why: From 5 pm to 3 am is 10 hours, which is two half-lives of 5 h. So 60 → 30 → 15 mg remains.

well-awkward-faq.title: Ask the awkward: questions people feel too shy to ask
well-awkward-faq.description: Big FAQ courses for every age band — kids, preteens, teens, older teens, adults and parents — answering the questions people never ask aloud, calmly, accurately and without judgment.

courses.title: Ask anything! Body & life questions for kids (6–10)
courses.summary: Simple, honest answers to the questions kids wonder about but feel shy to ask — bodies, babies, privacy, feelings, families and big life questions — best explored with a grown-up.
outcomes: Children can get simple, correct answers to common body questions
Children know that curiosity is normal and okay
Children know which questions to ask a trusted grown-up
courses.guardianNote: For ages 6–10 with a parent or teacher nearby: short, calm, accurate answers to the body and life questions young children ask (where babies come from, body differences, privacy, touching, death, words they've heard). Age-appropriate and non-explicit per UNESCO ITGSE 2018.

lessons.title: Bodies: why are we different?

scenes.text: At the pool, Aryan asks his dad, 'Why do girls have different private parts?'
His dad answers calmly with the right words.
Aryan says, 'Okay!' and jumps back into the water.

steps.title: All questions are okay
steps.body: Being curious about bodies is **normal**. You can ask a trusted grown-up anything. If they don't know, they can find out with you.

steps.title: Bodies differ
steps.body: Boys usually have a **penis** and **testicles**; girls usually have a **vulva**, and inside, a **vagina** and **uterus**. Bodies also differ in size, colour, hair and shape — all normal.

steps.title: Private parts stay private
steps.body: We keep private parts covered in public and don't touch other people's private parts. Your body belongs to you.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: Why do boys and girls have different private parts?
items.a: Bodies are made differently so that when people grow up they can, if they choose, make babies. Both kinds are normal.

items.q: Why does my body have a belly button?
items.a: Before you were born, a tube called the umbilical cord connected you to your mother and gave you food. After birth it was cut, and the belly button is where it was!

items.q: Why can't I see grown-ups' private parts?
items.a: Private parts are private for everyone, kids and grown-ups. That's about respect.

items.q: Is it okay to touch my own private parts?
items.a: Many kids touch their own private parts sometimes because it feels nice or they're curious. It's not harmful, but it's private — something for when you're alone, like in your bedroom or the bathroom. No one else should touch them or ask you to touch theirs.

items.q: Why are some people very tall or short, dark or fair?
items.a: Mostly because of genes — instructions from our families. Every size and skin colour is normal and good.

quiz.q: Is being curious about bodies normal?
quiz.why: Yes. It is normal to be curious about bodies. It is okay to ask a trusted grown-up.

quiz.q: Your belly button is where the… was
quiz.why: The belly button is the place where the umbilical cord was joined. The cord fed the baby before birth.
Private parts are private for everyone. We keep them covered, and nobody should touch them or ask to see them.
Skin colour comes mostly from genes, which we get from our parents. The sun can change it a little, but it is not the main reason.

lessons.title: Where do babies come from?

scenes.text: Mira notices Neha Aunty's tummy getting bigger.
'Is there a baby inside? How did it get there?'
Her mum explains simply and Mira is satisfied — for now!

steps.title: Simple answer
steps.body: A baby starts when a tiny **sperm** cell from a man and a tiny **egg** cell from a woman join together. The baby grows in the woman's **uterus** (womb) for about **9 months**, then is born — through the vagina or by an operation called a caesarean.

steps.title: Families are different
steps.body: Some children are adopted, some have one parent, two mums or two dads, grandparents as parents, or were born with help from doctors. **Families are about love and care.**

steps.title: Grown-up note
steps.body: Answer what's asked, simply and truthfully. Add more as the child grows. Avoid myths like storks — they confuse children later.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: How does the baby get out?
items.a: Most babies come out through the mother's vagina, which can stretch. Some are born by a caesarean, where doctors make a careful opening in the tummy.

items.q: How does the sperm get to the egg?
items.a: When grown-ups decide to have a baby, their bodies can bring sperm and egg together. It's something for grown-ups. (Grown-ups: give more detail as children get older.)

items.q: Can kids make babies?
items.a: No. Bodies need to grow up through puberty first, and making a baby is a grown-up decision.

items.q: What does the baby eat inside?
items.a: It gets food and oxygen from its mother's blood through the umbilical cord.

items.q: Was I adopted?
items.a: Ask your grown-up — every family has its own story, and every story is special.

quiz.why: A baby grows inside the mother, in a special part called the uterus (womb).
A baby grows inside the mother for about 9 months before it is born.
Families are about love and care. Families can look very different, and that is okay.
No. Storks do not bring babies. That is just a story. Babies grow inside the mother.

lessons.title: Feelings, families and big questions

scenes.text: Rohan's grandfather died last month.
Rohan asks, 'Will I die too? Is it my fault?'
His mother holds him and answers gently, honestly.

steps.title: Big feelings
steps.body: Sadness, anger, fear and confusion are all okay. Talking, drawing, crying and hugs help. No feeling is 'bad'.

steps.title: About death (simply)
steps.body: When someone dies, their body stops working and doesn't start again. It isn't like sleeping. It's never a child's fault. Most people live a long, long time.

steps.title: Help
steps.body: If you're worried, sad for a long time, or someone is hurting you — tell a trusted grown-up. Grown-ups can call **1098**.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: Will I die soon?
items.a: Most people live to be very old. Your grown-ups and doctors work hard to keep you safe and healthy.

items.q: Is it my fault someone died or my parents fought?
items.a: No. Grown-up problems and illnesses are never a child's fault.

items.q: Why do grown-ups kiss?
items.a: Grown-ups who love each other sometimes kiss to show it. Kids can show love with hugs, words and kindness.

items.q: Why do some boys like boys or girls like girls?
items.a: People can love people of any gender. It's a normal part of how people are.

items.q: Why do I feel angry for no reason?
items.a: Sometimes we're tired, hungry or worried. Taking slow breaths, a snack or a hug can help.

quiz.why: No. Dying is not like sleeping. When a body dies, it stops working and does not wake up. Sleeping bodies still work and wake up.

quiz.q: Is a grown-up's illness a child's fault?
quiz.why: No. A grown-up's illness is never a child's fault. Children do not make people sick by what they say or do.
All feelings are okay, including sad and angry ones. What matters is how we handle them, and we can talk to someone we trust.
1098 is Childline, a free helpline that grown-ups and children in India can call for help.

lessons.title: Words I heard: rude words and unkind words

scenes.text: On the playground, Kabir hears an older boy use a word he's never heard. Everyone laughs.
At home he asks his mum what it means.
She explains why some words are rude or hurtful, without needing to repeat it — and thanks him for asking.

steps.title: Rude words vs unkind words
steps.body:
- **Swear words** are words many people find rude, often about bodies, toilets or sex.
- **Slurs** are words used to insult people for their caste, religion, skin colour, disability, gender or who they love — these are **hurtful and not okay**.
When you hear a new word, ask a trusted grown-up what it means.

steps.title: What to do
steps.body: Don't repeat words you don't understand. If someone uses words to hurt someone, tell a grown-up. Use kind words — they make people feel safe.

steps.title: Grown-up note
steps.body: Stay calm and thank the child for asking. Explain in simple terms what kind of word it is and why it's hurtful, without shaming.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: What does that word mean?
items.a: Ask a trusted grown-up. They can explain what kind of word it is and whether it's rude or hurtful.

items.q: Why do people laugh at rude words?
items.a: Sometimes people laugh because they're nervous or want to fit in. It doesn't mean the word is okay.

items.q: Am I in trouble for hearing it?
items.a: No! Hearing a word isn't your fault. Asking about it is smart.

items.q: What if someone calls me a bad name?
items.a: Say 'Stop, I don't like that,' walk away, and tell a grown-up.

items.q: Is it okay to use slurs as a joke?
items.a: No. Slurs hurt people even as 'jokes'.

quiz.q: If you hear a new word, you should…
quiz.why: If you hear a new word and don't know it, ask a trusted grown-up what it means. Do not repeat it everywhere or shout it.

options: hurtful words about who people are
quiz.why: Slurs are hurtful words used about who people are. They can make others feel bad, so we do not use them.

quiz.q: Are you in trouble for hearing a word?
quiz.why: No. You are not in trouble for hearing a word. It is not your fault. You can ask a grown-up what it means.
If someone calls you a bad name, say 'stop' firmly, walk away, and tell a trusted grown-up. Hitting back can get you or others hurt.

questions.q: Being curious about bodies is…
questions.why: Being curious about bodies is normal. Everyone wonders about how bodies work.

questions.q: A baby grows in the…
questions.why: A baby grows in the mother's uterus (womb), not in the stomach or lungs.

questions.q: Childline:
questions.why: Childline is 1098, a free helpline for children.

questions.q: Private parts are…
questions.why: Private parts are private for everyone. Nobody should touch them or ask you to touch theirs.

questions.q: Families are about…
questions.why: Families are about love and care, not money or being the same.

questions.q: If you hear a new word, you…
questions.why: If you hear a new word, ask a grown-up you trust what it means.

questions.q: Is it a child's fault when grown-ups fight?
questions.why: No. When grown-ups fight, it is never a child's fault. Children can talk to a trusted adult about how they feel.

questions.q: Slurs as jokes are…
questions.why: Slurs used as jokes still hurt people, so they are not okay. Use kind words instead.

questions.q: A baby starts when…
questions.why: A baby starts when a sperm and an egg join. It is biology, not storks or wishes.

questions.q: Touching your own private parts is…
questions.why: Touching your own private parts is something to do in private. It does not harm you, but it is not for other people to see.

questions.q: Someone asks you to touch their private parts. You…
questions.why: If anyone asks you to touch their private parts, say 'No', go away, and tell a trusted grown-up. Do not keep it a secret. It is never your fault.

questions.q: Death means the body…
questions.why: Death means the body stops working and does not start again. It is not like sleeping or going on a holiday. It is good to explain it honestly.

questions.q: Why are bodies different sizes and colours?
questions.why: Bodies come in many sizes and colours mostly because of genes from our parents. All of these are normal.

questions.q: What should you do if someone uses a slur?
options: tell a grown-up and use kind words
questions.why: If someone uses a slur, tell a grown-up and use kind words. Do not laugh or repeat it, as it hurts people.

questions.q: Is asking questions about babies okay?
questions.why: Yes. Asking questions about babies is okay. Curious children can ask a trusted grown-up.

courses.title: The question box: puberty & growing-up questions (11–13)
courses.summary: The real questions from anonymous question boxes — 'Is my body normal?', periods, wet dreams, erections, smells, crushes, swear words and things seen online — answered calmly and accurately.
outcomes: Learners can get accurate answers to common puberty questions
Learners can recognise when something needs a doctor or trusted adult
Learners can handle swear words, rumours and online content safely
courses.guardianNote: Anonymous-question-box style answers for ages 11–13 about puberty, bodies, feelings, crushes, swear words and the internet. Calm, accurate and non-explicit (UNESCO ITGSE 2018), with trusted-adult and helpline guidance.

lessons.title: 'Is my body normal?'

scenes.text: Class 7's question box fills up in a week.
Almost every note starts with 'Is it normal…?'
The teacher smiles: 'The answer to most of these is yes.'

steps.title: Normal is a wide range
steps.body: Bodies change at different times and in different ways. Differences in size, shape, hair, skin and timing are **normal**.

steps.title: When to check
steps.body: Pain that doesn't go away, a lump that grows, bleeding that's very heavy, no signs of puberty by 13 (girls) / 14 (boys), or anything that worries you → talk to a parent and doctor.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **My breasts are different sizes. Normal?** Yes. Very common, especially while growing.
- **One testicle hangs lower. Normal?** Yes. Usually the left one does.
- **I have stretch marks. Normal?** Yes. Fast growth stretches the skin; marks fade over time.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: My breasts are different sizes. Normal?
items.a: Yes. Very common, especially while growing.

items.q: One testicle hangs lower. Normal?
items.a: Yes. Usually the left one does.

items.q: I have stretch marks. Normal?
items.a: Yes. Fast growth stretches the skin; marks fade over time.

items.q: I'm much shorter/taller than friends. Normal?
items.a: Usually yes — growth spurts happen at different ages.

items.q: I have hair on my upper lip/chest/toes. Normal?
items.a: Yes. Hair growth varies hugely with genes.

items.q: My penis/breasts seem small. Is that a problem?
items.a: No. Size varies a lot and doesn't affect health. Online images are not realistic.

items.q: My nipples hurt (I'm a boy). Normal?
items.a: Yes — tender breast tissue is common in boys during puberty and usually settles.

quiz.why: Breasts are often different in size, and this is normal. Most people have a small difference.
Stretch marks can appear when the body grows fast, as in puberty. They are normal and often fade with time.
A lump that keeps growing or that hurts should be checked by a doctor. Don't ignore it or squeeze it.
Body images online are often edited or filtered, so they are often unrealistic. Real bodies come in many shapes.

lessons.title: Periods, wet dreams and erections

scenes.text: Note 1: 'Can people tell when I'm on my period?' Note 2: 'Is it bad that I wake up with my shorts wet?'
The class goes quiet.
The teacher answers both calmly. Some students exhale with relief.

steps.title: Quick facts
steps.body: Periods: 2–7 days, every ~21–45 days in early years. Wet dreams: normal semen release in sleep. Erections: can happen randomly in puberty and go away on their own.

steps.title: More detail
steps.body: See the 'Puberty in depth' pack for full lessons on periods and wet dreams.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **Can people tell I'm on my period?** No, not unless you tell them. Pads and other products are discreet.
- **Can I play sports on my period?** Yes! Exercise can even ease cramps.
- **Is a wet dream bedwetting?** No. It's semen, not urine — and completely normal.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: Can people tell I'm on my period?
items.a: No, not unless you tell them. Pads and other products are discreet.

items.q: Can I play sports on my period?
items.a: Yes! Exercise can even ease cramps.

items.q: Is a wet dream bedwetting?
