items.a: No. It's semen, not urine — and completely normal.

items.q: Do wet dreams make you weak?
items.a: No. That's a myth. Your body keeps making semen.

items.q: Why do I get erections in class?
items.a: Hormones cause random erections in puberty. Think of something else; they pass in minutes.

items.q: Can boys get periods?
items.a: No. Periods come from the uterus. Boys can still be supportive friends!

items.q: What if my period starts at school?
items.a: Ask a teacher or nurse for a pad; tie a sweater if needed. It happens to lots of girls.

quiz.q: Can people tell you're on your period?
quiz.why: No. Other people cannot tell that you are on your period unless you tell them. Periods are normal, and pads or other products can be used discreetly.
Wet dreams happen when a boy's body releases semen while he sleeps. They are a normal part of puberty and are not bedwetting or an illness.
Random erections are common during puberty, because hormones change the body. They happen without any reason and pass on their own. They are not dangerous and need no treatment.
Doing sport or exercise during your period is fine and safe. Gentle activity can even help with cramps. Use a comfortable pad, cup or other product, and rest if you feel unwell.

lessons.title: Crushes, feelings and friends

scenes.text: Note: 'I have a crush on my best friend who is the same gender as me. Is something wrong with me?'
The teacher answers: 'Nothing is wrong with you.'
'Feelings at this age can be strong and confusing. You don't need a label.'

steps.title: Feelings are normal
steps.body: Crushes on anyone — or no crushes at all — are normal. Strong feelings and mood swings are part of puberty.

steps.title: Talk to someone
steps.body: A trusted adult or counsellor can help with confusing feelings. If you ever feel very sad for weeks, call **14416** or tell an adult.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **I have a crush on someone of the same gender. Is that okay?** Yes. People can be attracted to any gender, and feelings at this age can change and develop. Nothing is wrong with you.
- **I don't have any crushes. Am I weird?** No. Everyone develops at their own pace, and some people don't feel attraction much at all.
- **How do I stop thinking about my crush?** Keep busy with things you enjoy, spend time with friends, and give it time.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: I have a crush on someone of the same gender. Is that okay?
items.a: Yes. People can be attracted to any gender, and feelings at this age can change and develop. Nothing is wrong with you.

items.q: I don't have any crushes. Am I weird?
items.a: No. Everyone develops at their own pace, and some people don't feel attraction much at all.

items.q: How do I stop thinking about my crush?
items.a: Keep busy with things you enjoy, spend time with friends, and give it time.

items.q: My friend told everyone my crush. What now?
items.a: That hurts. Tell them how you felt. Real friends keep secrets that are safe to keep.

items.q: Why do I cry or get angry so easily now?
items.a: Hormones, growing up and stress make feelings stronger. Sleep, exercise, talking and breathing help.

quiz.why: A crush on someone of the same gender is okay and normal. Many young people have such feelings. It is not wrong or an illness.
Not having crushes at all is also normal. Young people develop at different times, and some never feel romantic attraction.
Mood swings are common in puberty, because hormones and the growing brain change how we feel. They usually settle with time. Talking and rest help.
If you feel sad for weeks, don't hide it. Tell a trusted adult or call Tele-MANAS (14416), the free helpline. Help is available and it works.

lessons.title: Swear words, sex talk and things seen online

scenes.text: At break, a classmate shows a few kids an adult video on his phone. Ravi feels shocked and confused.
He walks away and later tells his father, worried he'll be in trouble.
His father says, 'You're not in trouble. I'm glad you told me. Let's talk about it.'

steps.title: Swear words and sex words
steps.body: Many swear words are about bodies or sex. Older kids often use them to sound grown-up. Ask a trusted adult what a word means instead of repeating it. Words that insult people for who they are (slurs) are never okay.

steps.title: If you see sexual content
steps.body: It's common to come across it accidentally. It's **not your fault**. Close it, tell a trusted adult. Pornography is not real life, and showing it to children is not okay — if an adult shows you, that's abuse; tell someone and call **1098**.

steps.title: What is 'sex' (simply)?
steps.body: 'Sex' can mean whether a body is male or female. 'Having sex' means a kind of physical closeness between grown-ups that can make a baby. It's for adults, and needs both people's clear agreement. In India the law protects everyone under 18.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: What does that swear word mean?
items.a: Ask a trusted adult — they can explain what kind of word it is and why people find it rude. Avoid repeating words you don't understand.

items.q: Am I in trouble because I saw a sex video?
items.a: No. It's not your fault. Telling an adult is the right move.

items.q: Why do older kids talk about sex so much?
items.a: They're curious and often exaggerate. Much of what they say is myth.

items.q: Is it normal to be curious about sex?
items.a: Yes, curiosity is normal. Ask a trusted adult or use reliable sources made for your age.

items.q: Someone sent me a rude picture. What do I do?
items.a: Don't forward it. Tell a trusted adult. If it's from an adult, it's a serious matter — report it (1098, 1930).

quiz.q: If you see sexual content accidentally:
options: close it and tell an adult
quiz.why: If you see sexual content by accident, close it and tell a trusted adult. It is not your fault, and telling helps you feel safe. Don't share it or keep watching.

quiz.q: An adult showing a child sexual videos is…
quiz.why: An adult showing a child sexual videos is abuse, and it is never the child's fault. Tell a trusted adult and call Childline 1098 for help.
Slurs are never okay. They are hurtful words about who people are, so calling them 'jokes' does not make them kind.

quiz.q: Curiosity about sex at this age is…
quiz.why: Curiosity about sex at this age is normal as the body and mind grow. The safe way is to ask a trusted adult or use a reliable, age-appropriate source.

questions.q: Stretch marks during growth are…
questions.why: Stretch marks can appear when the body grows quickly, as in puberty. They are normal and often fade over time. They are not a disease and are not dangerous.

questions.q: Wet dreams are…
questions.why: Wet dreams happen when a boy's body releases semen during sleep. They are a normal part of puberty. They are not bedwetting and not an illness.

questions.q: Childline:
questions.why: Childline is 1098, a free helpline for children in need of care or protection. 14416 is Tele-MANAS and 1930 is for cybercrime.

questions.q: Can boys get periods?
questions.why: No. Periods come from the lining of the uterus (womb) shedding, and boys do not have a uterus. So boys cannot get periods.

questions.q: Same-gender crush:
questions.why: A crush on someone of the same gender is normal. It is not an illness, and it is not wrong.

questions.q: Seeing sexual content by accident is…
questions.why: Seeing sexual content by accident is not your fault. You can close it and tell a trusted adult, and you will not be in trouble.

questions.q: Boy's tender nipples in puberty usually…
questions.why: Tender or slightly swollen nipples can happen in boys during puberty because of hormone changes. It usually settles on its own and does not need surgery. See a doctor if it is painful or keeps growing.

questions.q: Someone forwards a rude picture to you:
questions.why: If someone forwards a rude picture to you, do not forward it. Tell a trusted adult. Sharing can hurt people and may be a crime.

questions.q: Wet dreams cause weakness?
questions.why: No. Wet dreams do not cause weakness. That is a myth. They are normal and the body stays healthy.

questions.q: Which needs a doctor?
questions.why: A painful, growing lump needs a doctor to check it. Stretch marks, a different breast size and hair in odd places are common, harmless changes.

questions.q: Why do older kids exaggerate about sex?
options: Curiosity and wanting to seem grown-up
questions.why: Older kids often exaggerate about sex because of curiosity and wanting to seem grown-up. So what they say is often wrong. Check facts with a reliable source.

questions.q: Cybercrime helpline:
questions.why: The cybercrime helpline number in India is 1930. Childline is 1098.

questions.q: An adult online sends a child sexual images. This is…
questions.why: An adult online sending a child sexual images is a serious offence. It should be reported to a trusted adult and the authorities, such as 1930 or Childline 1098. It is never the child's fault.

questions.q: Best source for questions about sex at 12:
options: trusted adult or age-appropriate reliable source
questions.why: At 12, the best sources of answers are a trusted adult or an age-appropriate reliable source. Porn is not real or accurate, and older kids' rumours are often wrong.

questions.q: Feeling very sad for weeks — best step?
questions.why: If you feel very sad for weeks, tell a trusted adult or call Tele-MANAS (14416). Hiding or ignoring it can make it worse, and help works.

courses.title: Too awkward to ask? Bodies, relationships & the internet (14–15)
courses.summary: The questions teens type into search bars at 2 am: readiness and the law, virginity myths, pregnancy myths, sexting and porn, 'am I normal?', mental health and identity — answered straight.
outcomes: Learners can correct common myths about sex, pregnancy and virginity
Learners can state the law on age of consent and sexting
Learners can find reliable help for body, relationship and mental-health concerns
courses.guardianNote: Frank, non-explicit answers for ages 14–15 about bodies, relationships, readiness and the law, sexting, pornography myths, virginity myths, mental health and identity. Accurate and judgment-free (UNESCO ITGSE 2018), with Indian law context (POCSO: age of consent 18) and helplines.

lessons.title: Readiness, the law and myths

scenes.text: In Arnav's group chat, boys brag about 'experience'. Arnav feels behind.
He wonders if something's wrong with him.
Health class shows most teens his age haven't had sex — and the law sets 18 as the age of consent.

steps.title: The law
steps.body: In India, the **age of consent is 18** (POCSO Act). Any sexual activity involving someone under 18 is an offence, even if both are teens and 'agree'. The law protects young people from exploitation.

steps.title: Readiness
steps.body: Being ready involves maturity, trust, knowing about consent, protection and consequences, and **never** being pressured. Waiting is common and completely normal — bragging in groups is often exaggerated.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **Is everyone my age having sex?** No. Most teens your age haven't, despite what people brag.
- **What's the age of consent in India?** 18, under the POCSO Act.
- **Can you get pregnant from kissing or a swimming pool?** No. Pregnancy requires sperm to reach an egg. Kissing and swimming pools can't cause pregnancy.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: Is everyone my age having sex?
items.a: No. Most teens your age haven't, despite what people brag.

items.q: What's the age of consent in India?
items.a: 18, under the POCSO Act.

items.q: Can you get pregnant from kissing or a swimming pool?
items.a: No. Pregnancy requires sperm to reach an egg. Kissing and swimming pools can't cause pregnancy.

items.q: Can you get pregnant the first time?
items.a: Yes. Any time sperm meets an egg, pregnancy is possible.

items.q: What is virginity?
items.a: It's a social idea, not a medical state. You can't tell by looking at a body, and the hymen is not a reliable sign. 'Virginity tests' have no medical basis.

items.q: Is it okay to wait?
items.a: Absolutely. Your timeline is yours.

quiz.why: The age of consent in India is 18. Under the POCSO Act, anyone under 18 is a child and cannot legally consent to sexual activity.
Pregnancy cannot come from kissing. Pregnancy needs a sperm to meet an egg, which does not happen through a kiss.

options: a social idea, not a medical state
quiz.why: Virginity is a social idea, not a medical state. There is no test to show it, and the hymen can stretch or tear in many ways, so bleeding or not proves nothing.
Yes. Waiting is normal. There is no deadline, and anyone, of any gender, can choose to wait until they feel ready and it is legal.

lessons.title: Sexting, nudes and porn

scenes.text: Riya's online boyfriend asks for a 'private pic, just for me'.
She remembers it's illegal for under-18s and risky. She says no.
He gets angry, so she blocks him and tells her sister. She feels proud of herself.

steps.title: Law & risk
steps.body: Sexual images of anyone **under 18** — including selfies — are illegal to make, share or keep (POCSO, IT Act 67B). Once sent, you lose control of them. Responsibility for harm lies with whoever shares or threatens.

steps.title: Porn ≠ reality
steps.body: Pornography is staged performance; it often shows unrealistic bodies and no consent or protection. It isn't sex education. If you feel you can't stop watching, talk to someone.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **Is it illegal if I send a nude of myself?** For under-18s, yes — it counts as child sexual material under Indian law. If you already did, tell a trusted adult; help (Take It Down, 1930) is available and the focus is on protecting you.
- **Someone is threatening to share my photo. What do I do?** Don't pay or send more. Save evidence, report at 1930/cybercrime.gov.in, block, tell an adult. It's not your fault.
- **Is watching porn normal?** Many teens come across it. It doesn't show real relationships, consent or bodies. Viewing child sexual material is a crime.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: Is it illegal if I send a nude of myself?
items.a: For under-18s, yes — it counts as child sexual material under Indian law. If you already did, tell a trusted adult; help (Take It Down, 1930) is available and the focus is on protecting you.

items.q: Someone is threatening to share my photo. What do I do?
items.a: Don't pay or send more. Save evidence, report at 1930/cybercrime.gov.in, block, tell an adult. It's not your fault.

items.q: Is watching porn normal?
items.a: Many teens come across it. It doesn't show real relationships, consent or bodies. Viewing child sexual material is a crime.

items.q: Will porn make me addicted?
items.a: Some people develop compulsive use. Signs: can't cut down, affects sleep or school. Talk to a counsellor or call 14416.

items.q: My friend forwarded someone's private photo. What should I do?
items.a: Don't share it further. Tell an adult and report it — it seriously harms the person.

quiz.why: Nude or sexual images of anyone under 18 are illegal in India, even if you take them yourself. It is treated as child sexual abuse material under the law.
In sextortion, someone threatens to share your private images unless you pay. Do not pay, as it usually leads to more demands. Save the evidence, tell a trusted adult and report it on 1930.
Porn is a staged, edited performance, not real life or sex education. It gives unrealistic ideas about bodies, consent and relationships.
1930 is India's cybercrime helpline. 1098 is Childline and 181 is the women's helpline.

lessons.title: 'Am I normal?' — bodies, hygiene and health

scenes.text: At 2 am Aditi types 'is white discharge normal' into her phone.
The results scare her.
Next day the school nurse explains it's normal — and which signs actually need a doctor.

steps.title: Search smart
steps.body: Late-night searching often shows rare or frightening results. Use trusted health sources and ask a doctor or nurse.

steps.title: See a doctor for
steps.body: Severe pain, unusual discharge with itching or smell, sores or lumps, very heavy or absent periods, sudden severe testicle pain (emergency).

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **Is white discharge normal?** Yes — clear or white discharge without itching is normal and healthy.
- **Is it normal to masturbate? Is it harmful?** Many people do and many don't. It's not physically harmful and doesn't cause weakness, acne or infertility. It's private.
- **Why do I smell 'down there'?** A mild natural smell is normal. Wash the outside daily with water; strong fishy smell, itching or unusual discharge → doctor.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: Is white discharge normal?
items.a: Yes — clear or white discharge without itching is normal and healthy.

items.q: Is it normal to masturbate? Is it harmful?
items.a: Many people do and many don't. It's not physically harmful and doesn't cause weakness, acne or infertility. It's private.

items.q: Why do I smell 'down there'?
items.a: A mild natural smell is normal. Wash the outside daily with water; strong fishy smell, itching or unusual discharge → doctor.

items.q: My periods are irregular. Problem?
items.a: Common in the first 2–3 years. See a doctor if cycles are under 21 or over 45 days, very heavy, or absent for 3+ months.

items.q: Can I get an STI without sex?
items.a: Some infections spread through blood (shared needles, razors) or from mother to baby. Most STIs spread through sexual contact.

quiz.why: A clear or white discharge without itching, smell or pain is normal for girls after puberty begins. It keeps the vagina clean and healthy. See a doctor if it changes colour, smells bad or itches.
No. Masturbation does not cause weakness or any lasting harm. That is a myth. It is a private and common behaviour.
Sudden severe testicle pain can be testicular torsion, where the testicle twists and loses its blood supply. It is an emergency that needs a hospital quickly.
Late-night searching often shows scary, rare results, which can increase worry. A doctor or reliable health source gives better answers than a random search.

lessons.title: Mind, identity and getting help

scenes.text: For weeks Siddharth feels empty and wonders if he's gay, if he's depressed, or both.
He calls Tele-MANAS at night and talks to a counsellor.
'One phone call didn't fix everything, but I didn't feel alone anymore.'

steps.title: You're not alone
steps.body: Many teens struggle with low mood, anxiety and questions about identity. Talking helps. Help: trusted adult, school counsellor, **14416** (24×7).

steps.title: Identity
steps.body: Questioning your sexual orientation or gender identity is okay. There's no deadline. You deserve respect and safety.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **How do I know if I'm depressed or just sad?** If low mood, losing interest, sleep or appetite changes last 2+ weeks and affect daily life, talk to someone — 14416 or a counsellor.
- **I think I might be gay/bi/trans. What do I do?** There's no rush to decide or label. Talk to someone you trust when you're ready. You deserve respect.
- **Can I talk to a counsellor without my parents knowing?** School counsellors and Tele-MANAS (14416) offer confidential support. For ongoing treatment of under-18s, parents are usually involved.

items.q: How do I know if I'm depressed or just sad?
items.a: If low mood, losing interest, sleep or appetite changes last 2+ weeks and affect daily life, talk to someone — 14416 or a counsellor.

items.q: I think I might be gay/bi/trans. What do I do?
items.a: There's no rush to decide or label. Talk to someone you trust when you're ready. You deserve respect.

items.q: Can I talk to a counsellor without my parents knowing?
items.a: School counsellors and Tele-MANAS (14416) offer confidential support. For ongoing treatment of under-18s, parents are usually involved.

items.q: I sometimes think about hurting myself.
items.a: Please tell someone today — a trusted adult, 14416 or 112 if you're in danger. You deserve support and things can get better.

items.q: My parents won't listen. What now?
items.a: Try another trusted adult: a relative, teacher or counsellor.

quiz.why: Low mood that lasts 2 weeks or more is a reason to talk to someone. Speak to a trusted adult, a doctor, or call Tele-MANAS (14416). It is treatable.
Questioning your identity or orientation is okay. It is a normal part of growing up for many people, and not an illness. You do not need to rush to label yourself.
If you have thoughts of self-harm, tell someone today. Talk to a trusted adult, call Tele-MANAS (14416), or call 112 if you are in danger. Hiding it or waiting can be risky.
If your parents won't listen, try another trusted adult, such as a relative, teacher, counsellor or doctor. Don't give up, because someone will listen.

questions.q: Age of consent:
questions.why: The age of consent in India is 18.

questions.q: Pregnancy from a swimming pool:
questions.why: Pregnancy cannot happen from a swimming pool. It needs sperm to meet an egg inside the body, and sperm do not survive in pool water.

questions.q: Tele-MANAS:
questions.why: Tele-MANAS, the free 24×7 mental-health helpline in India, is 14416.

questions.q: Under-18 nude selfie is…
questions.why: A nude selfie of someone under 18 is illegal in India, even if it is of yourself and kept private. It counts as child sexual abuse material.

questions.q: Porn is…
questions.why: Porn is a performance, scripted and edited. It is not realistic, and it is not a way to learn about sex or relationships.

questions.q: Pregnancy the first time:
questions.why: Pregnancy is possible the first time anyone has sex. It does not depend on marriage or on how many times.

questions.q: Virginity tests are…
questions.why: A virginity test has no medical meaning. The hymen can change from many activities, and tests are unreliable and violate a person's dignity.

questions.q: Sextortion step:
questions.why: In sextortion, don't pay. Save the evidence (screenshots), block the person, tell a trusted adult and report it on 1930.

questions.q: White discharge with no itch:
questions.why: White discharge with no itch or smell is normal for girls and women. It keeps the vagina clean.

questions.q: Irregular cycles in first 2–3 years are…
questions.why: Irregular periods in the first 2–3 years are common, as the hormones are still settling. See a doctor if periods are very heavy, very painful or stop for long.

questions.q: Case: A friend forwarded a classmate's private photo. Best?
options: Don't share; tell an adult; report
questions.why: Don't share a classmate's private photo. Sharing causes harm and may be illegal. Tell a trusted adult and report it, so that it can be taken down.

questions.q: Masturbation and infertility:
questions.why: There is no link between masturbation and infertility. It is a myth, and it does not affect the ability to have children later.

questions.q: Case: A 15-year-old says she might be bi and is scared. Best response?
options: Listen, respect, no pressure to label
questions.why: The best response is to listen, respect her feelings, and not pressure her to put a label on herself. Don't dismiss it as a phase or share it with others (outing her).

questions.q: Which statement is TRUE about teen sexting law in India?
options: Sexual images of under-18s are illegal even if self-made
questions.why: Under Indian law, sexual images of anyone under 18 are illegal, even if self-made or consensual. Sharing, keeping or sending them is an offence.

questions.q: Thoughts of self-harm — best first step?
questions.why: If you have thoughts of self-harm, tell someone today: a trusted adult, Tele-MANAS (14416), or 112 in an emergency. Don't hide it or wait.

lessons.title: Consent, pressure and relationships

scenes.text: Tara's boyfriend says 'everyone our age has done it' and keeps pushing.
Tara says she's not ready. He sulks for days.
With her best friend's support she ends the relationship. 'Pressure isn't love.'

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body: Consent = **FRIES** (freely given, reversible, informed, enthusiastic, specific). Pressure, guilt or threats aren't consent. Intoxicated or asleep people can't consent. Age of consent in India is **18**.

steps.title: Lines that work
steps.body: 'I'm not ready.' 'No means no.' 'If you respected me you'd stop asking.'

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **How do I say no without losing them?** Say it clearly and kindly. Someone who truly cares will respect it. If they don't, that tells you something important.
- **Is it still consent if I said yes earlier?** Consent can be withdrawn at any time. Today's 'no' counts.
- **What if we're both drunk?** Intoxication removes the ability to consent. Don't take advantage; get each other home safely.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: How do I say no without losing them?
items.a: Say it clearly and kindly. Someone who truly cares will respect it. If they don't, that tells you something important.

items.q: Is it still consent if I said yes earlier?
items.a: Consent can be withdrawn at any time. Today's 'no' counts.

items.q: What if we're both drunk?
items.a: Intoxication removes the ability to consent. Don't take advantage; get each other home safely.

items.q: Is it normal not to want sex at all?
items.a: Yes. Desire varies a lot; some people are asexual or simply not interested yet.

items.q: My partner checks my phone. Normal?
items.a: No — that's controlling behaviour. Healthy relationships respect privacy.

quiz.why: Yes. Consent can be withdrawn at any time, even after agreeing or during an activity. Saying 'yes' once does not mean 'yes' always.
A person who is drunk (or high) cannot give valid consent, since they cannot think clearly or decide freely. Even in a relationship, the answer is 'not valid'.
Checking a partner's phone is controlling, not caring. Trust and privacy are part of a healthy relationship.
Not wanting sex is normal. Some people never feel sexual attraction (asexuality), or they simply are not ready. It is not an illness.

lessons.title: Contraception & emergency contraception questions

scenes.text: Ritesh's cousin (19) asks him what to do after a condom broke.
Ritesh remembers his health class: emergency contraception, sooner is better.
They go to a pharmacy and then a clinic for advice.

steps.title: Quick reference
steps.body: Condoms (also prevent STIs) · pills · injectables · IUDs · emergency contraceptive pill ≤72 h (sooner better) · copper IUD ≤5 days (most effective EC). Free services at government health centres; confidential counselling at adolescent-friendly clinics.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **Can I buy emergency contraception without a prescription?** In India, levonorgestrel EC pills are sold at pharmacies. Take as soon as possible after unprotected sex or condom failure.
- **Is the emergency pill an abortion pill?** No. It mainly delays ovulation and won't end an established pregnancy.
- **Do condoms expire?** Yes. Check the date; store away from heat; don't use oil-based lubricants with latex.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body: Trusted adults first: a parent, relative, teacher, school nurse or counsellor. **Help in India:** 112 (any emergency) · 1098 (Childline, for anyone under 18) · 14416 (Tele-MANAS, free 24×7 mental-health support). Also: 1930 (cybercrime), 181 (women's helpline), 1097 (HIV/AIDS, NACO). This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: Can I buy emergency contraception without a prescription?
items.a: In India, levonorgestrel EC pills are sold at pharmacies. Take as soon as possible after unprotected sex or condom failure.

items.q: Is the emergency pill an abortion pill?
items.a: No. It mainly delays ovulation and won't end an established pregnancy.

items.q: Do condoms expire?
items.a: Yes. Check the date; store away from heat; don't use oil-based lubricants with latex.

items.q: Can the pill make me infertile?
items.a: No. Fertility returns after stopping.

items.q: Can you get pregnant during your period?
items.a: Less likely but possible, especially with short cycles.

items.q: Does withdrawal work?
items.a: It's unreliable — about 1 in 5 couples using it get pregnant in a year.

quiz.why: The emergency contraceptive pill works best when taken as soon as possible after unprotected sex, and within 72 hours. The sooner, the better.

quiz.q: EC pill is an abortion pill?
quiz.why: No. The emergency contraception pill is not an abortion pill. It works by delaying ovulation, so it does not end an existing pregnancy.
The withdrawal ('pull-out') method is unreliable: about 1 in 5 couples using it for a year get pregnant. Sperm can also be present before ejaculation.
Yes, condoms expire. Old condoms can be weak and may break, so always check the date and the packet.

lessons.title: STIs, testing and doctor visits

scenes.text: At 17, Meher has painful periods and finally sees a gynaecologist with her mother.
The doctor asks questions, examines her abdomen and explains options; no internal exam was needed.
'I was terrified for nothing — she was kind and explained everything.'

steps.title: What to expect
steps.body: Doctors take a history (periods, symptoms, sometimes sexual history — you can ask for privacy). Examinations are explained first and need your consent; you can ask for a female/male doctor or a chaperone. Many visits need no internal exam.

steps.title: Confidentiality
steps.body: Doctors keep information confidential. For under-18s, parents are often involved in treatment decisions, and doctors must report sexual offences under POCSO — but their aim is to protect you. Adolescent-friendly health clinics (RKSK) and ICTCs offer confidential counselling.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **Do I have to tell the doctor if I've had sex?** It helps them give correct care. Information is confidential; you can ask to speak privately.
- **How do I know if I have an STI?** Many have no symptoms. Testing is the only way to know. ICTCs and Suraksha clinics offer confidential tests.
- **Is a pelvic exam always needed?** No. Many problems are assessed with questions, abdominal exam or ultrasound. You can always ask why and say no.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: Do I have to tell the doctor if I've had sex?
items.a: It helps them give correct care. Information is confidential; you can ask to speak privately.

items.q: How do I know if I have an STI?
items.a: Many have no symptoms. Testing is the only way to know. ICTCs and Suraksha clinics offer confidential tests.

items.q: Is a pelvic exam always needed?
items.a: No. Many problems are assessed with questions, abdominal exam or ultrasound. You can always ask why and say no.

items.q: Can boys see a doctor about their genitals?
items.a: Yes — a family doctor, paediatrician or urologist. Sudden severe testicle pain is an emergency.

items.q: Will the doctor judge me?
items.a: Good doctors don't. If one does, you can see another.

quiz.why: Many STIs have no symptoms, so a person can have one without knowing. That is why testing matters, and not just waiting for signs.

quiz.q: Can you ask for a chaperone?
quiz.why: Yes. You can ask for a chaperone (a trusted person or staff member) during a medical examination. It is your right.
ICTC and Suraksha clinics provide confidential STI and HIV testing and counselling. A bank or school office does not.
Any medical examination needs a clear explanation and your consent. You can ask questions and say no, and a parental order alone is not enough.

lessons.title: Size, performance, porn and identity worries

scenes.text: After watching online videos, Kunal worries his body is 'not enough'.
A doctor reassures him: wide natural variation; online content is unrealistic and edited.
His anxiety drops when he stops comparing.

steps.title: Reality check
steps.body: Body size and shape vary widely and are not linked to health, masculinity, femininity or a partner's satisfaction. Porn performers are selected, filmed and edited. Anxiety itself can affect bodies — talking to a doctor or counsellor helps.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **Is my penis size normal?** Almost certainly yes. Most worries come from comparison with unrealistic media. A doctor can reassure you.
- **Are big breasts/small breasts better?** No. Size has nothing to do with health, feeding a baby or worth.
- **Does porn show what partners like?** No. Real intimacy is about communication, consent and respect.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body: Trusted adults first: a parent, relative, teacher, school nurse or counsellor. **Help in India:** 112 (any emergency) · 1098 (Childline, for anyone under 18) · 14416 (Tele-MANAS, free 24×7 mental-health support). Also: 1930 (cybercrime), 181 (women's helpline), 1097 (HIV/AIDS, NACO). This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: Is my penis size normal?
items.a: Almost certainly yes. Most worries come from comparison with unrealistic media. A doctor can reassure you.

items.q: Are big breasts/small breasts better?
items.a: No. Size has nothing to do with health, feeding a baby or worth.

items.q: Does porn show what partners like?
items.a: No. Real intimacy is about communication, consent and respect.

items.q: I think I'm attracted to more than one gender. Is that okay?
items.a: Yes. Bisexuality and other orientations are normal variations.

items.q: I'm worried about 'performance' some day.
items.a: Anxiety is common; good communication and health matter far more than performance myths.

quiz.q: Body size is linked to health?
quiz.why: Body size does not tell you how healthy a person is. Health depends on many things, such as food, activity, sleep and genes.
Porn shows a staged, edited performance. It is not real life or medical fact, so it gives unrealistic ideas about bodies and sex.
Bisexuality is a normal variation in human sexuality. It is not a phase, and it is not an illness.
Comparing yourself with media images causes unnecessary anxiety, as those images are edited and unrealistic. Real bodies vary widely.

questions.q: FRIES 'F' stands for…
questions.why: In the FRIES model of consent, F means Freely given: without pressure, threats or tricks. The others are Reversible, Informed, Enthusiastic and Specific.

questions.q: Age of consent:
questions.why: The age of consent in India is 18.

questions.q: EC pill window:
questions.why: The emergency contraceptive pill should be taken as soon as possible, and within 72 hours of unprotected sex.

questions.q: Condoms with oil-based lubes:
questions.why: Avoid oil-based lubricants (like oil or petroleum jelly) with latex condoms. They weaken latex, so the condom may break. Use water-based lubricant.

questions.q: STI status known only by…
questions.why: You can only know your STI status by testing, because many infections have no symptoms. Guessing or looking is not reliable.

questions.q: Drunk consent:
questions.why: Consent given while drunk is invalid, because the person cannot decide clearly. Being a partner does not change this.

questions.q: Is the EC pill an abortion pill?
questions.why: No. The emergency contraception pill does not end a pregnancy. It prevents or delays ovulation, so no pregnancy starts.

questions.q: Many gynae visits need an internal exam?
questions.why: Not always. Many gynaecology visits (for periods, acne, contraception advice, etc.) do not need an internal exam. It is done only when needed, with your consent.

questions.q: Checking a partner's phone:
questions.why: Checking a partner's phone is control, not trust or care. Healthy partners respect each other's privacy.

questions.q: Withdrawal typical failure about:
questions.why: The withdrawal method fails in about 20% of couples (about 1 in 5) in a year of typical use, so it is unreliable.

questions.q: Case: Condom broke 20 hours ago. Best?
questions.why: After a broken condom, take emergency contraception as soon as possible. 20 hours is well within the 72-hour window, and earlier works better. Think about an STI test as well.

questions.q: Doctors must report sexual offences involving under-18s under…
questions.why: Under the POCSO Act, doctors (and others) must report sexual offences involving under-18s. This is called mandatory reporting, and it is meant to protect children.

questions.q: Case: Partner sulks for days after a no. This shows…
questions.why: Sulking or punishing someone for days after they say no is pressure, a red flag of coercion. In a respectful relationship, 'no' is accepted without punishment.

questions.q: Why are size anxieties usually misplaced?
options: Wide natural variation; media is unrealistic
questions.why: Size worries are mostly misplaced, as there is wide natural variation in bodies. Media and porn show unrealistic images, and size does not predict health.

questions.q: Best place for confidential teen counselling:
questions.why: Adolescent-friendly health clinics (AFHC, under RKSK) offer confidential counselling and care for teens. Social media and rumours are not reliable.

lessons.title: Marriage, wedding-night myths and desire

story.title: The pressure of the first night

scenes.text: Newly married Anil and Rekha feel pressure from relatives' jokes about the 'first night'.
They agree to take their time and talk openly.
'There's no exam. We're building trust,' says Rekha.

steps.title: Myths
steps.body:
- 'Bleeding proves virginity' — false; many people don't bleed; hymens vary; 'virginity tests' are medically meaningless.
- 'Semen loss weakens men' — false.
- 'There must be sex on the first night' — no; consent and comfort come first, always, including within marriage.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **Is it normal for partners to want sex at different frequencies?** Very common. Talking openly, scheduling time together and addressing stress, health or relationship issues helps; a counsellor can too.
- **Is it okay to take time after marriage?** Yes. Comfort, consent and trust matter more than any timeline or relative's expectations.
- **Does every woman bleed the first time?** No. Bleeding varies and proves nothing.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body: Trusted people first: a doctor, counsellor, or someone you trust. **Help in India:** 112 (any emergency) · 1098 (Childline, for anyone under 18) · 14416 (Tele-MANAS, free 24×7 mental-health support). Also: 1930 (cybercrime), 181 (women's helpline), 1097 (HIV/AIDS, NACO). This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

items.a: Very common. Talking openly, scheduling time together and addressing stress, health or relationship issues helps; a counsellor can too.

items.a: Yes. Comfort, consent and trust matter more than any timeline or relative's expectations.

items.q: Does every woman bleed the first time?
items.a: No. Bleeding varies and proves nothing.

items.q: Low desire — is something wrong?
items.a: It can relate to stress, depression, medicines, hormones, pain or relationship issues. A doctor can help.

items.q: Can we see a sex therapist in India?
items.a: Yes — qualified psychiatrists, psychologists and sexual-medicine specialists. Avoid unqualified 'sexologists' advertising cures.

quiz.why: No. Bleeding does not prove virginity. Many women do not bleed the first time, and the hymen can stretch or change from many causes.
Different levels of desire between partners are common, and they change with stress, health and life stage. They are not abnormal.
Consent matters always, including within marriage. Marriage does not give automatic or lasting consent, and either partner can say no.
Qualified help comes from a psychiatrist, psychologist or sexual-medicine specialist. Wall-ad clinics and online powders are unreliable and may be unsafe.

lessons.title: Pain, erections, ejaculation — medical, not shameful

scenes.text: For two years after childbirth, Shalini has pain during sex and stays silent.
A gynaecologist finds treatable causes and suggests pelvic-floor physiotherapy.
'I wish I'd asked sooner.'

steps.title: Common, treatable
steps.body: Pain during sex (infections, dryness, scarring after birth, endometriosis, vaginismus) · erectile difficulty (often linked to diabetes, BP, smoking, stress) · premature ejaculation · delayed ejaculation · low desire. All are health topics with effective treatment.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **Pain during sex after childbirth — normal?** It's common but not something to endure. Lubricants, time, pelvic-floor physiotherapy and medical treatment help.
- **Erection problems at 40 — should I worry?** See a doctor: it can be an early sign of diabetes or heart disease, and it's treatable.
- **Are online 'stamina' pills safe?** Many unregulated products contain hidden drugs. Use only prescribed treatment.

steps.title: Where to get help

Also: 1930 (cybercrime), 181 (women's helpline), 1097 (HIV/AIDS, NACO). This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

items.a: See a doctor: it can be an early sign of diabetes or heart disease, and it's treatable.

items.a: Many unregulated products contain hidden drugs. Use only prescribed treatment.

items.q: Is premature ejaculation treatable?
items.a: Yes — behavioural techniques, counselling and medicines help.

items.q: What is vaginismus?
items.a: Involuntary tightening of pelvic muscles making penetration painful or impossible; treatable with therapy and physiotherapy.

Online 'stamina' pills may contain hidden drugs that can be harmful, such as unlisted prescription medicines. See a qualified doctor instead.
Vaginismus (involuntary tightening of the vaginal muscles) is real and treatable, with therapy, counselling and physiotherapy.

lessons.title: Talking to partners about STIs, testing and health

scenes.text: Before marriage, Sameer suggests both get health check-ups including STI tests.
Neha is surprised, then agrees.
'It felt like a team decision about our future.'

steps.title: How to bring it up
steps.body: 'I care about us, so I'd like us both to get a check-up and STI tests. I'll go first.' Testing is routine health care, not an accusation.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **How do I ask a partner to get tested?** Frame it as caring for both of you; offer to test together.
- **If I test positive, must I tell my partner?** Telling partners allows them to get tested and treated; doctors and counsellors can help with how to tell.
- **Can a married couple get STIs?** Yes, if either has an infection from before or outside the relationship. Testing helps.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body: Trusted people first: a doctor, counsellor, or someone you trust. **Help in India:** 112 (any emergency) · 1098 (Childline, for anyone under 18) · 14416 (Tele-MANAS, free 24×7 mental-health support). Also: 1930 (cybercrime), 181 (women's helpline), 1097 (HIV/AIDS, NACO). This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

items.q: How do I ask a partner to get tested?
items.a: Frame it as caring for both of you; offer to test together.

items.q: If I test positive, must I tell my partner?
items.a: Telling partners allows them to get tested and treated; doctors and counsellors can help with how to tell.

items.q: Can a married couple get STIs?
items.a: Yes, if either has an infection from before or outside the relationship. Testing helps.

items.q: Is HPV vaccination useful for adults?
items.a: Benefit is highest before exposure, but some adults may still benefit — ask a doctor.

quiz.why: STI testing is routine health care, like checking blood pressure. It is not an accusation or an insult, and it is legal.
If a test is positive, partners should be told so they can be tested and treated too, which prevents re-infection and spread.
Yes. Married couples can have STIs, as some infections have no symptoms and can be present for years. Testing and treatment are still important.
The best way to raise it is with care, as a shared health step, and suggest testing together. Accusing or hiding makes it harder.

lessons.title: Mental health, therapy and life stages

scenes.text: After years of feeling flat, Rajesh, 45, sees a psychologist for the first time.
He learns he has had depression for years.
With therapy and treatment he feels like himself again.

steps.title: It's never too late
steps.body: Depression, anxiety, grief, burnout and relationship issues are common in adults. Therapy and, when needed, medicines are effective. Help: GP, psychologist, psychiatrist, **14416**.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **Is therapy only for 'serious' problems?** No. People go for stress, relationships, grief, decisions and growth.
- **How do I find a qualified therapist?** Look for a licensed clinical psychologist (RCI-registered) or a psychiatrist; ask about approach and fees.
- **Is menopause affecting my mood normal?** Yes, hormone changes can affect mood and sleep; doctors can help.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body: Trusted people first: a doctor, counsellor, or someone you trust. **Help in India:** 112 (any emergency) · 1098 (Childline, for anyone under 18) · 14416 (Tele-MANAS, free 24×7 mental-health support). Also: 1930 (cybercrime), 181 (women's helpline), 1097 (HIV/AIDS, NACO). This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

items.q: Is menopause affecting my mood normal?
items.a: Yes, hormone changes can affect mood and sleep; doctors can help.

items.q: Do older adults still have sexual lives?
items.a: Many do. Health, comfort and communication matter at every age.

items.q: Is postnatal depression real?
items.a: Yes — it's common and treatable; it can affect fathers too.

quiz.why: Therapy is for many kinds of problems, from stress and relationships to illness. Seeking it is a sign of strength, not weakness.

quiz.q: Qualified psychologists in India are registered with…
quiz.why: Qualified clinical psychologists in India are registered with the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI).
Postnatal depression is real and treatable. It affects many new parents, and support, therapy and sometimes medicine help.
Tele-MANAS, India's free 24×7 mental-health helpline, is 14416.

questions.q: Bleeding proves virginity?
questions.why: Bleeding does not prove virginity. Many women do not bleed the first time, and a torn hymen is not a reliable sign.

questions.q: Tele-MANAS:
questions.why: Tele-MANAS, India's free mental-health helpline, is 14416.

questions.q: Pain during sex should be…
questions.why: Pain during sex should be checked by a doctor. It is common and usually treatable, and it should not be ignored or endured.

questions.q: Desire differences between partners are…
questions.why: Differences in desire between partners are common, so they are not an illness or a sign that something is wrong.

questions.q: STI testing is…
questions.why: STI testing is routine care. It is not illegal or an insult, and it protects both partners.

questions.q: RCI registers…
questions.why: The Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) registers clinical psychologists and other rehabilitation professionals.

questions.q: Erectile difficulty at 40 may signal…
questions.why: Erectile difficulty at 40 may signal vascular disease or diabetes, as erections depend on healthy blood vessels and nerves. It is a reason to see a doctor.

questions.q: Consent within marriage:
questions.why: Consent is always required, including in marriage. It cannot be assumed to last forever.

questions.q: Postnatal depression can affect…
questions.why: Postnatal depression can affect both mothers and fathers. Getting help early works.

questions.q: Case: Online pill promises 'instant stamina'. Best?
questions.why: Pills promising instant stamina may have hidden drugs. Avoid them and see a doctor, who can find the real cause safely. Doubling a dose can be dangerous.

questions.q: Case: Partner tests positive for an STI. Next?
questions.why: If a partner tests positive for an STI, both should be tested and treated, so that it does not pass back and forth. Counselling can help the couple talk calmly, without blame.

questions.q: Vaginismus treatment:
questions.why: Vaginismus is treatable with therapy (including relaxation and gradual exposure) and pelvic-floor physiotherapy. Surgery is not usually needed.

questions.q: Case: Relatives pressure a newly-wed couple about the 'first night'. Best?
options: Couple decides together; consent and comfort first
questions.why: The couple should decide together, with consent and comfort first. Pressure from relatives or a demand to 'prove virginity' is wrong and has no medical basis.

questions.q: Which is a qualified source of sexual-health care?
questions.why: A sexual-medicine specialist, psychiatrist or gynaecologist is qualified. Influencers and wall-ad clinics are not reliable.

questions.q: Why is 'semen loss causes weakness' harmful?
options: Creates needless anxiety and exploitation by quacks
questions.why: The belief that semen loss causes weakness is a myth. It creates needless anxiety, and quacks exploit that fear by selling useless treatments.

courses.title: For parents & carers: answering children's awkward questions
courses.summary: Scripts and principles for parents, grandparents and teachers: answering 'where do babies come from', a child touching their genitals, first periods and wet dreams, finding a child watching porn, a child coming out, signs of abuse, and handling swear words — calmly and accurately at each age.
outcomes: Parents can answer common questions with age-appropriate, accurate words
Parents can respond calmly to surprising moments
Parents can recognise warning signs of abuse and respond
Parents can keep communication open through the teen years

lessons.title: Principles: calm, correct, ongoing

scenes.text: In a supermarket queue, 5-year-old Diya loudly asks, 'Mummy, why does that man have a big tummy — is there a baby?'
Her mother smiles: 'Only women can grow babies. People have all kinds of tummies.'
Diya moves on. Simple, calm, true.

steps.title: Five principles
steps.body:
1. **Stay calm** — your reaction teaches more than words.
2. **Find out what they're asking**: 'What made you wonder?'
3. **Answer simply and truthfully**; correct names.
4. **It's fine to say** 'Good question — let me find out.'
5. **Keep it ongoing** — many small talks, not one big one.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **What if I get embarrassed?** That's normal. Say, 'I feel a bit shy talking about this, but it's important.' Honesty models openness.
- **Won't talking about sex make children curious too early?** Evidence (UNESCO ITGSE) shows good sexuality education doesn't hasten sexual activity; it tends to delay it and make it safer.
- **What age should I start?** From toddlerhood: body names, privacy, consent basics. Then build up.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body: Trusted people first: a doctor, counsellor, or someone you trust. **Help in India:** 112 (any emergency) · 1098 (Childline, for anyone under 18) · 14416 (Tele-MANAS, free 24×7 mental-health support). Also: 1930 (cybercrime), 181 (women's helpline), 1097 (HIV/AIDS, NACO). This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: What if I get embarrassed?
items.a: That's normal. Say, 'I feel a bit shy talking about this, but it's important.' Honesty models openness.

items.q: Won't talking about sex make children curious too early?
items.a: Evidence (UNESCO ITGSE) shows good sexuality education doesn't hasten sexual activity; it tends to delay it and make it safer.

items.q: What age should I start?
items.a: From toddlerhood: body names, privacy, consent basics. Then build up.

items.q: What if my child asks in public?
items.a: Give a short answer and promise more at home: 'Great question — let's talk about it in the car.'

quiz.why: The first principle is to stay calm. A calm response tells the child it is safe to ask. Scolding or changing the subject teaches them to hide questions.

options: Evidence says no; it tends to delay and make safer
quiz.why: Evidence from large reviews (such as UNESCO's) shows that comprehensive sexuality education does not make young people start sex earlier. It tends to delay it and make it safer.
If you don't know the answer, be honest: say you'll find out and come back. Making things up spreads wrong information.
Talks about bodies, relationships and safety should be ongoing, with small chats as the child grows, not a single big talk.

lessons.title: Surprising moments: touching, porn, swear words

scenes.text: Mr. Khan finds adult sites in his 11-year-old son's browsing history.
His first urge is to shout.
Instead he says, 'I saw this. You're not in trouble — I want to understand and help.' They talk about what porn is and isn't, and set up filters together.

steps.title: Respond, don't react
steps.body: Breathe. Separate your feelings from the child's need. Avoid shame — shame drives secrecy, which increases risk.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **My toddler touches their genitals. Should I stop it?** It's common and normal self-exploration. Calmly teach privacy: 'That's something we do in private, like in your room.' Don't shame.
- **I found my child watching porn.** Stay calm. Explain porn is not real life, shows unrealistic and sometimes harmful behaviour, and isn't meant for children. Ask how they found it; set filters; keep talking. If an adult showed it to them, that's abuse — contact 1098.
- **My child used a swear word.** Ask what they think it means; explain briefly why it's hurtful or rude; set family expectations without big drama.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body: Trusted people first: a doctor, counsellor, or someone you trust. **Help in India:** 112 (any emergency) · 1098 (Childline, for anyone under 18) · 14416 (Tele-MANAS, free 24×7 mental-health support). Also: 1930 (cybercrime), 181 (women's helpline), 1097 (HIV/AIDS, NACO). This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: My toddler touches their genitals. Should I stop it?
items.a: It's common and normal self-exploration. Calmly teach privacy: 'That's something we do in private, like in your room.' Don't shame.

items.q: I found my child watching porn.
items.a: Stay calm. Explain porn is not real life, shows unrealistic and sometimes harmful behaviour, and isn't meant for children. Ask how they found it; set filters; keep talking. If an adult showed it to them, that's abuse — contact 1098.

items.q: My child used a swear word.
items.a: Ask what they think it means; explain briefly why it's hurtful or rude; set family expectations without big drama.

items.q: My child asked about a news story on rape.
items.a: Use simple words: 'Someone forced another person to do something sexual without their permission. That's a crime and it's never the victim's fault.' Reassure them about safety.

quiz.why: Toddlers exploring their genitals is normal curiosity. Calmly teach privacy ('that's for private time'), without shaming.
Shame drives secrecy: children who feel ashamed hide things, which increases risk. Openness and calm replies keep them safe.
An adult showing a child pornography is child sexual abuse. Stay calm, support the child, and contact Childline 1098 or the police.
Respond calmly and listen. An angry, shocked reaction can make the child stop telling you things.

lessons.title: Puberty, periods and wet dreams: preparing your child

scenes.text: Mrs. Rao packs a small period kit in her 9-year-old's bag — and also explains periods to her 10-year-old son.
'Why tell him?' her husband asks.
'So he understands, doesn't tease, and knows his own changes too.'

steps.title: Timing
steps.body: Talk **before** changes start: around 8–9 for periods and breast changes; 9–10 for wet dreams and erections. Tell **all** children about **all** genders' puberty.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **How do I explain periods to my daughter?** Simply: 'Every month the uterus builds a soft lining in case of a baby; when there isn't one, it leaves as a little blood. It's healthy.' Show products; pack a kit.
- **How do I talk to my son about wet dreams?** 'As you grow, your body may release semen in your sleep. It's normal, not bedwetting, and doesn't make you weak.'
- **Should fathers talk about periods?** Yes. Every parent can; it normalises the topic.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body: Trusted people first: a doctor, counsellor, or someone you trust. **Help in India:** 112 (any emergency) · 1098 (Childline, for anyone under 18) · 14416 (Tele-MANAS, free 24×7 mental-health support). Also: 1930 (cybercrime), 181 (women's helpline), 1097 (HIV/AIDS, NACO). This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: How do I explain periods to my daughter?
items.a: Simply: 'Every month the uterus builds a soft lining in case of a baby; when there isn't one, it leaves as a little blood. It's healthy.' Show products; pack a kit.

items.q: How do I talk to my son about wet dreams?
items.a: 'As you grow, your body may release semen in your sleep. It's normal, not bedwetting, and doesn't make you weak.'

items.q: Should fathers talk about periods?
items.a: Yes. Every parent can; it normalises the topic.

items.q: My child started puberty at 8 — is that early?
items.a: Signs before 8 (girls) or 9 (boys) warrant a doctor's check.

quiz.why: Talk about periods before the body changes, around age 8–9, so a girl is not frightened when they start. Waiting until after is too late.
Yes, teach boys about periods too. It builds respect and understanding, and helps them support others.
No. Wet dreams do not make boys weak. They are normal in puberty, and the myth causes needless worry.
Breast development or other puberty signs before age 8 in girls are early puberty, and a doctor should check it to find the cause and advise.

lessons.title: Abuse warning signs, coming out, and keeping teens talking

scenes.text: Nine-year-old Aarav suddenly refuses to go to tuition and has nightmares.
His mother gently asks, listens, and he discloses inappropriate touching by the tutor.
She believes him, contacts 1098 and the police; Aarav gets counselling.

steps.title: Possible warning signs of abuse
steps.body: Sudden fear of a person/place · sleep problems or bed-wetting returning · sexual knowledge or behaviour unusual for age · unexplained injuries or genital pain · withdrawal, anger, falling grades · secret gifts or phone. None proves abuse alone — but they're reasons to gently ask.

steps.title: If a child discloses
steps.body: Stay calm · believe · 'It's not your fault; you did the right thing telling me' · don't interrogate or confront the abuser in front of the child · write down what they said · get help: **1098**, police (POCSO requires reporting), doctor, counsellor.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **My teen came out as gay. How do I respond?** Thank them for trusting you; say you love them. You can have questions — seek reliable information and support. Acceptance strongly protects teens' mental health.
- **My teen won't talk to me anymore.** Keep low-pressure time together (car rides, cooking). Listen more than lecture. Let them know your door is open.
- **How do I talk to my teen about consent and the law?** Use examples from films or news; explain FRIES and that 18 is the legal age of consent; talk about sexting laws.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: My teen came out as gay. How do I respond?
items.a: Thank them for trusting you; say you love them. You can have questions — seek reliable information and support. Acceptance strongly protects teens' mental health.

items.q: My teen won't talk to me anymore.
items.a: Keep low-pressure time together (car rides, cooking). Listen more than lecture. Let them know your door is open.

items.q: How do I talk to my teen about consent and the law?
items.a: Use examples from films or news; explain FRIES and that 18 is the legal age of consent; talk about sexting laws.

items.q: Should I read my teen's messages?
items.a: Respect privacy while setting clear safety rules. If you have a specific safety concern, talk openly first; seek help if needed.

quiz.q: If a child discloses abuse, first:
quiz.why: If a child tells you about abuse, stay calm and believe them. Reassure them it is not their fault, and don't interrogate or punish.
Acceptance and support from family protect the mental health of an LGBTQ+ teen. Rejection raises the risk of depression and self-harm.
Under the POCSO Act, anyone who knows of a sexual offence against a child must report it. Hiding it or settling it within the family is not allowed.

quiz.q: Sudden fear of a tutor may be…
quiz.why: A sudden fear of a tutor or another adult may be a warning sign. It is a reason to ask gently and listen, not to dismiss it as laziness.

questions.q: First principle for awkward questions:
questions.why: Staying calm is the first principle. It shows the child that questions are welcome.

questions.q: Childline:
questions.why: Childline is 1098. 1930 is cybercrime, and 14416 is Tele-MANAS.

questions.q: Talks should be…
questions.why: Talks should be ongoing, with many small conversations as the child grows, not a single talk.

questions.q: Toddler touching genitals:
questions.why: A toddler touching their genitals is normal exploration. Teach privacy calmly. It is not always a sign of abuse, and punishing it can cause shame.

questions.q: Teach boys about periods?
questions.why: Yes, boys should be taught about periods. This helps them understand and respect girls, and be supportive.

questions.q: A child discloses abuse — say:
questions.why: When a child discloses abuse, say 'It's not your fault' and believe them. Blame or silence can make it worse.

questions.q: Does sexuality education hasten sexual activity?
questions.why: Evidence says sexuality education does not hasten sexual activity. It tends to delay it and make it safer.

questions.q: Found child watching porn — best first response?
questions.why: If you find a child watching porn, respond calmly. Talk about what they saw, use filters, and keep the conversation going. Shouting or silent bans push the behaviour into secrecy.

questions.q: Puberty in a girl at 7 →
questions.why: Puberty signs at age 7 in a girl are early puberty, and a doctor should check her. It is not normal at that age, and ignoring it can miss a treatable cause.

questions.q: Warning sign of abuse:
questions.why: Sexual knowledge or behaviour that is unusual for the child's age is a warning sign of possible abuse. It is a reason to ask gently and seek help.

questions.q: Teen comes out — protective response:
questions.why: When a teen comes out, love and acceptance are protective for their mental health. Denial or punishment raises the risk of harm.

questions.q: If a child discloses, you should…
options: write down what they said and get help
confront the abuser in front of the child
questions.why: If a child discloses abuse, write down (in their words) what they said and get help, such as Childline 1098 or the police. Keeping it in the family or confronting the abuser in front of the child can cause harm.

questions.q: Case: A 10-year-old asks about rape after the news. Best?
options: Simple, accurate explanation; never the victim's fault; reassure
questions.why: Give a simple, accurate explanation, reassure the child, and say it is never the victim's fault. Details that are too graphic frighten a 10-year-old, and refusing teaches them not to ask.

questions.q: Why avoid shaming children's questions?
options: Shame drives secrecy and increases risk
questions.why: Shaming a child's question drives secrecy, so they stop asking and may seek wrong or unsafe sources. That increases risk.

questions.q: Which is most protective for children?
options: Correct body names, open talk, trusted adults, consent at home
questions.why: Protection comes from correct body names, open talk, trusted adults and consent at home. Silence and nicknames leave children without the words to tell.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Myth-busting quiz for every age
courses.summary: A mixed review of the most-asked awkward questions across all age bands: myths vs facts, safety numbers, laws and where to get help — with a 20-question mock.
outcomes: Learners can bust the most common myths about bodies, sex and mental health
Learners can recall helplines and key laws
Learners can choose the right help for a question
courses.guardianNote: Mixed-age myth-busting revision of awkward questions on bodies, sex, safety and mental health; non-explicit, accurate and help-focused.

lessons.title: Top 20 myths, busted

scenes.text: A youth club holds 'Myth Night'. Each team reads a myth; the others vote fact or myth.
Most people get at least five wrong.
By the end, everyone has a shortlist to share at home.

steps.title: Ten big myths
steps.body: 1. Semen loss causes weakness. 2. Periods make you impure. 3. Virginity can be tested. 4. You can't get pregnant the first time. 5. EC is an abortion pill. 6. HIV spreads through food or mosquitoes. 7. Depression is laziness. 8. Asking about suicide gives people ideas. 9. Orientation can be 'cured'. 10. Masturbation causes infertility. — **All myths.**

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **Myth: semen loss weakens you?** Myth — no evidence.
- **Myth: you can't get pregnant during your period?** Myth — less likely but possible.
- **Myth: talking about sex makes teens have sex earlier?** Myth — quality sexuality education tends to delay and make it safer.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: Myth: semen loss weakens you?
items.a: Myth — no evidence.

items.q: Myth: you can't get pregnant during your period?
items.a: Myth — less likely but possible.

items.q: Myth: talking about sex makes teens have sex earlier?
items.a: Myth — quality sexuality education tends to delay and make it safer.

items.q: Myth: mental illness is a weakness?
items.a: Myth — it's health, and treatable.

items.q: Myth: only strangers abuse children?
items.a: Myth — most often it's someone known.

items.q: Myth: condoms are 100%?
items.a: Myth — high but not perfect; consistent correct use matters.

quiz.why: The belief that semen loss causes weakness is a myth. Semen is replaced by the body, and there is no harm.
Pregnancy is possible during a period, though the chance is lower, as ovulation timing varies and sperm can live for days.
Most child abuse is by someone the child knows (a relative, neighbour or acquaintance), not a stranger.
Asking someone about suicidal thoughts does not plant the idea. It helps, because they feel heard and can get support.

lessons.title: Which help for which question?

scenes.text: Students build a pocket directory of helplines.
Each number gets a 'when to call' line.
They tape copies inside their diaries.

steps.title: Directory
steps.body: 112 emergency · 1098 Childline · 14416 mental health · 1930 cybercrime · 181 women's helpline · 1097 HIV/AIDS (NACO) · 14446 drug-abuse help · 1800-180-5522 anti-ragging.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **Being blackmailed with a photo?** 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in; 1098 if under 18; tell an adult.
- **Feeling hopeless at night?** 14416 (24×7). 112 if in danger.
- **Questions about HIV testing?** 1097 (NACO) or an ICTC.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body: Trusted adults first: a parent, relative, teacher, school nurse or counsellor. **Help in India:** 112 (any emergency) · 1098 (Childline, for anyone under 18) · 14416 (Tele-MANAS, free 24×7 mental-health support). Also: 1930 (cybercrime), 181 (women's helpline), 1097 (HIV/AIDS, NACO). This is general education, not medical or legal advice.

items.a: 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in; 1098 if under 18; tell an adult.

items.q: Feeling hopeless at night?
Questions about HIV testing?
items.a: 1097 (NACO) or an ICTC.

items.q: Being ragged in hostel?
A child is being harmed?
items.a: 1098; 112 in danger.

quiz.why: The national HIV/AIDS helpline (NACO) is 1097.
The anti-ragging helpline in India is 1800-180-5522.
Tele-MANAS, the 24×7 free mental-health helpline, is 14416.
The drug-abuse (Nasha Mukt Bharat) helpline is 14446.

lessons.title: How to ask anything (and where to look)

scenes.text: Shy Komal finally asks her school nurse a question she'd carried for a year.
The answer takes one minute — and relieves a year of worry.
'Asking is a skill. It gets easier.'

steps.title: Asking scripts
steps.body: 'Can I ask you something private?' · 'I read something online and I'm worried — is it true?' · 'I don't know how to say this, but…'

steps.title: Trusted sources
steps.body: Doctors, nurses, counsellors, WHO, MoHFW, NACO, UNESCO materials, this site. Be wary of forums, rumours and ads promising cures.

steps.title: Key answers in brief
steps.body:
- **What if the adult laughs at me?** That's their problem, not yours. Ask another trusted adult.
- **Can I ask anonymously?** Many schools have question boxes; helplines like 14416 and 1098 are confidential.
- **Is the internet reliable for health questions?** Some sites are; prefer official health sources and check with a professional.

activity.prompt: Questions people don't ask out loud

items.q: What if the adult laughs at me?
items.a: That's their problem, not yours. Ask another trusted adult.

items.q: Can I ask anonymously?
items.a: Many schools have question boxes; helplines like 14416 and 1098 are confidential.

items.q: Is the internet reliable for health questions?
items.a: Some sites are; prefer official health sources and check with a professional.

quiz.q: If an adult laughs at your question:
quiz.why: If an adult laughs at your question, don't feel ashamed. Ask another trusted adult or a reliable source. Your question is valid.
Reliable sources are official health bodies such as WHO, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and NACO. Ads and rumours are not.
Anonymous options like question boxes and helplines let you ask without giving your name. Posting publicly is not private.

questions.q: Semen-loss weakness:
questions.why: Semen-loss weakness is a myth. The body makes semen all the time and nothing is lost.

questions.q: Childline:
questions.why: Childline is 1098, the free helpline for children.

questions.q: Cybercrime helpline:
questions.why: The cybercrime helpline is 1930.

questions.q: Tele-MANAS:
questions.why: Tele-MANAS is 14416. 14446 is the drug-abuse helpline, and 1097 is for HIV/AIDS.

questions.q: Periods make you impure:
questions.why: The idea that periods make you impure is a myth. A period is a natural body process and does not make anyone unclean.

questions.q: EC pill is an abortion pill:
questions.why: The emergency contraception pill is not an abortion pill. It works before pregnancy starts, by delaying ovulation.

questions.q: HIV through mosquitoes:
questions.why: HIV does not spread through mosquito bites. It spreads through blood, certain body fluids and from mother to child. The idea is a myth.

questions.q: Women's helpline:
questions.why: The women's helpline in India is 181. 1098 is Childline, and 1097 is for HIV/AIDS.

questions.q: Virginity tests are…
questions.why: Virginity tests have no medical meaning. They are unreliable and violate a person's dignity.

questions.q: Depression is laziness:
questions.why: Depression is a medical condition, not laziness. It is treatable with therapy and sometimes medicine.

questions.q: Asking about suicide gives ideas:
questions.why: Asking about suicide does not give someone the idea. It is a myth, and asking can help the person feel supported.

questions.q: Age of consent in India:
questions.why: The age of consent in India is 18.

questions.q: Case: Teen blackmailed with a photo. Best first numbers?
questions.why: If a teen is being blackmailed with a photo, call the cybercrime helpline 1930 and Childline 1098. Save the evidence and tell a trusted adult. Do not pay.

questions.q: Case: Fresher ragged in hostel. Number?
questions.why: The anti-ragging helpline is 1800-180-5522. 181 is the women's helpline, and 1097 is for HIV/AIDS.

questions.q: Pregnancy the first time:
questions.why: Pregnancy is possible the first time someone has sex. It does not depend on marriage.

questions.q: Masturbation causes infertility:
questions.why: Masturbation does not cause infertility. It is a myth.

questions.q: Which is TRUE?
options: Most child abuse is by someone the child knows
questions.why: Most child abuse is by someone the child knows. It is not rare, and children rarely lie about abuse.

questions.q: Which is TRUE about sexuality education?
options: It tends to delay first sex and make it safer
questions.why: Evidence shows that sexuality education tends to delay first sex and make it safer. It does not hasten sex, and it is not illegal.

questions.q: Which statement is FALSE?
questions.why: Sexual orientation cannot be 'cured', as it is not an illness. The HPV vaccine does prevent cervical cancer, PEP must start within 72 hours, and condoms reduce STI risk.

questions.q: Case: Friend says 'I want to disappear' at midnight. Best?
options: Stay with them, tell an adult, 14416/112
questions.why: If a friend says they want to disappear, stay with them, take it seriously, tell an adult, and call Tele-MANAS (14416), or 112 in an emergency.

well-mind.title: Mind matters: stress, emotions & mental health
well-mind.description: Stress and exam anxiety skills, anxiety and depression awareness, self-harm and suicide safety, and substance-use awareness — evidence-based, kind and help-focused.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Emotions, stress & a coping toolkit
courses.summary: What emotions are for, how stress works in body and brain, good stress vs harmful stress, and a tested toolkit: breathing, grounding, movement, sleep, talking, problem-solving and self-kindness.
outcomes: Learners can name emotions and explain their purpose
Learners can describe the stress response and its body signs
Learners can tell helpful from harmful stress
Learners can use at least five evidence-based coping strategies
Learners can identify when stress needs professional help
courses.guardianNote: General mental-health education about stress and coping for teenagers; no clinical diagnosis. It teaches practical coping skills and when and where to seek help (trusted adults, school counsellor, Tele-MANAS 14416).

lessons.title: Emotions: signals, not enemies

scenes.text: Rehan reads a message in his group: friends made plans without him.
He types an angry reply… then pauses.
He names it: 'I feel left out and hurt.' He messages one friend privately instead. It turns out it was a mix-up.

steps.title: What emotions do
steps.body: Emotions are fast body-and-brain signals that tell us something matters: **fear** (danger), **anger** (unfairness or a boundary crossed), **sadness** (loss), **joy** (something good), **disgust** (something harmful), **surprise**. All emotions are normal; what we **do** with them is a choice.

steps.title: Name it to tame it
steps.body: Putting feelings into words ('I feel nervous', 'I feel disappointed') can calm the brain's alarm system. Try being precise: not just 'bad' but *jealous, embarrassed, lonely, overwhelmed*.

steps.title: Solved example: the STOP skill
steps.body:
**S**top — pause before reacting.
**T**ake a breath — one slow breath.
**O**bserve — what am I feeling, thinking, sensing?
**P**roceed — choose a response that fits your values.

Rehan: Stop (doesn't send), Breath, Observe ('hurt, left out; thinking they don't like me'), Proceed (asks privately).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Boys don't cry' / 'Good girls don't get angry' — everyone has every emotion.
- Bottling up feelings until they burst.
- Believing every thought ('they hate me') is a fact.

activity.prompt: Match the emotion to the message it often carries
pairs: Something feels unfair or a boundary was crossed
I may have acted against my values

quiz.why: Emotions are signals, giving information about what matters to us or what is going on around us. They are not weaknesses.
Naming a feeling precisely (like 'disappointed' instead of just 'bad') helps calm the brain's alarm centre. This is called affect labelling.
In the STOP skill: Stop, Take a breath, Observe what is happening in you and around you, then Proceed mindfully. So 'O' stands for Observe.
'Boys don't cry' is a harmful myth. Crying is a natural human response, and holding feelings in can be bad for health.
Thoughts are not always facts. They can be wrong or one-sided, so it helps to check the evidence.

lessons.title: How stress works in body and brain

scenes.text: At the starting line Aisha's heart pounds, hands shake, stomach churns.
The gun fires and she runs her best time ever.
Her coach: 'That was stress helping you. The trick is not letting it stay switched on all day.'

steps.title: The stress response
steps.body: When the brain senses a threat (a tiger — or an exam), the **amygdala** raises the alarm; the **hypothalamus** activates the **sympathetic nervous system** and the **adrenal glands**: **adrenaline** (fast) and **cortisol** (slower). Heart rate and breathing rise, muscles tense, digestion slows, attention narrows — 'fight, flight or freeze'. Afterwards, the **parasympathetic** system ('rest and digest') calms things down.

steps.title: Helpful vs harmful stress
steps.body: Short, manageable stress (a match, a presentation) can sharpen performance. Long-lasting, overwhelming stress (**chronic stress**) — constant pressure, conflict at home, bullying — can disturb sleep, appetite, immunity, concentration and mood. A classic idea (the **Yerkes–Dodson** curve) says performance rises with arousal up to a point, then falls.

steps.title: Solved example: body signs
steps.body:
List of signs: racing heart, sweaty palms, headache, tight shoulders, stomach ache, trouble sleeping, irritability, forgetting things, biting nails.
- Physical: heart, palms, headache, shoulders, stomach.
- Mental/behaviour: sleep, irritability, forgetting, nail-biting.
**Takeaway:** stress shows up in the body, not just the mind.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trying to remove all stress — impossible and unnecessary.
- Ignoring long-term stress signs.
- Physical symptoms can also have medical causes — a doctor can check if they persist.

activity.label: How stressed do you feel today?

bands.text: Calm zone — good time to plan and learn.
Alert zone — stress may be helping you focus; take short breaks.
Overload zone — use a coping tool now: breathe, move, talk.
Red zone — pause, get support from someone you trust today. If you feel unsafe, call 14416 or 112.

quiz.why: Adrenaline is the fast stress hormone, released by the adrenal glands. It raises heart rate for quick action.
The 'rest and digest' system is the parasympathetic nervous system, which calms the body after stress.
Long-lasting (chronic) stress can affect many systems of the body, including sleep, immunity and mood.

options: moderate arousal helps, too much hurts
