quiz.why: The Yerkes–Dodson idea is that moderate arousal helps performance, but too much hurts it. So some stress can be useful, but too much is not.
The amygdala is the brain's alarm centre, which detects threats and triggers fear.

lessons.title: The coping toolkit: body-based skills

scenes.text: Kiran feels panicky in a crowded bus.
She counts: in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4.
After six rounds her shoulders drop. She notices 5 things she can see out the window.

steps.title: Slow breathing
steps.body: Breathing out slowly (longer out-breath than in-breath) activates the calming parasympathetic system. Try **box breathing (4-4-4-4)** or **4-in, 6-out**. 1–3 minutes is enough to feel a change.

steps.title: Grounding: 5-4-3-2-1
steps.body: Name **5** things you see, **4** you can touch, **3** you hear, **2** you smell, **1** you taste. It brings the mind back to the present.

steps.title: Move, sleep, eat, connect
steps.body:
- **Movement**: a 10-minute walk or dance reduces stress hormones and lifts mood.
- **Sleep**: 8–10 h for teens.
- **Regular meals**, water; limit caffeine.
- **Connection**: time with people who feel safe; pets; nature.
- **Muscle relaxation**: tense a muscle group for 5 s, release for 10 s, move up the body.

steps.title: Solved example: build a 10-minute reset
steps.body:
Feeling overwhelmed after school:
1. 2 min box breathing.
2. 5 min walk or stretching.
3. 1 min grounding.
4. 2 min writing: 'What's one small next step?'
Total = 10 minutes.

steps.title: Unhelpful 'coping'
steps.body: Scrolling for hours, energy drinks, skipping meals, smoking/vaping, alcohol, isolating, hurting yourself — they may give quick relief but make stress worse later. If you're using any of these, you deserve support, not blame.

activity.label: Box breathing: in 4 · hold 4 · out 4 · hold 4

quiz.why: Longer out-breaths activate the parasympathetic (calming) system, which slows the heart rate and eases stress.
5-4-3-2-1 is a grounding skill. You name 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear, 2 you smell and 1 you taste, to bring attention to the present.

quiz.q: Which is an unhelpful coping habit?
quiz.why: Hours of scrolling is an avoidant habit. It gives quick relief but doesn't solve the problem and can worsen sleep and mood. Talking, sleep and walks are helpful.
In progressive muscle relaxation, you tense a muscle group for a few seconds and then release it, moving through the body. This lowers physical tension.
Box breathing is 4-4-4-4: breathe in for 4, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4.

lessons.title: Thinking skills: problem-solving and self-talk

scenes.text: Harsh gets a low mark on his science project.
Thought: 'I'm useless. I'll fail everything.'
His counsellor helps him challenge it: 'One low mark. I did well in maths. I can ask what went wrong.'

steps.title: Thinking traps
steps.body:
- **All-or-nothing**: 'If it's not perfect, it's a failure.'
- **Catastrophising**: 'This will ruin my life.'
- **Mind-reading**: 'They think I'm stupid.'
- **Overgeneralising**: 'I always mess up.'
- **Labelling**: 'I'm a loser.'
These are common in everyone, especially under stress.

steps.title: Solved example: the thought check
steps.body:
Thought: 'I'll fail everything.'
1. Evidence for? One low project mark.
2. Evidence against? Passed last 5 tests; teacher said my research was good.
3. Balanced thought: 'I didn't do well on this; I can learn what to fix.'
4. Action: ask the teacher for feedback this week.

steps.title: Solved example: problem-solving steps
steps.body:
Problem: too much homework and tuition, no time to rest.
1. Define: 'I have 4 hours of work and 2 hours free.'
2. Brainstorm: talk to parents about tuition; plan; drop one activity; ask teacher about deadline.
3. Choose: talk to parents + plan.
4. Try it for a week.
5. Review and adjust.

steps.title: Self-compassion
steps.body: Talk to yourself like you would to a good friend. 'This is hard. Lots of people struggle with this. What would help right now?' Self-compassion is linked to more resilience, not laziness.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forcing 'positive thinking' that you don't believe — aim for **balanced**, not fake-happy.
- Trying to solve everything at once.

activity.prompt: Which thinking trap is this?

items.text: If I fumble this speech my life is over
They're laughing — must be at me
Either I'm the best or I'm nothing
One mistake and I'll be expelled

quiz.q: 'I'm a loser' is an example of…
quiz.why: 'I'm a loser' is labelling: putting a harsh, fixed label on yourself. It is one of the common thinking traps.
The first step of problem-solving is to define the problem clearly. Then you brainstorm, choose, try and review.
A balanced thought is realistic and fair. It is not overly negative, and it is not a fake positive either.

options: treating yourself like a good friend
quiz.why: Self-compassion means treating yourself with the kindness you would show a good friend. It is not weakness or selfishness.
'They think I'm stupid' with no evidence is mind-reading, a thinking trap where we assume we know what others think.

lessons.title: When stress is too much: getting support

scenes.text: Neha, a topper, stops eating lunch and cries in the washroom most days.
A classmate notices and walks with her to the school counsellor.
With weekly sessions and a talk with her parents about expectations, things slowly get lighter.

steps.title: Signs you need more help
steps.body: Stress or low mood most days for **2+ weeks**; not sleeping or sleeping too much; can't concentrate; avoiding school or friends; panic attacks; using substances to cope; thoughts of hurting yourself or not wanting to live.

steps.title: Who can help
steps.body: Trusted family member · teacher or school counsellor · family doctor · psychologist (talk therapy) · psychiatrist (a medical doctor who can also prescribe) · **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7, many Indian languages) · **112** for emergencies · **1098** Childline for under-18s.

steps.title: Solved example: how to start the conversation
steps.body: Script: 'Can I talk to you about something? I've been feeling really stressed/low for a few weeks. It's affecting my sleep and studies. I don't know what to do.' If the first person doesn't listen well, **try another**.

steps.title: Before a counselling visit
steps.body: Note what you've noticed (sleep, mood, worries), when it started, and what you want help with. Counselling is confidential — except when someone's safety is at risk.

activity.prompt: Write the script you would use to ask an adult for help, and who you'd ask first.
activity.hint: 'I've been feeling ___ for ___. It's affecting ___. Can you help me figure out what to do?'

quiz.q: Low mood most days for 2+ weeks means…
quiz.why: Low mood on most days for 2 weeks or more is a sign to get support. Talk to a trusted adult, counsellor or doctor. Ignoring it can make it worse.

options: a medical doctor for mental health
quiz.why: A psychiatrist is a medical doctor who specialises in mental health, and can diagnose and prescribe medicines.
Tele-MANAS is India's free 24×7 mental-health helpline. The number is 14416.

quiz.q: If the first adult doesn't listen…
quiz.why: If the first adult doesn't listen, try another trusted adult. Keep trying until someone hears you.
Counselling is confidential, except when safety is at risk, for example if someone may harm themselves or be harmed. Then the counsellor may need to involve others.

questions.q: Emotions are…
questions.why: Emotions are signals, not dangers or weaknesses. They tell us about our needs and situation.

questions.q: Adrenaline is released by…
questions.why: Adrenaline is released by the adrenal glands, which sit above the kidneys.

questions.q: Tele-MANAS number:
questions.why: Tele-MANAS is 14416. 1098 is Childline, 100 is police and 911 is not an Indian number.

questions.q: Box breathing count:
questions.why: Box breathing uses equal counts: in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4.

questions.q: Which is a thinking trap?
questions.why: Catastrophising, imagining the worst outcome, is a thinking trap. Grounding, problem-solving and sleep are helpful.

questions.q: A healthy coping strategy:
questions.why: A short walk is a healthy way to cope, since movement lowers stress. Isolation, vaping and energy drinks make problems worse.

questions.q: Assertion: Some stress improves performance. Reason: Moderate arousal sharpens attention.
questions.why: Both are true. Moderate arousal sharpens attention and gives energy, so some stress improves performance. Too much hurts it. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: The calming nervous system:
questions.why: The calming part of the nervous system is the parasympathetic system ('rest and digest'). The sympathetic system is for fight or flight.

questions.q: 'I failed one test so I'll fail life' is…
questions.why: 'I failed one test so I'll fail at life' is catastrophising and overgeneralising: one event is stretched into a total conclusion.

questions.q: Case: Arjun's heart races and palms sweat before a debate. What's happening?
questions.why: A racing heart and sweaty palms before a debate come from adrenaline, part of the normal stress response. They are not a sign of disease.

questions.q: Which balanced thought fits 'Nobody likes me' after one friend cancelled?
options: 'One friend cancelled; others texted today; I'll ask what happened.'
questions.why: A balanced thought uses evidence and is fair: 'One friend cancelled; others texted today; I'll ask what happened.' The others are all-or-nothing and catastrophic.

questions.q: Why are scrolling marathons poor coping?
options: Quick relief but worse sleep and mood later
questions.why: Long scrolling gives quick relief but avoids the problem. It worsens sleep and mood later, so it does not build coping skills.

questions.q: Order the problem-solving steps:
questions.why: The steps of problem-solving in order are: define the problem, brainstorm solutions, choose one, try it and review how it went.

questions.q: Case: For three weeks Meera can't sleep, cries daily and avoids friends. Best step?
options: Talk to a trusted adult/counsellor or 14416 now
questions.why: Not sleeping, crying daily and avoiding friends for three weeks is a sign that support is needed. She should talk to a trusted adult or counsellor, or call 14416, now. It is treatable, and waiting makes it harder.

questions.q: Which shows self-compassion?
options: 'This is hard; many people struggle; what would help?'
questions.why: Self-compassion sounds like 'This is hard; many people struggle; what would help?'. It recognises pain and responds kindly. 'I'm pathetic' and 'I must be perfect' are harsh.

questions.q: Chronic stress harms the body partly because…
options: cortisol stays high, affecting sleep, immunity and mood
questions.why: In chronic stress, cortisol stays high for long. This can affect sleep, the immune system and mood.

questions.q: Case: A friend says they've been using vaping to cope with stress and feel ashamed. Best response?
options: Listen without blame, suggest healthier tools and support from an adult
questions.why: Listen without blame, offer healthier ways to cope and encourage them to speak to an adult. Shaming or joining in does not help, and vaping is harmful.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Exam stress, study smarts & coping with results
courses.summary: Beat exam anxiety with evidence-based study methods (active recall, spacing, interleaving), a realistic timetable, test-day calm, handling family and peer pressure, and coping with results — good, bad or unexpected.
outcomes: Learners can use active recall, spaced practice and interleaving
Learners can build a realistic study timetable with breaks and sleep
Learners can manage test-day anxiety with practical skills
Learners can handle pressure from family, coaching and comparison
Learners can cope with disappointing results and plan next steps
courses.guardianNote: Practical study, planning and exam-anxiety skills for students facing board, entrance and school exams, plus coping with results and family pressure. Includes supportive help-seeking (Tele-MANAS 14416) and no clinical diagnosis.

lessons.title: Study methods that actually work

scenes.text: Aryan highlights the whole chapter in yellow. It looks productive.
In the test he remembers almost nothing.
His sister shows him flashcards and self-testing. Next test: much better.

steps.title: What research supports
steps.body:
- **Active recall (retrieval practice)**: test yourself — close the book and write what you remember, answer questions, use flashcards. Stronger than re-reading.
- **Spaced repetition**: review after 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks — instead of cramming.
- **Interleaving**: mix problem types (e.g. different maths chapters) in one session.
- **Elaboration**: explain *why* and *how* — teach it to a friend or an imaginary student.
- **Dual coding**: combine words with diagrams.

steps.title: Solved example: spacing schedule
steps.body:
Learn the 'Heart' chapter on Monday 1st.
- Review 1: Tuesday 2nd (1 day)
- Review 2: Thursday 4th (3 days)
- Review 3: Monday 8th (1 week)
- Review 4: Monday 22nd (2 weeks)
Each review = self-test first, then check notes for gaps.

steps.title: Solved example: Pomodoro maths
steps.body:
Pomodoro = 25 min focus + 5 min break; after 4 rounds, a 15–30 min break.
In 2 hours (120 min): 4 × (25+5) = 120 → **100 minutes of focused work** and 20 minutes of breaks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Re-reading and highlighting as the main method (feels easy, learns little).
- Studying with the phone next to you — even a silent phone in view can reduce focus. Put it in another room.
- Skipping past papers.

activity.prompt: Strong or weak study method?

quiz.why: Active recall means testing yourself from memory, which strengthens learning. Re-reading and highlighting are less effective.
Spaced practice means reviewing material over increasing gaps of time. It is better for long-term memory than cramming once.
Interleaving means mixing different problem types or topics in one session. It improves learning compared with practising one type in a block.

quiz.q: 3 Pomodoros give how many focus minutes?
quiz.why: One Pomodoro is 25 minutes of focus. Three Pomodoros are 3 × 25 = 75 minutes.

quiz.q: Best place for your phone while studying:
quiz.why: Keep your phone in another room while studying. Even a phone on the desk distracts you.

lessons.title: A realistic timetable (with sleep and rest)

scenes.text: Priya makes a plan to study 16 hours a day for board exams.
By day 3 she's exhausted and has a headache.
Her teacher helps her make a 7-hour plan with breaks, exercise and 8.5 hours of sleep. She sticks to it for months.

steps.title: Timetable rules
steps.body:
1. Start with fixed things: school, meals, **sleep (8–10 h for teens)**, travel.
2. Put the hardest subject in your best-energy time.
3. Blocks of 25–50 min with short breaks.
4. Daily: 30–60 min of movement and some downtime.
5. One lighter half-day per week.
6. Weekly review: what worked? adjust.

steps.title: Solved example: count real study time
steps.body:
After-school window: 4:30–9:30 pm = 5 h.
- Snack/rest 30 min, exercise 30 min, dinner 45 min → 1 h 45 min.
- Left: 5 h − 1 h 45 = **3 h 15 min** of study.
- At 50/10 blocks: about 3 blocks of 50 min = 2 h 30 min focused study + breaks. Realistic and sustainable.

steps.title: Solved example: the 6-week countdown
steps.body: Weeks 6–4: finish syllabus gaps + spaced reviews. Weeks 3–2: past papers under timed conditions, mark them, fix weak topics. Final week: light revision, formula sheets, sleep normal hours, no new topics the night before.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Planning perfect 14-hour days you can't keep.
- Cutting sleep — it's when memory consolidates.
- Not leaving buffer time for surprises.

activity.prompt: You have 4 hours free after school. You need 30 min for a snack/rest and 30 min for exercise. How many minutes are left for study?

quiz.q: First things to put in a timetable:
quiz.why: In a timetable, first block in the fixed things: sleep, meals and school. Then fit study around them.
Teenagers need 8–10 hours of sleep even during exams, as sleep helps memory and mood.
Put the hardest subject in your best-energy time, when you are most alert.
The night before an exam, do a light review and sleep normally. Learning new chapters all night tires you and hurts recall.
A weekly review shows what is working, so you can adjust the plan.

lessons.title: Test-day anxiety: calm under pressure

scenes.text: Zara opens the maths paper and her mind goes blank.
She puts the pen down, breathes out slowly three times and reads question 1 again.
She starts with a question she knows. By question 4, her memory is back.

steps.title: Why we 'blank'
steps.body: High stress narrows attention and can block recall from working memory. It's temporary. Calming the body helps the thinking brain come back online.

steps.title: Before and during the exam
steps.body:
- **Night before**: pack the kit (admit card, pens, ID, water, watch), sleep normal hours.
- **Morning**: breakfast you're used to, arrive early, avoid last-minute panic chats outside the hall.
- **In the hall**: 3 slow breaths; read all instructions; spend 5–10 min reading the paper; start with a question you can do; watch the clock (marks ÷ total time); if stuck, mark and move on.
- **Reframe**: 'My heart is racing because I care and my body is getting ready.' Research suggests reappraising anxiety as energy can help performance.

steps.title: Solved example: time per mark
steps.body:
Paper: 80 marks, 180 minutes, 15 min reading time.
- Writing time = 180 − 15 = 165 min.
- Time per mark = 165 ÷ 80 ≈ **2 min per mark**.
- A 5-mark question ≈ 10 min; leave ~10 min to check.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Discussing answers right before the exam — increases panic.
- Getting stuck on one hard question for 20 minutes.
- Comparing how fast others are writing.

activity.prompt: Order your first 10 minutes in the exam hall
items: Skim the whole paper and mark questions you know
Note the time plan (minutes per mark)
Start with a question you're confident about

options: pause, breathe, start an easier question
quiz.why: If your mind goes blank, pause, take a slow breath, and start an easier question. The answer often comes back once you relax.
Time per mark = 180 minutes ÷ 90 marks = 2 minutes per mark.

options: seeing body arousal as energy for performance
quiz.why: Reframing anxiety means seeing the body's arousal (fast heartbeat, butterflies) as energy that helps performance, rather than as a sign of failure.

quiz.q: Stuck on a question for long:
options: mark it, move on, return later
quiz.why: If you are stuck on a question, mark it, move on and return later. This saves time, and your mind may solve it in the background.
Right before the exam, avoid discussions of panic and answers, as they raise anxiety. A pen, breathing and water are useful.

lessons.title: Pressure from parents, coaching and comparison

scenes.text: At a family function an uncle asks Arnav his JEE rank — and compares him with a cousin.
Arnav feels small and angry.
Later he tells his parents calmly how the comparisons feel. His mother says, 'We'll stop. We're proud of your effort.'

steps.title: Why pressure builds
steps.body: Parents often worry about the future and show it as pressure. Coaching culture, rankings and social media 'topper' posts add comparison. Your worth is **not** your rank or marks. Many routes lead to good careers and lives — there are many colleges, courses, skills and second attempts.

steps.title: Solved example: the 'I-statement' conversation
steps.body:
Formula: **I feel ___ when ___ because ___. Could we ___?**
'I feel anxious when my marks are compared with my cousin's, because it makes me feel I'm never enough. Could we talk about my effort and plan instead?'
Pick a calm time, not right after a fight.

steps.title: Handle comparison
steps.body:
- Compare yourself with **your past self** (progress), not others' highlight reels.
- Mute 'topper' accounts during exam months.
- Have a 'why': what do you enjoy, what kind of life do you want?
- Talk to a counsellor about career options — streams and careers are wider than a few famous ones.

steps.title: When pressure turns dangerous
steps.body: If you feel hopeless, trapped, or have thoughts of ending your life because of exams or results — **you are not alone and help works**. Talk to someone today. **Tele-MANAS 14416** or **112**. (See Unit 5 for safety planning.)

activity.prompt: Build an I-statement
activity.text: I feel ___ when you compare my marks, because it makes me feel ___. Could we talk about my effort instead?
answers: not good enough|like a failure|worthless|small|never enough|bad|useless

quiz.why: Your worth is not your rank or marks. Results show how you did on one test, not who you are.
An I-statement begins with 'I feel…', so you state your feelings without blaming. 'You always…' sounds like blame.
A healthy comparison is with your past self, which shows your own progress. Comparing with toppers or influencers is not fair.
If you have hopeless thoughts about exams, talk to someone today, such as a trusted adult or Tele-MANAS (14416). Hiding it makes it heavier.

quiz.q: Best time for a hard conversation:
quiz.why: The best time for a hard conversation is a calm moment, when everyone can listen. In the middle of an argument or late at night it goes badly.

lessons.title: Results day and bouncing back

scenes.text: Sameer's board result is 20% lower than his target.
He doesn't want to see anyone.
A week later, with his family and counsellor, he lists options: re-evaluation, a different course, a gap-year plan. 'It's a setback, not the end.'

steps.title: Feelings are normal
steps.body: Disappointment, shame, anger or numbness after results are normal. Give yourself a day or two; then move to options. Celebrate effort even when results disappoint.

steps.title: Solved example: the options map
steps.body:
1. Check: re-evaluation / re-totalling / supplementary or improvement exam options (check your board's official notice and deadlines).
2. Explore: other colleges, courses, diplomas, skill programmes.
3. Plan: if retaking an entrance exam, analyse what went wrong (topics, test strategy, health) and make a new plan.
4. Support: talk to a counsellor and family.

steps.title: Resilience skills
steps.body: Separate **the event** ('I didn't get the rank') from **identity** ('I'm a failure'). Remember past setbacks you came through. Keep sleep, food and movement going. Help a friend — it lifts mood too.

steps.title: Look out for each other
steps.body: Results season is when friends may struggle quietly. If someone goes silent, says 'there's no point' or gives things away, check in and tell an adult. **14416 / 112**.

a.text: Results are out. Yours are lower than hoped. Group chat is full of celebrations.

choices.label: Mute the chat for now and talk to someone you trust
Stay in the chat comparing marks all night

x.text: You feel worse and can't sleep.

choices.label: Put the phone away and talk to a family member

b.text: Next day you feel a bit steadier. What now?

choices.label: Make an options map with a counsellor or parent
Decide your life is ruined

b2.text: A friend reminds you of times you bounced back before.

choices.label: Ask for help to make a plan

end1.text: You have options and support. The result is one chapter, not the whole story.

quiz.why: After disappointing results, first allow yourself to feel the feelings. Then, calmly explore options. Deciding that life is over, or hiding, is not helpful.
Re-evaluation and other options should be checked on the board's official notice, not on social media or rumours.

options: 'I didn't get the rank' ≠ 'I'm a failure'
quiz.why: Separating the event from your identity means 'I didn't get the rank' is not the same as 'I'm a failure'. It protects your confidence.

quiz.q: A friend says 'there's no point' after results:
options: check in and tell an adult
quiz.why: If a friend says 'there's no point' after results, check in with them kindly and tell a trusted adult. Take it seriously, and don't leave them alone with it.
Muting chats full of celebration for a while can protect your mood. It is a healthy boundary, not rude.

questions.q: Active recall is…
questions.why: Active recall is self-testing, trying to remember without looking. It is one of the best ways to study.

questions.q: Teens' sleep in exam season:
questions.why: Teenagers need 8–10 hours of sleep even in exam season, since sleep helps learning and memory.

questions.q: Tele-MANAS:
questions.why: Tele-MANAS, the free 24×7 mental-health helpline, is 14416.

questions.q: Pomodoro is…
questions.why: The Pomodoro technique splits study into 25 minutes of focused work followed by a 5-minute break. Short breaks help you keep your attention fresh.

questions.q: Which is weak study?
questions.why: Highlighting only is a passive, weak study method, as it feels productive but doesn't test memory. Flashcards, explaining aloud and past papers force you to recall.

questions.q: An I-statement example:
questions.why: An I-statement tells how you feel, without blaming: 'I feel stressed when…'. Statements starting with 'You always…' blame and start arguments.

questions.q: Assertion: Spaced practice beats cramming for long-term memory. Reason: Repeated retrieval over time strengthens memory.
questions.why: Both are true. With spaced practice, you retrieve the material again and again over time, and each retrieval strengthens memory. That is why it beats cramming.

questions.q: Mind goes blank in exam — best step?
options: Breathe slowly and start an easier question
questions.why: If your mind goes blank, breathe slowly to calm down and start an easier question. This builds confidence and the answer often returns. Leaving or panicking does not help.

questions.q: Which comparison is healthiest?
questions.why: The healthiest comparison is with your past self, as it shows your own progress. Comparing with toppers, cousins or celebrities is unfair as everyone's path differs.

questions.q: Case: Riya plans 15 hours of study daily and sleeps 4 h. Best advice?
options: Reduce to realistic blocks and keep 8–10 h sleep
questions.why: 15 hours of study with only 4 hours of sleep is not sustainable. Sleep helps memory and mood, so reduce to realistic study blocks and keep 8–10 hours of sleep.

questions.q: 100 marks in 180 min with 20 min reserved for checking: minutes per mark?
questions.why: Time left for writing = 180 − 20 = 160 minutes. 160 ÷ 100 marks = 1.6 minutes per mark.

questions.q: 5 h free; 1 h 30 min for meals/exercise. Study time?
questions.why: Study time = 5 h − 1 h 30 min = 3 h 30 min.

questions.q: A spaced schedule after learning on day 1 might review on days…
questions.why: A spaced schedule uses expanding gaps between reviews: for example on days 2, 4, 8 and 22. Reviewing on the same day or only on day 30 is less effective.

questions.q: Case: Uncle compares your rank publicly. Most constructive response later?
options: Calm I-statement with parents about how comparisons feel
questions.why: Later, in a calm moment, tell your parents using an I-statement ('I feel hurt when my rank is compared in public'). Posting online or yelling doesn't help, and stopping study only hurts you.

questions.q: Case: After results a friend gives away his things and says he won't be around. Best action?
options: Stay with him, tell a trusted adult right away, call 14416/112
questions.why: Giving away belongings and saying he won't be around are warning signs of suicide risk. Stay with him, tell a trusted adult right away, and call 14416 or 112. Never keep it secret or wait.

questions.q: Why is putting the phone in another room better than face-down on the desk?
options: Its presence can still pull attention
questions.why: Even a phone face-down on the desk can pull your attention, since part of the mind stays on it. Putting it in another room removes the temptation.

questions.q: Which reflects interleaving in maths revision?
options: Mixing trigonometry, algebra and geometry problems in one session
questions.why: Interleaving means mixing different types of problems (trigonometry, algebra, geometry) in one session. It trains you to pick the right method and improves long-term learning.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Anxiety, panic & fears: understanding and managing
courses.summary: What anxiety is and when it becomes a disorder, what a panic attack feels like and how to ride it out, phobias and social anxiety, CBT-style tools like exposure ladders and worry time, and when and how to get professional help.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish everyday worry from an anxiety disorder
Learners can describe a panic attack and help themselves or a friend through one
Learners can build a step-by-step exposure ladder for a fear
Learners can use worry time and thought-checking
Learners can describe treatment options and where to get help in India
courses.guardianNote: Awareness of anxiety, panic attacks and phobias for teenagers, with self-help skills based on CBT principles and clear guidance on seeking professional help. General education, not diagnosis or treatment.

lessons.title: Worry vs anxiety disorder

scenes.text: Every Sunday evening Tanmay gets stomach aches and can't sleep, worrying about school.
His doctor finds nothing physically wrong and asks about worries.
He's referred to a counsellor. 'Anxiety is real, common and treatable,' she says.

steps.title: Anxiety is normal — up to a point
steps.body: Anxiety is the feeling of worry, unease or fear about what might happen. It helps us prepare. It becomes an **anxiety disorder** when it is **intense, long-lasting (often months), out of proportion**, and **gets in the way** of daily life — school, friendships, sleep.

steps.title: Common types
steps.body:
- **Generalised anxiety**: worrying about many things most days.
- **Panic disorder**: repeated unexpected panic attacks and fear of more.
- **Social anxiety**: intense fear of being judged or embarrassed.
- **Specific phobias**: fear of dogs, heights, injections, water, darkness, etc.
- **Separation anxiety** (common in younger children).
Related: **OCD** (unwanted repeated thoughts and rituals), **PTSD** (after trauma).

steps.title: Solved example: everyday or disorder?
steps.body:
(a) Nervous the night before a debate → **everyday**.
(b) Avoids all group projects and the canteen for 6 months, fearing judgement; grades drop → **possible social anxiety** → professional assessment.
(c) Fear of big dogs, crosses the road when one passes, otherwise fine → mild **specific fear**; may not need treatment unless it limits life.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Just stop worrying' — anxiety isn't a choice.
- Avoiding everything that causes anxiety — gives short relief, but makes the fear grow.
- Assuming physical symptoms are 'all in the head' — they're real body reactions; a doctor can also rule out other causes.

activity.prompt: Everyday worry or worth checking with a professional?

items.text: Avoiding school for weeks due to fear
Daily worry about everything for months
Nervous meeting new people at a party

quiz.q: Anxiety becomes a disorder when it…
options: is intense, long-lasting and disrupts life
quiz.why: Anxiety becomes a disorder when it is intense, long-lasting and disrupts daily life, such as school, sleep or friendships. Mild, short-term anxiety is normal.

quiz.q: Fear of being judged in social situations:
quiz.why: A fear of being judged or embarrassed in social situations is social anxiety. A phobia of dogs is a specific phobia.
Avoiding what we fear brings relief, but the fear grows over time because the brain never learns that the situation is safe.
Anxiety disorders are common and treatable, usually with therapy such as CBT, and sometimes medicine. They are not a choice or a weakness.

quiz.q: Sunday stomach aches from school worry are…
quiz.why: Stomach aches from school worry are real body reactions. Anxiety causes real physical symptoms (the gut and brain are linked), so they are not faked or imaginary.

lessons.title: Panic attacks: what they are and how to ride the wave

scenes.text: In a packed metro, Divya's heart races, she can't catch her breath, her hands tingle. She thinks she's dying.
An older woman notices, says calmly, 'Breathe out slowly with me,' and stays beside her.
Within ten minutes it eases. Later a doctor confirms her heart is fine — it was a panic attack.

steps.title: What a panic attack is
steps.body: A sudden surge of intense fear that peaks within about **10 minutes**: racing or pounding heart, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness, tingling, shaking, sweating, feeling unreal, fear of losing control or dying. It is **frightening but not dangerous** in itself, and it passes.

steps.title: Ride the wave
steps.body:
1. Name it: 'This is panic. It will pass.'
2. Slow the out-breath (in 4, out 6–8); don't gulp air.
3. Ground: feet on floor, 5-4-3-2-1.
4. Don't fight or flee — let the wave rise and fall.
5. Afterwards, return to what you were doing if possible (prevents avoidance).

steps.title: Solved example: helping a friend
steps.body:
- Stay calm and with them; speak slowly.
- 'You're having a panic attack. You're safe. Breathe out slowly with me.'
- Don't crowd them or say 'calm down'.
- **If chest pain, fainting, or it's their first ever episode with unusual symptoms, or they have heart/asthma conditions → seek medical help / 112.** You can't always tell panic from a medical problem.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Breathing into a paper bag — not recommended (can be unsafe).
- Avoiding all places where an attack happened — leads to shrinking life.
- Assuming it's 'just panic' when symptoms are new and severe — get checked first.

activity.label: Ride the wave: breathe in 4, out slowly for 7

quiz.q: A panic attack usually peaks within…
quiz.why: A panic attack usually peaks within about 10 minutes and then settles, though the person may feel tired after.

options: frightening but not dangerous in themselves
quiz.why: Panic attacks are frightening but not dangerous in themselves. They are not contagious and not always a heart attack.

options: 'You're safe. Breathe out slowly with me.'
quiz.why: Calm, supportive words like 'You're safe. Breathe out slowly with me.' help a person in panic. 'Calm down!' or 'Stop faking' can make it worse.
Paper-bag breathing is not recommended, since it can reduce oxygen and may hide a medical problem. Slow breathing with long out-breaths is safer.

quiz.q: New severe chest pain with fainting →
quiz.why: Severe chest pain with fainting, especially if it is new, could be a medical emergency. Seek medical help or call 112, and do not assume it is just panic.

lessons.title: Facing fears step by step: the exposure ladder

scenes.text: Vikram, 15, panics near swimming pools since nearly drowning at 7.
With a swim coach and counsellor he builds a ladder: watch from the side → sit with feet in → stand in the shallow end → float with support.
Three months later he swims a length. Fear shrank because he faced it gradually.

steps.title: How exposure works
steps.body: Fear reduces when we **gradually and repeatedly** face the feared thing **safely**, staying long enough for anxiety to drop (or to learn the feared outcome doesn't happen). This is a core part of **cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)**, the best-studied talk therapy for anxiety.

steps.title: Solved example: build a ladder for stage fear
steps.body:
Rate each step 0–10 for fear:
1. Read aloud alone (2)
2. Read aloud to a family member (3)
3. Speak 1 min to 2 friends (4)
4. Answer a question in class (5)
5. Present 2 min in a small group (6)
6. Speak at the class assembly (8)
7. Speak on stage at the annual day (10)
Start at the lowest; repeat each step until fear drops to about half, then move up.

steps.title: Solved example: fear of the dark (younger sibling)
steps.body: Night light → dim it over a week → 1 minute in dark with parent → 5 minutes → falls asleep with door ajar. Praise courage at each step.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Jumping straight to the top step ('flooding') without support.
- Leaving as soon as anxiety rises — teaches the brain the danger was real.
- Exposure to **genuinely dangerous** things — exposure is only for safe situations, and trauma-related fears are best done with a professional.

activity.prompt: Order this exposure ladder for fear of dogs (easiest first)
items: Watch a calm dog from across the park
Stand near a calm, leashed dog with its owner
Gently pet a calm, friendly dog with the owner's permission

quiz.why: Exposure therapy means gradually facing a feared but safe situation, step by step, so the brain learns it is safe. It is not forcing someone into real danger.

quiz.q: Move to the next step when…
options: fear on the current step has dropped noticeably
quiz.why: In exposure, move to the next step when the fear on the current step has dropped noticeably, as the brain has got used to it (habituation).

quiz.q: The best-studied talk therapy for anxiety:
quiz.why: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is the best-studied talk therapy for anxiety. It changes unhelpful thoughts and avoidance behaviours.

quiz.q: Leaving as soon as anxiety rises teaches the brain…
quiz.why: Leaving as soon as anxiety rises teaches the brain that the danger was real and that escape was needed. So the fear stays or grows.
Exposure is used only for safe situations that feel scary, such as speaking in class. It is never for real danger, such as fire or strangers' cars.

lessons.title: Worry time, thought checks and getting treatment

scenes.text: Ananya worries all day — in class, at meals, in bed.
Her counsellor suggests '15-minute worry time' at 6 pm. During the day she jots worries down and postpones them.
By 6 pm many worries feel smaller. Some she solves; others she lets go.

steps.title: Worry time
steps.body: Choose a daily 15–20 min slot (not near bedtime). When worries pop up, write them down: 'later'. In worry time, sort each: **solvable now?** → make a step. **Not solvable / hypothetical?** → practise letting it pass (breathing, an activity).

steps.title: Solved example: the 'what's likely' check
steps.body:
Worry: 'If I answer wrong, everyone will laugh and I'll be humiliated forever.'
- Worst case? Some laugh briefly.
- Best case? Teacher praises the attempt.
- Most likely? Teacher corrects kindly; no one remembers next day.
- Could I cope with the worst? Yes — I've coped with embarrassment before.

steps.title: Treatment options
steps.body:
- **Talk therapy** (CBT, others) with a psychologist or counsellor — usually first choice for teens.
- **Medicines** prescribed by a psychiatrist for moderate–severe anxiety; safe when monitored; not 'addictive' in the way many fear (some sedatives are, which is why doctors manage them carefully).
- Lifestyle: sleep, exercise, less caffeine, limiting doom-scrolling.
Help: school counsellor, government hospital psychiatry OPD, **Tele-MANAS 14416**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Searching symptoms online at night.
- Seeking constant reassurance ('Are you sure it's fine?') — relief fades and worry returns stronger.
- Stopping prescribed medicines suddenly without the doctor.

activity.prompt: Anxiety questions people don't ask

items.q: Is anxiety a sign of weakness?
items.a: No. It's a common health condition, like asthma, and has nothing to do with character.

items.q: Will I always feel this way?
items.a: Most people improve a lot with the right support and skills.

items.q: Can I go to a counsellor without my parents knowing?
items.a: School counsellors and Tele-MANAS can talk with you confidentially. For ongoing treatment of under-18s, parents are usually involved, and that's often helpful.

items.q: Does medicine change my personality?
items.a: Properly prescribed medicine aims to reduce symptoms, not change who you are. Discuss side effects with your doctor.

items.q: Is it OK to avoid things that make me anxious?
items.a: A little rest is fine, but long-term avoidance tends to make fear grow.

options: postponing worries to a set slot
quiz.why: Worry time means postponing worries to a set daily slot (like 15 minutes), so worry does not take over the whole day.
Constant reassurance-seeking brings brief relief, but it keeps the worry going, because the person never learns to cope with uncertainty.

quiz.q: Usually the first treatment for teen anxiety:
quiz.why: Talk therapy such as CBT is usually the first treatment for teen anxiety. Medicine is considered only when needed.
Only a psychiatrist (a medical doctor) or another qualified doctor can prescribe medicine. Not a teacher, influencer or friend.

options: should be discussed with the doctor first
quiz.why: Stopping prescribed medicines suddenly can cause withdrawal or relapse. Discuss any changes with the doctor first, who may reduce the dose slowly.

questions.q: Anxiety in small amounts is…
options: normal and can help you prepare
questions.why: A small amount of anxiety is normal and can even help you prepare, for example before an exam. It becomes a problem when it is intense and long-lasting.

questions.q: A panic attack is…
questions.why: A panic attack is a sudden wave of intense fear with body symptoms, which passes in minutes. It is not fake and not necessarily a heart attack.

questions.q: Tele-MANAS:
questions.why: Tele-MANAS, the free 24×7 mental-health helpline in India, is 14416.

questions.q: Exposure means…
options: facing safe fears step by step
questions.why: Exposure means facing safe but feared situations step by step, so the brain learns that they are safe.

questions.q: A specific phobia example:
questions.why: A specific phobia is an intense fear of one thing or situation, such as injections. Worrying about everything is generalised anxiety, and OCD involves rituals.

questions.q: Helpful breathing during panic:
questions.why: During panic, a slow breath with a longer out-breath helps calm the body. Rapid gulps, long breath-holding or paper bags are not helpful.

questions.q: Assertion: Avoiding feared situations maintains anxiety. Reason: The brain never learns the situation is safe.
questions.why: Both are true. When we avoid a feared situation, the brain never gets a chance to learn it is safe, so anxiety continues. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is a sign of an anxiety disorder?
options: Fear that disrupts school for months
questions.why: Anxiety is a disorder when fear is strong, lasts long (for months) and disrupts life, such as school. Nerves at an interview, butterflies or worry about one test are normal.

questions.q: Case: Kabir's friend hyperventilates in the canteen, says her chest is tight; she's had this before and was told it's panic. First step?
options: Calmly stay, guide slow breathing; seek help if symptoms are unusual
questions.why: Stay calm with her and guide slow breathing. Seek help if the symptoms are unusual (such as new, severe chest pain). Shouting 'calm down' or leaving her does not help.

questions.q: CBT stands for…
questions.why: CBT stands for cognitive behavioural therapy, a talking therapy that changes unhelpful thoughts and behaviours.

questions.q: Fear ratings: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9. Where should exposure start?
questions.why: Exposure starts with the least scary step on the ladder, rated 2. You then work up gradually as each step gets easier.

questions.q: Why is reassurance-seeking unhelpful long-term?
options: Relief is brief and worry returns stronger
questions.why: Reassurance brings brief relief, but the worry returns stronger and the person learns to depend on others. So it is unhelpful in the long run.

questions.q: Worry: 'If I'm late, I'll be expelled.' Most likely outcome?
questions.why: Being late once is most likely to get a warning or a late mark, not expulsion. Testing a worry against realistic outcomes reduces anxiety.

questions.q: Which is TRUE about anxiety medicines?
options: All are addictive and should be avoided
Prescribed by psychiatrists and monitored; some sedatives need careful limits
questions.why: Anxiety medicines are prescribed by psychiatrists and monitored, and some sedatives need careful limits. Not all are addictive, and they should never be bought from friends.

questions.q: Case: A teen avoids school for 8 weeks due to fear of panic attacks. Best plan?
questions.why: Avoiding school for 8 weeks needs professional help and a gradual return plan (exposure with support). Punishment, ignoring or staying home indefinitely makes the fear worse.

questions.q: Why should first-ever severe chest pain not be assumed to be panic?
options: Medical causes must be ruled out
questions.why: First-ever severe chest pain must be checked, because heart or lung problems must be ruled out. Do not assume it is panic.

questions.q: Which worry is best handled in worry time by making a step?
options: 'I haven't started my project due Friday'
questions.why: 'I haven't started my project due Friday' is a real, solvable worry, so make a small plan or step. Worries about asteroids or far-off 'what ifs' cannot be solved.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Low mood & depression: signs, support and recovery
courses.summary: The difference between sadness and depression, how depression shows up in teens, what causes it, myths that stop people getting help, everyday steps that help, how to support a friend, and how treatment works.
outcomes: Learners can tell everyday sadness from depression
Learners can list common signs of depression in teens
Learners can correct myths about depression and treatment
Learners can use behavioural activation and other self-help steps
Learners can support a friend and know how to get professional help
courses.guardianNote: Awareness of depression for teenagers: signs, causes, myths, self-care, helping a friend and treatment options. Non-graphic, hopeful and help-focused, consistent with WHO guidance; includes Tele-MANAS 14416 and 112.

lessons.title: Sadness vs depression

scenes.text: Since the summer, Ritvik has stopped playing football, sleeps in, and says nothing feels fun.
His parents call him lazy. He feels guilty and even worse.
A doctor explains this could be depression — an illness, not laziness — and that it's treatable.

steps.title: Sadness
steps.body: A normal response to loss, disappointment or stress. It usually comes in waves, eases with time and support, and you can still enjoy some things.

steps.title: Depression
steps.body: A common health condition (WHO estimates it affects millions worldwide, including many teens) where low or irritable mood and/or **loss of interest or pleasure** last **most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 2 weeks**, along with other changes: sleep (too little/too much), appetite or weight changes, tiredness, trouble concentrating, feeling worthless or excessively guilty, moving or speaking slowly or being restless, and sometimes thoughts of death or suicide.

steps.title: How it can look in teens
steps.body: Irritability and anger more than sadness · withdrawing from friends and hobbies · falling grades · headaches or stomach aches · more screen time to escape · self-criticism · risky behaviour or substance use.

steps.title: Solved example: sort the situation
steps.body:
(a) Sad for a week after a pet died, still meets friends → **grief, normal**; support helps.
(b) 5 weeks of no interest in anything, sleeping 12 h, failing tests, saying 'I'm worthless' → **possible depression** → get assessed.
(c) One bad day after a fight → **normal sadness**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling depression laziness or 'attitude'.
- 'Snap out of it' — people can't, any more than they could snap out of a fever.
- Thinking only people with 'big problems' get depressed — it can happen to anyone.

statements.s: Depression is the same as feeling sad for a day.
statements.why: It lasts 2+ weeks and affects daily life.

statements.s: In teens, depression can show as irritability.
Losing interest in things you used to enjoy can be a key sign.
Depression is caused by weak character.
statements.why: It has biological, psychological and social causes.

statements.s: Depression is treatable.

quiz.why: Depression is diagnosed when symptoms, such as low mood or loss of interest, last at least 2 weeks and affect daily life.
A key sign of depression is a loss of interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy (anhedonia). One bad day is not depression.

quiz.q: In teens, depression may look like…
quiz.why: In teens, depression often shows as irritability and withdrawal rather than just sadness.
Grief after a loss is a normal response, not weakness or illness. If it is very long or disabling, a professional can help.
'Snap out of it' is unhelpful, as depression is a health condition, not a choice. Support and treatment work better.

lessons.title: Causes, myths and the brain

scenes.text: Fatima learns her mother had depression after her birth and recovered with treatment.
'So it can run in families?'
'Genes can raise risk, but life events, stress and support matter too — and help works.'

steps.title: Many causes together
steps.body:
- **Biological**: genes/family history, hormone changes, illness, brain chemistry and circuits, poor sleep.
- **Psychological**: harsh self-criticism, perfectionism, past trauma.
- **Social**: bullying, family conflict, loss, loneliness, academic pressure, discrimination, poverty.
Often it's a mix; sometimes there's no clear reason — that's OK too.

steps.title: Myths vs facts
steps.body:
- 'Only adults get depressed' → teens and even children can.
- 'Talking about it makes it worse' → talking usually helps.
- 'Medicines are addictive and make you a zombie' → antidepressants are not addictive; side effects are discussed with the doctor; many people feel more like themselves.
- 'Seeking help means you're mad' → it means you're taking care of your health.
- 'Boys don't get depressed' → they do, and may hide it more.

steps.title: Solved example: spot the myth
steps.body:
Statement: 'He has a nice house and good marks, so he can't be depressed.'
- Step 1: Does depression depend on wealth or marks? No.
- Step 2: Depression can occur with or without obvious problems.
- **Conclusion:** myth — check in with him.

steps.title: Protective factors
steps.body: Supportive relationships, sleep, physical activity, time outdoors, a sense of purpose, skills for coping, and getting help early.

activity.prompt: Match the myth to the fact
pairs: They are not addictive; doctors monitor them
Boys do, and may hide it

options: a mix of biological, psychological and social factors
quiz.why: Depression comes from a mix of biological (genes, brain chemistry), psychological (thinking patterns) and social (stress, relationships) factors.
Antidepressants are not addictive, but they should be taken as the doctor advises. They take a few weeks to work.
Seeking help means looking after your health, like going to a doctor for a fever. It is not weakness or being 'mad'.
Supportive relationships are a protective factor. Bullying, isolation and lack of sleep raise the risk.

options: can raise risk but isn't destiny
quiz.why: A family history of depression can raise the risk, but it is not destiny. Many people with a family history never become depressed.

lessons.title: Small steps that help: behavioural activation

scenes.text: Ritvik's counsellor asks him to do one small thing each day — even if he doesn't feel like it.
Day 1: a 10-minute walk. Day 3: text a friend. Day 6: 15 minutes of football.
Mood follows action, slowly. 'I didn't wait to feel better — I did things and then felt a little better.'

steps.title: Why action comes first
steps.body: Depression tells you to withdraw, which removes things that give pleasure or achievement, which deepens low mood — a downward spiral. **Behavioural activation** reverses it: plan small, doable activities that bring **pleasure**, **achievement** or **connection**, and do them even before motivation returns.

steps.title: Solved example: plan a week
steps.body:
Rate mood 0–10 before and after each activity.
- Mon: 10-min walk (mood 3 → 4)
- Tue: help cook dinner (3 → 4)
- Wed: call cousin (2 → 4)
- Thu: 20 min drawing (3 → 5)
- Fri: football 15 min (3 → 5)
Average rise ≈ (1+1+2+2+2)/5 = **1.6 points**. Evidence for your brain that action helps.

steps.title: Other daily supports
steps.body: Regular sleep–wake times · sunlight in the morning · movement most days · regular meals · limit alcohol/drugs (they worsen mood) · reduce doom-scrolling · break tasks into tiny steps · be kind in self-talk · stay connected even briefly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Waiting to 'feel motivated' first.
- Setting huge goals and then feeling like a failure — start tiny.
- Self-help replacing professional help when symptoms are moderate or severe — use both.

activity.prompt: My small-steps plan for this week
items: Do one thing I used to enjoy for 15 minutes
Rate my mood before and after

options: planning small rewarding activities even before motivation
quiz.why: Behavioural activation means planning small, rewarding activities even before you feel motivated. Action helps lift mood.
Mood often follows action. Doing small activities first can improve how you feel, so waiting to feel better is less effective.
Alcohol is a depressant and tends to worsen mood and sleep, so it is not a cure for depression.
Goals should start tiny and doable, like a 10-minute walk. Small wins build momentum.
The rises are 4 − 2 = 2 and 5 − 3 = 2. The average rise is (2 + 2)/2 = 2.

lessons.title: Helping a friend and getting treatment

scenes.text: At midnight Siya gets a text from her friend: 'I'm so tired of everything.'
She replies: 'I'm here. Are you safe right now? Can I call?'
Next morning they go together to the school counsellor. Siya also tells her own mum, so she isn't carrying it alone.

steps.title: How to help a friend
steps.body:
- **Notice** changes and **ask**: 'You've seemed down lately. How are you really?'
- **Listen** more than you talk; don't judge or rush to fix.
- **Validate**: 'That sounds really hard.'
- **Encourage help**: offer to go with them to a counsellor or trusted adult.
- **Stay in touch** — small messages matter.
- **Look after yourself** too; you're a friend, not a therapist.

steps.title: If they mention suicide or self-harm
steps.body: Take it seriously. It's OK to ask directly: 'Are you thinking about suicide?' Asking does **not** put the idea in someone's head. Don't promise secrecy. Stay with them if they're in danger and **get an adult immediately**; call **112** or **14416**.

steps.title: How treatment works
steps.body:
- **Mild**: counselling, behavioural activation, problem-solving, sleep/activity changes.
- **Moderate–severe**: psychological therapy (e.g. CBT, interpersonal therapy) and sometimes antidepressant medicine from a psychiatrist; regular follow-up.
- Recovery often takes **weeks to months**; ups and downs are normal.
Where: school counsellor, district hospital psychiatry OPD (District Mental Health Programme), private psychologists/psychiatrists, **Tele-MANAS 14416**.

steps.title: Solved example: what to say / not say
steps.body:
Say: 'I'm here.' 'You're not a burden.' 'Let's find someone who can help.'
Avoid: 'Others have it worse.' 'Just be positive.' 'It's all in your head.'

a.text: Your friend has skipped football for weeks and says, 'Nothing matters anymore.'

choices.label: 'I've noticed you seem down. Want to talk? I'm here.'
'Stop being dramatic.'
choices.feedback: That can make them shut down.

x.text: Your friend goes quiet and walks off. Try again later?

choices.label: Text: 'Sorry, that came out wrong. I care. Can we talk?'

b.text: They say they feel like a burden and sometimes think everyone would be better off without them.

choices.label: Ask directly if they're thinking of suicide, stay with them and tell an adult now
Promise to keep it secret
choices.feedback: Their safety matters more than secrecy.

b2.text: You feel worried and alone with this.

choices.label: Tell a trusted adult and call 14416 together

end1.text: An adult gets involved and your friend starts getting support. You did the right thing.

options: does not put the idea in their head
quiz.why: Asking directly 'Are you thinking about suicide?' does not put the idea in someone's head. It shows you care and opens the door to help.

quiz.q: If a friend shares suicidal thoughts:
options: don't promise secrecy; get an adult
quiz.why: If a friend shares suicidal thoughts, don't promise secrecy. Their safety matters more, so get a trusted adult involved.
'You're not a burden' is validating and supportive. 'Just be positive' or 'Others have it worse' dismisses the person's feelings.
Recovery from depression usually takes weeks to months with treatment and support, and many people recover fully.
Tele-MANAS (14416) is a free, 24×7 helpline for mental health in India.

questions.q: Depression lasts at least…
questions.why: Depression is diagnosed when symptoms last at least 2 weeks.

questions.q: Depression is…
questions.why: Depression is treatable. It is not contagious or laziness, and most people improve with therapy and sometimes medicine.

questions.q: Tele-MANAS:
questions.why: Tele-MANAS, the free mental-health helpline, is 14416.

questions.q: A key sign of depression:
questions.why: A key sign of depression is loss of interest in activities once enjoyed.

questions.q: Antidepressants are…
questions.why: Antidepressants are not addictive. They are prescribed by a doctor and should not be stopped suddenly.

questions.q: Behavioural activation:
questions.why: Behavioural activation means doing small, rewarding actions, even when you don't feel like it, to lift mood step by step.

questions.q: Assertion: Asking about suicide directly can help. Reason: It shows care and opens a conversation without planting the idea.
questions.why: Both are true. Asking directly shows care and opens a conversation, and research shows it does not plant the idea. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: In teens, depression often shows as…
questions.why: In teens, depression often shows as irritability (being easily annoyed) rather than only sadness.

questions.q: Which is a myth?
questions.why: 'Boys don't get depressed' is a myth. Boys and men also get depressed, though they may show it as anger or withdrawal.

questions.q: Case: Sana is sad for 4 days after moving schools but still enjoys drawing. Most likely?
questions.why: Four days of sadness after moving schools, while still enjoying drawing, is normal adjustment sadness. Depression needs 2 weeks or more of symptoms and loss of interest.

questions.q: Mood rises: 2→5, 3→4, 1→4. Average rise?
questions.why: The rises are 3, 1 and 3. Average = (3 + 1 + 3)/3 = 7/3 ≈ 2.33.

questions.q: Why does withdrawal deepen depression?
questions.why: Withdrawal removes pleasure, achievement and connection, which are things that lift mood. So low mood deepens in a downward spiral.

questions.q: Case: A friend texts 'I can't do this anymore' at night. First reply?
options: 'I'm here. Are you safe right now?'
questions.why: A message like 'I can't do this anymore' may mean distress or suicidal thoughts. A caring reply, 'I'm here. Are you safe right now?', checks safety and shows support.

questions.q: Moderate–severe depression treatment typically includes…
options: therapy and sometimes medicine with follow-up
questions.why: Moderate to severe depression is typically treated with therapy and sometimes medicine, with follow-up from a doctor.

questions.q: Case: A friend says everyone would be better off without them and they've 'made a plan'. Correct action?
options: Stay with them, get an adult immediately, call 112
questions.why: A friend saying everyone would be better off without them and that they have made a plan is an emergency. Stay with them, get an adult at once, and call 112. Don't keep it secret.

questions.q: Which statement reflects the biopsychosocial view?
options: Genes, thinking patterns and life circumstances interact
questions.why: The biopsychosocial view says genes, thinking patterns and life circumstances all interact to cause depression. It is not only chemicals or willpower.

questions.q: Best way to look after yourself while helping a depressed friend?
options: Share the load with a trusted adult and keep your own routines
questions.why: Helping a friend is easier when you share the load with a trusted adult and keep your own routines, like sleep. You should not be the only support.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Self-harm & suicide: understanding, safety and hope
courses.summary: A careful, non-graphic course on why people may hurt themselves, warning signs of suicide, how to respond if you or a friend is struggling, making a personal safety plan, safer coping, and where to get help in India 24×7.
outcomes: Learners can describe self-harm as a sign of distress, not attention-seeking
Learners can recognise warning signs of suicide
Learners can respond to a friend using ask–listen–stay–get help
Learners can create a personal safety plan
Learners can name helplines and emergency steps
courses.guardianNote: Sensitive: self-harm and suicide prevention. Content follows safe-messaging principles: no methods or graphic detail, hope and help-seeking emphasised, how to support others, safety planning, and Indian helplines (Tele-MANAS 14416, 112, 1098). Strongly recommended that a trusted adult is available to talk with afterwards.

lessons.title: Understanding self-harm

scenes.text: In May heat, Jiya always wears long sleeves.
Her friend Mansi notices and gently asks if she's okay.
Jiya admits she has been hurting herself when feelings get overwhelming. Mansi listens, doesn't panic, and helps her talk to the school counsellor.

steps.title: What self-harm is
steps.body: **Self-harm** means a person deliberately hurts themselves, often to cope with overwhelming emotions such as pain, anger, numbness, shame or stress. It is **a sign of serious distress**, not 'attention-seeking' — and if someone is seeking attention, they need it. It does not always mean the person wants to die, but it does increase future risk, so it should always be taken seriously.

steps.title: Possible signs
steps.body: Unexplained injuries, covering up in hot weather, withdrawing, low mood, avoiding activities like swimming, keeping sharp objects, saying they deserve to be hurt.

steps.title: Solved example: respond, don't react
steps.body:
Friend shows you an injury.
- Don't: gasp, shout, threaten to tell everyone, or demand they stop immediately.
- Do: stay calm; 'Thank you for telling me. I'm glad you did.' Ask if they need medical care now. Ask what's been happening. Encourage — and help — them to talk to a trusted adult or counsellor. Tell an adult yourself if there's a risk to safety.
- If the injury is serious → first aid and **112**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'They're just doing it for attention.'
- Promising total secrecy.
- Focusing only on the injury and not the feelings behind it.
- Sharing photos or stories of self-harm online — this can harm others.

statements.s: Self-harm is usually a way of coping with overwhelming emotions.
People who self-harm are just seeking attention.
Self-harm should always be taken seriously.
You should promise to keep a friend's self-harm secret.

quiz.why: Self-harm is mainly a sign of serious emotional distress, a way of coping with pain. It is not just attention-seeking or a trend, and it should be taken seriously.
A calm first response is 'Thank you for telling me.' It shows trust was respected. Shock, threats or gossip make the person hide more.
A serious injury needs first aid and a call to 112. Hiding it or waiting can be dangerous.
Sharing self-harm images online can harm others who are vulnerable, since it may trigger them. It is better to avoid it.

options: raises risk, so take it seriously
quiz.why: Self-harm raises the risk of future suicide attempts, so it must be taken seriously and the person should get support.

lessons.title: Suicide: warning signs and myths

scenes.text: Before the holidays, Aakash gives his favourite cricket bat to his friend Neel and says, 'You keep it. I won't need it.'
Neel feels uneasy and remembers a lesson on warning signs.
He tells his teacher that day. Aakash gets help in time.

steps.title: Warning signs — act on these
steps.body:
- Talking about wanting to die, being a burden, feeling trapped or having no reason to live.
- Saying goodbye, giving away important things, writing about death.
- Withdrawing from friends and activities.
- Sudden calm after a period of deep depression.
- Increased alcohol or drug use; reckless behaviour.
- Big mood swings, rage, extreme hopelessness.
- Looking for ways to harm themselves.

steps.title: Risk factors (not causes)
steps.body: Depression and other mental-health conditions, previous attempts, self-harm, substance use, bullying (including cyberbullying), abuse, loss, exam or family pressure, isolation, discrimination. **Suicide is rarely caused by one thing**, and it is preventable — most people who feel suicidal do not want to die; they want the pain to stop.

steps.title: Myths vs facts
steps.body:
- 'People who talk about it won't do it' → many who die by suicide told someone. Always take it seriously.
- 'Asking about suicide gives people ideas' → no; it opens the door to help.
- 'Once suicidal, always suicidal' → feelings pass; with help, people recover.
- 'Nothing can stop it' → support, treatment and safety steps save lives.

steps.title: Solved example: which signs are present?
steps.body:
Aakash: gives away bat ✔, says 'won't need it' ✔ (talking about not being around), recent withdrawal ✔.
→ **Three warning signs** → tell an adult **today**.

activity.prompt: Is this a warning sign to act on?
buckets: Usually not a warning sign alone

items.text: Saying 'everyone would be better off without me'
Being sad for a day after losing a match
Sudden calm after weeks of deep depression
Searching for ways to hurt themselves

quiz.q: Talking about being a burden is…
quiz.why: Talking about being a burden to others is a warning sign of suicide risk. It should be taken seriously and an adult should be told.
Asking about suicide does not plant the idea. It opens the door to help, as the person feels heard.
Suicide usually has several causes together, such as distress, loss, bullying, illness and lack of support. It is rarely one cause, and it can be prevented.
Most people who feel suicidal want the pain to stop, and not necessarily to die. They are often unsure, which is why support can help.

quiz.q: Sudden calm after deep depression can be…
quiz.why: A sudden calm after deep depression can be a warning sign. It can sometimes follow a decision to end life, so stay alert and check in.

lessons.title: How to help: Ask, Listen, Stay, Get help

scenes.text: Late at night Kavya calls her cousin Ravi: 'I don't want to be here anymore.'
Ravi stays on the phone, asks if she's safe, and gets his parents to call 112 and her family.
Weeks later, in treatment, Kavya says, 'You staying on the line mattered.'

steps.title: A-L-S-G
steps.body:
- **Ask** directly: 'Are you thinking about suicide?'
- **Listen** without judging; let them talk; don't argue or lecture.
- **Stay** with them (in person or on the phone) if they are at risk; help remove things they could use to harm themselves, if safe to do so.
- **Get help**: a trusted adult **immediately**; **112** if in immediate danger; **Tele-MANAS 14416**; **1098** for under-18s.

steps.title: Solved example: words that help
steps.body:
- 'I'm really glad you told me.'
- 'You don't have to go through this alone.'
- 'Let's call someone together right now.'
- 'Will you stay safe while we get help?'
Avoid: 'Don't be stupid', 'Think of your parents', 'You have so much to live for' (said as a lecture).

steps.title: You are not responsible for fixing it
steps.body: Your job is to **connect them to help**, not to be their counsellor. It's not betrayal to tell an adult — it's care. Afterwards, talk to someone about how you feel too.

steps.title: In an emergency
steps.body: If someone has harmed themselves seriously or taken something harmful → call **112**, give first aid if trained, stay with them, don't leave them alone, and tell paramedics what you know.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to help someone at risk
items: Stay with them and keep them safe

quiz.why: A-L-S-G: Ask directly, Listen without judging, Stay with them, and Get help (an adult or helpline).

quiz.q: If someone is in immediate danger:
quiz.why: If someone is in immediate danger, call 112 right away. Don't wait for morning or send a text.

quiz.q: Telling an adult about a friend's suicidal thoughts is…
quiz.why: Telling an adult about a friend's suicidal thoughts is care, not betrayal. It may save their life.

quiz.q: 'You don't have to go through this alone' is…
quiz.why: 'You don't have to go through this alone' is a supportive statement. It reduces isolation and shows you are there.
Your role as a friend is to connect them to help (a trusted adult, doctor or helpline). You cannot be their therapist or fix everything.

lessons.title: Your personal safety plan and safer coping

scenes.text: After a hard winter, Arjun and his counsellor write a safety plan and save it on his phone.
One bad evening, he opens it: warning signs, things that calm him, people to call.
He calls his elder sister and walks with her. The urge passes. 'The plan worked.'

steps.title: What a safety plan includes
steps.body:
1. **My warning signs** (thoughts, feelings, situations).
2. **Things I can do on my own** to cope (music, walk, shower, breathing, writing).
3. **People and places** that help distract me.
4. **People I can ask for help** (names and numbers).
5. **Professionals & helplines**: counsellor, doctor, **14416**, **112**, **1098**.
6. **Making my environment safer** — with a trusted adult, keeping things I could use to harm myself out of easy reach.

steps.title: Safer ways to get through an urge
steps.body: Urges usually rise and fall like a wave. Try: hold an ice cube or splash cold water on your face; intense exercise for a few minutes; squeeze a stress ball; tear paper; write feelings and rip it up; call or text someone; go to a public or shared space; slow breathing. These don't fix the cause but can help you **delay** until the urge passes — and then talk to someone.

steps.title: Solved example: fill one section
steps.body:
Warning signs: 'Lying awake replaying mistakes; thinking I'm a burden; staying in my room.'
On my own: '10-min walk, cold shower, playlist, box breathing.'
People: 'Didi, Rohan, Mrs Pillai (counsellor).'
Helplines: '14416, 112.'

steps.title: Hope is real
steps.body: Many people who once felt suicidal go on to live full, meaningful lives. Feelings change; help works. If you're struggling right now, please reach out today: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7) or **112**.

activity.prompt: Start your safety plan: write two warning signs, three things that help you cope, and two people you could call.
activity.hint: Keep it somewhere easy to find, like your phone notes. Share it with a trusted adult or counsellor.

quiz.why: A safety plan starts with your own warning signs: the thoughts, feelings or situations that tell you a crisis may be near.

options: rise and fall like a wave
quiz.why: Urges rise and fall like a wave. They usually pass in time if you ride them out using coping skills and support.

quiz.q: Cold water on your face can help…
options: delay an urge and calm the body
quiz.why: Cold water on the face can calm the body and delay an urge, since it triggers a calming reflex. It does not cure depression, but it gives time.

quiz.q: Making the environment safer is done…
quiz.why: Making the environment safer by putting away items that could be used for harm should be done with a trusted adult, not alone in secret.

options: go on to live full lives
quiz.why: Many people who once felt suicidal get help and go on to live full lives. Feelings of despair can pass.

questions.q: Self-harm is mainly a sign of…
questions.why: Self-harm is mainly a sign of distress, a way of coping with emotional pain. It deserves care and support.

questions.q: Emergency number:
questions.why: 112 is the single emergency number in India.

questions.q: Tele-MANAS:
questions.why: Tele-MANAS, the free mental-health helpline, is 14416.

questions.q: A warning sign of suicide:
questions.why: Giving away treasured things is a warning sign of suicide risk. Take it seriously and ask the person about it.

questions.q: Asking directly about suicide…
questions.why: Asking directly about suicide helps. It does not plant the idea, and it shows you care.

questions.q: A safety plan includes…
questions.why: A safety plan lists warning signs, coping steps, and people and helplines to contact in a crisis.

questions.q: Assertion: You should not promise secrecy when a friend shares suicidal thoughts. Reason: Their safety requires an adult's help.
questions.why: Both are true. You should not promise secrecy if a friend shares suicidal thoughts, because keeping them safe needs an adult's help. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: 'People who talk about suicide won't do it' is…
questions.why: 'People who talk about suicide won't do it' is a myth. Most people who die by suicide gave some warning, so every mention should be taken seriously.

questions.q: Which is a safer coping strategy during an urge?
options: Splash cold water and call a friend
Be alone in a locked room
questions.why: During an urge, splashing cold water on your face and calling a friend are safer coping strategies. Alcohol, being alone or searching methods raise risk.

questions.q: Case: A friend shows you a fresh injury and asks you not to tell. First response?
options: Stay calm, thank them, check if they need medical care, and help them tell an adult
questions.why: Stay calm, thank your friend for trusting you, check whether they need medical care, and help them tell an adult. Don't promise secrecy, as it is not safe.

questions.q: Which combination counts as multiple warning signs?
options: Withdrawing + giving things away + saying goodbye
questions.why: Withdrawing, giving things away and saying goodbye together are multiple warning signs. When several appear together, act and get help.

questions.q: Why is 'sudden calm' after deep depression a concern?
options: It can sometimes follow a decision to end life
questions.why: A sudden calm after deep depression can sometimes follow a decision to end life, as the person feels relief at having decided. So it needs attention, not relief.

questions.q: Which response is BEST?
options: 'I'm glad you told me. Let's call someone together now.'
questions.why: 'I'm glad you told me. Let's call someone together now.' is the best response: it is caring and leads to action. Minimising or guilt-tripping does not help.

questions.q: Your role helping a friend at risk is to…
options: connect them with adult and professional help
questions.why: Your role is to connect them with adult and professional help. You cannot be their only counsellor or keep it secret.

questions.q: Case: At 1 am a friend says they have taken something to harm themselves. Correct action?
options: Call 112 immediately, stay on the line/with them, inform an adult
questions.why: If someone has taken something to harm themselves, it is an emergency. Call 112 immediately, stay with them, and inform an adult. Do not wait for morning.

questions.q: Why is suicide described as preventable?
options: Support, treatment and safety steps reduce risk
questions.why: Suicide is preventable because support, treatment and safety steps can reduce risk. Many people recover when they get help.

questions.q: Which is the best long-term goal after a self-harm disclosure?
options: Ongoing support for the underlying distress
questions.why: After a disclosure of self-harm, the best long-term goal is ongoing support for the underlying distress. Ignoring or punishing does not address the cause.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Tobacco, alcohol, drugs & screen habits: addiction awareness
courses.summary: How addictive substances act on the brain, the facts on tobacco, vapes, alcohol, cannabis and pill misuse, what Indian law says, behavioural addictions like gaming and scrolling, refusal skills, and how to get help for yourself or someone else.
outcomes: Learners can explain how addiction affects the brain's reward system
Learners can state health effects of tobacco, vaping, alcohol and cannabis
Learners can outline key Indian laws on tobacco, e-cigarettes and drugs
Learners can use refusal skills under peer pressure
Learners can recognise problem gaming/screen use and know where to get help
courses.guardianNote: Factual awareness of tobacco, vaping, alcohol, cannabis and other drugs, behavioural addictions (gaming, scrolling), Indian law basics, refusal skills and getting help. No instructions for use; harm-prevention and help-seeking focus.

lessons.title: The brain on rewards: how addiction works

scenes.text: At a farewell party, Rohit, 16, is told 'just once' — first a cigarette, later a drink.
By Class 12 he smokes daily and feels restless without it.
A doctor explains: 'Nicotine hijacked your reward system. The good news — brains recover.'

steps.title: Reward system
steps.body: Pleasurable things (food, friends, music) release **dopamine** in the brain's reward circuits, teaching us to repeat them. Addictive substances cause **bigger, faster** surges. Over time the brain adapts: **tolerance** (needing more for the same effect), **cravings**, and **withdrawal** (feeling bad without it).

steps.title: Why teens are more at risk
steps.body: The brain's reward system matures earlier than the **prefrontal cortex** (self-control, planning), which keeps developing into the mid-20s. Starting substances in the teens is linked to **higher risk of addiction** later and can affect memory, learning and mood.

steps.title: Solved example: spot the stage
steps.body:
Signs: (1) tries at a party; (2) uses every weekend; (3) needs more for same effect; (4) feels irritable without it; (5) skips class to use.
- Experimentation: 1
- Regular use: 2
- Tolerance: 3
- Withdrawal/dependence: 4
- Harm to life: 5
Help can start at **any** stage — earlier is easier.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'I can stop anytime' — dependence often feels like that until you try.
- 'Natural means safe' — tobacco and cannabis are plants.
- 'Addiction = weak character' — it's a health condition; people recover.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Brain chemical in the reward system
Needing more for the same effect

options: needing more for the same effect
quiz.why: Tolerance means needing more of a substance to get the same effect. It is a sign the body is adapting, and it can lead to addiction.

quiz.q: Teens are at higher risk because…
quiz.why: Teens are at higher risk because the prefrontal cortex (the brain's self-control area) matures later, so impulses are harder to control.
'Natural' does not mean safe. Many natural substances, like tobacco and some plants, are harmful.

options: a health condition people recover from
