outcomes: Learners can explain why body diversity is normal
Learners can spot edited and filtered images and marketing tricks
Learners can respond to body-shaming comments
Learners can describe a healthy relationship with food and exercise
Learners can recognise warning signs of disordered eating and know where to get help
courses.guardianNote: Discusses body image, social-media filters, teasing about bodies, weight and healthy eating, and early signs of eating problems, without numbers that could trigger comparison. Language is kind and non-judgmental, and the lessons point to trusted adults and Tele-MANAS 14416 for support.

lessons.title: Every body is different — and that's the design

scenes.text: Tara flips through her family album and notices her nose is like Nani's and her height like her father's.
'So I didn't choose any of this?' she laughs.
She realises comparing herself to a film star is like comparing a mango to an apple.

steps.title: What shapes your body
steps.body: Genes (height, build, skin tone, hair, where fat is stored), puberty timing, food, activity, sleep and health conditions. Healthy bodies come in **many sizes and shapes**. During puberty, gaining some weight and body fat (especially for girls around hips and thighs) is a normal part of growth, not something to 'fix'.

steps.title: Skin colour
steps.body: Skin tone depends mostly on **melanin** levels set by genes, plus sun exposure. No shade is healthier or 'better'. Colourism (valuing lighter skin) is a social bias, not biology.

steps.title: Solved example: reframe a thought
steps.body:
Thought: 'My thighs are too big.'
- Step 1: Fact-check — is this based on health or on ads/comparison?
- Step 2: Function — 'My legs carry me through kabaddi and stairs.'
- Step 3: Kinder sentence — 'My body is growing the way it's meant to.'
- Step 4: Action — focus on strength, energy and fun, not a number.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using weight as a measure of worth.
- Commenting on others' bodies, even as 'compliments' about weight loss — you don't know what's behind it.
- Thinking body confidence means loving everything all the time — **body neutrality** (respecting and caring for your body) is a fine goal too.

activity.prompt: Write three things your body lets you do that you're grateful for (not about looks).
activity.hint: Think: dancing, climbing stairs, hugging, laughing, playing, tasting food, healing a cut.

quiz.q: Body shape is mostly influenced by…
quiz.why: Body shape comes mainly from genes and growth patterns, plus lifestyle such as food and activity. It is not decided by willpower alone or by star signs.

quiz.q: Gaining some body fat in puberty is…
quiz.why: Gaining some body fat during puberty is normal and part of healthy growth. It is not a disease and not always unhealthy.
Colourism is a social bias that treats lighter skin as better. It has no medical basis; skin tone is simply natural variation.

options: respecting and caring for your body without needing to love every part
quiz.why: Body neutrality means respecting and caring for your body for what it does, without having to love every part. It is not hating your body, ignoring health, or dieting.

options: can be hurtful; you don't know the cause
quiz.why: Commenting on someone's weight loss can hurt, because you don't know the cause (it might be illness or stress). It is safer not to comment on bodies.

lessons.title: Filters, ads and the comparison trap

scenes.text: Dhruv follows a fitness influencer with perfect abs and feels terrible about his own body.
Then the influencer posts a 'behind the scenes': lighting, posing, dehydration before shoots, and editing apps.
'So even he doesn't look like that most days?'

steps.title: How images are edited
steps.body: Lighting, angles, posing, make-up, filters that smooth skin and reshape faces, apps that slim waists or add muscle, choosing 1 photo out of 200. Many ads use digital retouching. Some influencers are paid to promote products — look for 'ad', 'sponsored' or 'paid partnership'.

steps.title: Solved example: spot the edit
steps.body: Clues an image is edited: wavy door frames or tiles near the body; skin with no pores; identical 'perfect' faces across posts; unusually long legs. Count: if you scroll 100 posts and 80 are edited or posed, your idea of 'normal' gets distorted by **80%**.

steps.title: Clean your feed
steps.body: Unfollow or mute accounts that leave you feeling worse. Follow people of different shapes, abilities and skin tones; follow hobbies (art, science, sport skills). Take screen breaks. Ask: 'Is this showing me something real, or selling me something?'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing 'before/after' ads.
- Buying fairness creams, slimming teas, height pills or 'detox' products — often useless or harmful.
- Thinking you're the only one who feels this — most teens do.

statements.s: Most professional ad photos are retouched.
Slimming teas are a safe, proven way to lose fat.
statements.why: Often laxatives; not safe or proven.

statements.s: Muting accounts that make you feel worse is a healthy choice.
Bent tiles near someone's waist can be a sign of editing.

options: the creator is paid to promote
quiz.why: A 'paid partnership' label means the creator is paid to promote the product. So it is advertising, not neutral advice or science.
A healthy feed shows varied bodies and hobbies, which gives a realistic picture. Seeing only 'perfect' bodies or ads can make you feel bad about yourself.

options: can contain harmful ingredients; skin tone is healthy as it is
quiz.why: Fairness creams can contain harmful ingredients and cannot change your genes. Skin tone is healthy just as it is.

quiz.q: A sign an image is edited:
quiz.why: Warped or bent background lines (like a curved door frame) are a sign a picture was edited. Natural pores, shadows and messy hair appear in real photos.

quiz.q: Feeling bad after scrolling is a cue to…
quiz.why: If scrolling makes you feel bad, take a break or mute those accounts. Buying products, scrolling more or dieting makes the problem worse.

lessons.title: Food, movement and a healthy relationship with both

scenes.text: Ritika starts skipping lunch to 'lose weight' before a wedding.
By afternoon she's dizzy and snappy in class.
The school counsellor talks with her about regular meals and feeling strong instead of 'small'.

steps.title: Regular eating
steps.body: Growing bodies need **three meals and 1–2 snacks** a day. Skipping meals often leads to tiredness, poor concentration, irritability and later overeating. No food is 'good' or 'bad' — think 'everyday foods' and 'sometimes foods'.

steps.title: Movement for joy
steps.body: Aim for about **60 minutes of activity a day** (WHO, for 5–17-year-olds) — sport, dance, cycling, walking, games. Exercise is for energy, strength, mood and fun, **not punishment** for eating.

steps.title: Solved example: build a balanced day
steps.body: Breakfast: vegetable poha + milk. Snack: fruit + roasted chana. Lunch: roti, dal, sabzi, curd. After-school: peanut chikki or sprouts. Dinner: rice, rajma, salad. Sometimes food: a samosa or sweet at a party — fully fine.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Crash diets and 'detox' juices for teens.
- Labelling yourself 'bad' for eating a sweet.
- Over-exercising while injured or exhausted.
- If you have a medical condition (e.g. diabetes, coeliac disease), follow your doctor's plan.

activity.prompt: Helpful or unhelpful food & exercise thinking?

items.text: I eat regular meals so I have energy
I must run 10 km because I ate a laddoo
I'll skip lunch to look thinner
Foods are either good or evil

quiz.q: Teens need about ___ of activity daily
quiz.why: The WHO advises teens to get about 60 minutes of physical activity every day for health and growth.
Skipping meals often leaves you tired and unable to focus, because the body and brain lack fuel. It does not improve focus or growth.

quiz.q: Exercise as punishment for eating is…
quiz.why: Using exercise as punishment for eating creates an unhelpful, unhealthy link between food and guilt. Exercise should be for enjoyment and health.
Calling foods 'everyday' and 'sometimes' foods is neutral and balanced. Labels like good, evil or forbidden create guilt and unhealthy rules.
Crash diets don't give the energy and nutrients a growing body needs, so they can harm growth. They are not recommended for teens.

lessons.title: Eating disorders: know the signs, know where to turn

scenes.text: Sneha notices her friend Divya always says she 'already ate', wears baggy clothes and runs extra laps.
Divya gets angry if anyone mentions food.
Sneha tells their class teacher privately. The teacher contacts Divya's family and a counsellor gently.

steps.title: What eating disorders are
steps.body: **Eating disorders** are serious but treatable mental-health conditions — not choices or phases. They affect all genders, body sizes and backgrounds. Types include **anorexia nervosa** (severe restriction and intense fear of weight gain), **bulimia nervosa** (cycles of binge eating and compensating, e.g. vomiting or over-exercise), **binge-eating disorder**, and **ARFID** (avoiding many foods due to fear or sensory issues — not about weight).

steps.title: Warning signs
steps.body: Skipping meals often, rigid food rules, hiding food, frequent trips to the toilet after meals, intense exercise despite illness or injury, rapid weight change, dizziness or fainting, periods stopping, preoccupation with weight or shape, withdrawing from meals with others, mood changes.

steps.title: Solved example: how to help a friend
steps.body:
1. Choose a private, calm time.
2. Use 'I' statements: 'I've noticed you skip lunch and seem tired. I'm worried about you.'
3. Don't comment on weight or appearance; don't argue about food.
4. Encourage talking to a trusted adult, counsellor or doctor — offer to go with them.
5. Tell an adult yourself if you're worried about their safety — that's caring, not betraying.

steps.title: Where to get help
steps.body: A parent or trusted adult, school counsellor, family doctor, psychiatrist/psychologist. **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free, 24×7). If someone faints, has chest pain or talks about wanting to die → **112**. Early help leads to better recovery.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'They look fine, so they can't be ill' — eating disorders occur at any weight.
- 'Only girls get them' — boys do too.
- Making jokes about 'anorexic' or 'fat'.

a.text: Your friend skips lunch every day, says she's 'fat' though she's tired all the time, and got dizzy in PE.

choices.label: Talk to her privately and kindly, then involve a trusted adult
Tell her she looks too thin in front of everyone
choices.feedback: Public comments about bodies cause shame.

choices.label: Ignore it — not my business
choices.feedback: Early help matters; you can help gently.

x.text: She seems more withdrawn. Want to try another way?

choices.label: Yes — speak privately with kindness

b.text: She says, 'Promise you won't tell anyone.'

choices.label: 'I care about you. I can't keep a secret if you might be unwell, but I'll come with you to talk to someone.'
Promise and do nothing
choices.feedback: Secrets about health risks can be dangerous.

b2.text: A week later she faints in assembly.

choices.label: Get the teacher immediately and share your worry

end1.text: A counsellor and her family get involved. Recovery takes time, and your friendship helps.

quiz.why: Eating disorders are serious but treatable health conditions. They can affect anyone, of any size or gender, and are not simply a choice.

options: rigid food rules and hiding food
quiz.why: Rigid food rules and hiding food are warning signs of an eating disorder. Drinking water and enjoying meals or snacks are normal.

quiz.q: Best first approach to a friend:
quiz.why: Talk to a friend privately and kindly using 'I' statements, such as 'I'm worried about you'. Public comments, jokes or weighing them can shame and hurt.
Tele-MANAS, India's mental health helpline, is 14416. 100 is police, 108 is ambulance and 1098 is Childline.
Eating disorders can occur at any weight, so you cannot tell by looking at someone. They are not only for very thin people, adults or athletes.

questions.q: Body shape is mainly influenced by…
questions.why: Body shape is mainly shaped by genes and growth. Willpower alone, shoe size or horoscope do not decide it.

questions.q: Teens need activity daily of about…
questions.why: Teens need about 60 minutes of activity every day for healthy growth and mood. 5 minutes or none is too little.

questions.q: Tele-MANAS:
questions.why: Tele-MANAS, the mental health helpline in India, is 14416. 100 is police, 101 is fire and 1098 is Childline.

questions.q: Filters on photos…
questions.why: Filters change how real faces look, smoothing skin and reshaping features. So filtered pictures do not show reality.

questions.q: Which is a healthy food idea?
questions.why: Splitting foods into 'everyday' and 'sometimes' foods is a balanced idea. Skipping breakfast, banning sweets forever and detox juices are not healthy.

questions.q: Eating disorders affect…
questions.why: Eating disorders affect people of all genders and sizes, not only girls, adults or models. Anyone can need help.

questions.q: Assertion: Comparing yourself to edited images harms body image. Reason: Edited images distort what normal looks like.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Edited images distort what a normal body looks like, so comparing yourself with them harms body image.

questions.q: Which is a red flag for an eating disorder?
options: Frequent toilet trips right after meals
questions.why: Frequent toilet trips right after meals can be a way of getting rid of food, a red flag for an eating disorder. Liking fruit, eating with friends and drinking water are healthy.

questions.q: A good reply to body-shaming:
options: 'Not funny. Stop.' and tell a teacher if it continues
questions.why: Say clearly 'Not funny. Stop.' and tell a teacher if it continues. That sets a boundary; shaming back, stopping eating or hiding does not solve the problem.

questions.q: Case: A boy runs 2 hours daily even with a leg injury and panics if he misses a day. This suggests…
options: a possible compulsive exercise problem worth discussing with an adult
questions.why: Exercising for 2 hours despite injury and panicking if a day is missed suggests compulsive exercise, which can be harmful. Talk to a trusted adult; it is not laziness or healthy dedication.

questions.q: If 70 of 100 posts in your feed are edited, roughly what share of what you see is unrealistic?
questions.why: 70 of 100 posts is 70/100 = 70%, so about 70% of what you see is edited and unrealistic.

questions.q: Why is skipping meals counter-productive for teens?
options: Causes low energy and often later overeating
questions.why: Skipping meals leaves the body low on energy and often leads to overeating later. It does not boost growth or sleep.

questions.q: Which statement is MOST accurate about eating disorders?
options: They are treatable; early help improves recovery
Just eat more and it's fixed
questions.why: Eating disorders are real, treatable health conditions, and getting help early improves recovery. They are not attention-seeking and recovery is possible; 'just eat more' ignores their causes.

questions.q: A friend asks you to keep their purging a secret. Best response?
options: Say you care, can't keep health-risk secrets, and help them reach an adult
questions.why: Say you care, explain you can't keep secrets that risk their health, and help them reach a trusted adult. Keeping the secret leaves them in danger; telling the class or posting online shames them.

questions.q: Case: Ads say a tea will 'melt fat in 7 days'. Best analysis?
options: Unrealistic claim; may contain laxatives; avoid
questions.why: A tea that 'melts fat in 7 days' is an unrealistic claim and may contain laxatives that harm the body. It is not scientific or safe for children, so avoid it.

questions.q: Which choice reflects body neutrality?
options: 'I'll fix my body with a crash diet.'
'I must love every part every day.'
'My legs are strong enough to carry me through practice.'
questions.why: Body neutrality is respecting what your body can do, like strong legs carrying you through practice. It does not require loving every part, hating it or crash dieting.

questions.q: Case: Someone with an eating disorder faints and has chest pain. Correct action?
options: Give them a snack and leave
questions.why: Fainting with chest pain in someone with an eating disorder is a medical emergency, so call 112. Lecturing, waiting or leaving them with a snack could cost a life.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Body care during puberty: sweat, hair, discharge & daily hygiene
courses.summary: Hands-on self-care for changing bodies: why sweat starts to smell and how to manage it, choices about body hair, normal vaginal discharge and vulval care, smegma and genital care for boys, feet, breath and underwear — and when an itch, smell or rash needs a doctor.
outcomes: Learners can explain body odour and choose deodorant or antiperspirant
Learners can make safe, personal choices about hair removal
Learners can tell normal discharge from signs of infection
Learners can follow a daily hygiene routine and know when to see a doctor
courses.guardianNote: Practical body-care for puberty: sweat and deodorant, hair-removal choices, normal vaginal discharge and vulval care, foot, mouth and underwear hygiene. Medically accurate and non-explicit, encouraging self-care and asking a doctor about anything unusual.

lessons.title: Sweat, smell and deodorant

scenes.text: After PE, Class 7's room smells strongly of sweat.
Kunal didn't realise it was partly him.
A friend quietly lends him a roll-on deodorant and tips. No drama, just help.

steps.title: Why sweat starts to smell
steps.body: At puberty, **apocrine sweat glands** in the armpits and groin switch on. Their sweat is not smelly itself, but **skin bacteria** break it down and produce odour. Hair traps sweat, so smells can be stronger there.

steps.title: Deodorant vs antiperspirant
steps.body:
- **Deodorant**: masks or reduces smell (often antibacterial).
- **Antiperspirant**: reduces sweating (usually aluminium salts).
Use on **clean, dry** skin, after bathing. Roll-ons are gentler for many; patch-test if skin is sensitive. Large studies have not shown a clear link between antiperspirants and breast cancer.

steps.title: Solved example: fix the smell
steps.body:
Problem: smell by afternoon even after a morning bath.
- Step 1: Clean T-shirt/vest daily; cotton breathes better than polyester.
- Step 2: Apply deodorant to dry armpits after bath.
- Step 3: Carry a spare vest for PE days; wash after sport.
- Step 4: Drink water; some foods (garlic, onion) may affect smell slightly.
- When to see a doctor: sweating that soaks clothes without heat or exercise (possible **hyperhidrosis**) — treatable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Spraying deodorant on top of yesterday's sweat.
- Using perfume instead of washing.
- Mocking someone about smell — help privately instead.

statements.s: Fresh sweat itself is almost odourless.
Antiperspirant reduces sweating; deodorant reduces smell.
Perfume is a substitute for washing.
Very heavy sweating without heat can be treated by a doctor.

quiz.why: Sweat itself is almost odourless. Body odour appears when bacteria on the skin break down sweat. Sleep, rice or thoughts do not cause it.
Deodorant works best on clean, dry skin. On wet or sweaty skin it does not stay or work well, and putting it on clothes only misses the point.
Cotton is a natural fabric that lets air and sweat pass through, so it breathes better. Plastic, rubber and leather trap moisture.
Apocrine sweat glands, found in armpits and groin, become active at puberty. That is why body odour often starts then.

quiz.q: If a classmate smells, kindest action:
quiz.why: If a classmate has body odour, help them privately and kindly, for example by suggesting a bath, deodorant and clean clothes. Announcing it or posting a meme humiliates them.

lessons.title: Body hair: your choice, done safely

scenes.text: A cousin tells Zainab, 12, 'Your arms are so hairy, wax them!'
Zainab isn't sure she wants to.
Her aunt says: 'Body hair is natural. Removing it is a personal choice — not a rule.'

steps.title: Body hair is normal
steps.body: Hair grows on arms, legs, underarms and the pubic area for everyone after puberty; amount and colour depend on genes. It protects skin and reduces friction. Removing it is **optional** — for any gender.

steps.title: Methods (pros & cautions)
steps.body:
- **Trimming**: easiest, least irritation.
- **Shaving**: quick; may cause nicks and bumps; never share razors.
- **Hair-removal creams**: patch-test first; follow timing exactly; never use on broken skin or the genitals' inner areas.
- **Waxing / threading**: lasts longer; can be painful; go to hygienic salons; avoid on irritated or sunburnt skin.
- **Laser**: by qualified professionals only, usually for adults.

steps.title: Solved example: razor bumps
steps.body:
Red bumps after shaving the underarm.
- Cause: hairs curling back into skin + irritation.
- Fix: shave with the direction of growth, use a sharp clean blade and gel, don't stretch skin hard, moisturise, give skin a break. Infected bumps (pus, pain, spreading redness) → doctor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Feeling pressured — your body, your choice.
- Using a rusty or shared razor.
- Waxing over cuts or pimples.
- Sudden heavy hair growth with irregular periods in girls → mention to a doctor (possible PCOS).

activity.prompt: Match the method to its main caution
pairs: Use a clean, sharp, unshared razor
Avoid on cuts or irritated skin

quiz.why: Removing body hair is a personal choice. It is not medically required and not compulsory for boys or girls.
Patch-test a small spot of skin first to check for allergy or irritation. Never use on cuts, mix with soap or leave on overnight.
Shaving in the direction of hair growth with a clean blade reduces razor bumps. Dry shaving, rusty blades or pressing hard irritate the skin.

quiz.q: Sudden heavy hair growth + irregular periods →
quiz.why: Sudden heavy hair growth with irregular periods can signal a hormone problem such as PCOS, so see a doctor. Waxing more only treats the surface.
Body hair protects skin and reduces friction. It does not cause illness and is not harmful.

lessons.title: Vaginal discharge and vulval care

scenes.text: Pooja, 11, notices a whitish stain in her underwear and thinks she's ill.
At her check-up, the doctor says: 'That's normal discharge — a sign your body is starting puberty.'
'Just wash outside with water and wear cotton underwear.'

steps.title: Normal discharge
steps.body: Starting 6–12 months before the first period, girls notice **clear or white discharge** that may dry yellowish on underwear. It keeps the vagina healthy and self-cleaning. Amount and texture change through the cycle (e.g. slippery and clear around ovulation). Mild smell is normal.

steps.title: Care
steps.body:
- Wash the **vulva (outside)** with plain water or mild unscented soap; **never douche** or wash inside the vagina — it upsets healthy bacteria.
- Wipe **front to back** after the toilet.
- Cotton underwear; change daily; avoid very tight synthetic clothes for long hours.
- Avoid scented sprays, powders and 'intimate washes' with perfumes.

steps.title: Solved example: normal or check?
steps.body:
(a) Clear-white, no itching → **normal**.
(b) Thick white 'curdy' discharge with itching → possible **yeast (thrush)** infection → doctor/pharmacist advice.
(c) Grey, fishy-smelling discharge → possible **bacterial vaginosis** → doctor.
(d) Green/yellow discharge, pain, fever, sores → **doctor soon**.
Yeast infections are common, not caused by being 'dirty', and treatable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Douching or using antiseptic liquids inside.
- Thinking discharge means 'weakness' (a myth, similar to the semen myth).
- Using pantyliners all day every day — let skin breathe; change often if you use them.

activity.prompt: Normal, or see a doctor?

items.text: Clear or white discharge, no itch

quiz.why: Clear or white vaginal discharge often starts about 6–12 months before the first period. It is a normal sign of hormone changes.
Douching (washing inside the vagina) is not recommended because it disrupts the healthy bacteria that protect against infection. The vagina cleans itself.
Always wipe front to back, so germs from the anus are not pushed toward the urethra and vagina. This helps prevent urinary tract infections.
Itchy, thick, curd-like discharge is typical of a yeast infection (thrush), which a doctor or pharmacist can treat. It is not pregnancy or normal discharge.
Normal discharge does not cause weakness; this is a myth. It is a natural body process.

lessons.title: Feet, mouth, underwear and a whole-body routine

scenes.text: At a friend's house everyone takes off shoes — and Raghav's feet smell strongly.
He learns about cotton socks, drying feet and airing shoes.
A week later: problem solved, confidence back.

steps.title: Feet
steps.body: Wash and **dry between toes**, change socks daily (cotton), air shoes and alternate pairs, use foot powder if you sweat a lot. Itchy peeling between toes → athlete's foot (fungal) → keep dry; antifungal cream as advised.

steps.title: Breath & teeth
steps.body: Brush twice for 2 minutes with fluoride toothpaste, clean the tongue, floss or use interdental brushes, drink water, limit sugary drinks. Bad breath lasting despite this may mean gum disease or tooth decay → dentist. **Gutkha, paan masala and tobacco** stain teeth and cause mouth cancer.

steps.title: Underwear & clothes
steps.body: Clean underwear daily, cotton crotch, change after sport. Wash sports kit after each use. Sleep in loose clothes. Boys: supportive underwear for sport.

steps.title: Solved example: weekly plan
steps.body:
Daily: bath, underwear, socks, brush ×2, deodorant.
Every 2–3 days: hair wash (or as your hair needs).
Weekly: change bed sheets & towel, trim nails, clean shoes.
Monthly: replace toothbrush every ~3 months (or when bristles splay).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wearing the same socks two days.
- Sharing towels or razors.
- Scrubbing skin harshly — gentle is better.

activity.prompt: My puberty hygiene routine
items: Clean underwear and cotton socks daily
Brush teeth twice and clean tongue

quiz.why: Athlete's foot is a fungal infection of the skin, usually between the toes. It is not viral or an allergy.
Replace your toothbrush about every 3 months, or sooner when the bristles fray, because old brushes clean poorly and hold germs.
Gutkha contains tobacco and other chemicals that raise the risk of mouth cancer. It does not whiten teeth or freshen breath.

quiz.q: Best sock material for sweaty feet:
quiz.why: Cotton socks absorb sweat and let feet breathe, which helps prevent smell and fungal infection. Nylon and plastic trap moisture.
Bad breath that continues despite brushing may signal a dental problem such as cavities or gum disease, so see a dentist. Mints only mask it.

questions.q: Body odour comes from…
questions.why: Body odour comes from bacteria on the skin breaking down sweat. Water, sleep or washing do not cause it.

questions.q: Wipe after the toilet…
questions.why: Wiping front to back keeps germs from the anus away from the urethra and vagina, helping prevent infections. Back to front spreads them forward.

questions.q: Never share…
questions.why: Razors and towels can carry skin germs or blood, so sharing them can spread infections. Pencils, music and books are safe to share.

questions.q: Antiperspirant…
questions.why: Antiperspirants contain aluminium salts that reduce sweating. Deodorants mainly control smell, and neither kills hair or whitens skin.

questions.q: Normal discharge is…
questions.why: Normal discharge is clear or white and not strongly smelly. Green discharge with fever suggests infection and needs a doctor.

questions.q: Hair removal is…
questions.why: Hair removal is optional, a personal choice. It is not compulsory, not medically needed, and not always harmful.

questions.q: Assertion: Douching is not advised. Reason: It disturbs the vagina's healthy bacteria.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Douching disturbs the vagina's healthy bacteria, which is exactly why it is not advised.

questions.q: Razor bumps are best prevented by…
options: sharp clean blade, gel, shaving with hair direction
questions.why: Razor bumps are prevented by using a sharp, clean blade, shaving gel, and shaving with the hair direction. Sharing a razor, pressing hard or dry shaving irritate the skin.

questions.q: Itchy peeling skin between toes is likely…
questions.why: Itchy, peeling skin between the toes is typical of athlete's foot, a fungal infection (tinea pedis). Scurvy and fractures do not cause this.

questions.q: Case: A girl has thick white itchy discharge after antibiotics. Likely?
questions.why: Antibiotics can kill the healthy bacteria that keep yeast in check, so thick white itchy discharge afterwards suggests a yeast infection (thrush). It is not a period or pregnancy.

questions.q: Case: Heavy sweating soaks a boy's shirt in an AC classroom. Best advice?
options: See a doctor; hyperhidrosis is treatable
questions.why: Very heavy sweating that soaks clothes even in cool rooms may be hyperhidrosis, which is treatable, so see a doctor. Stopping water or using more perfume does not help.

questions.q: Which daily routine is MOST complete?
options: Bath, clean underwear and socks, brush twice, deodorant
questions.why: The most complete routine includes bathing, clean underwear and socks, brushing twice and deodorant. Weekly baths, perfume alone or one brushing leave gaps.

questions.q: Grey discharge with a fishy smell suggests…
questions.why: Grey discharge with a fishy smell suggests bacterial vaginosis, a common imbalance of vaginal bacteria that a doctor can treat. It is not normal ovulation discharge or a period.

questions.q: Why does underarm smell increase in puberty?
options: Apocrine glands start + hair traps sweat for bacteria
questions.why: In puberty apocrine glands start working and underarm hair holds sweat, so bacteria break it down into smelly compounds. Weather or washing less are not the main reason.

questions.q: Case: An aunt says a 'feminine wash' with perfume is needed daily. Best evidence-based response?
options: Plain water/mild unscented soap outside only is enough; scented washes can irritate
questions.why: Plain water or mild unscented soap on the outside is enough, because the vagina cleans itself. Scented washes can irritate, and antiseptic or bleach inside is harmful.

questions.q: A teen wants to start waxing. Which is safest advice?
options: Hygienic salon, avoid irritated/broken skin, it's your choice
questions.why: Waxing is a personal choice. Do it in a hygienic place and avoid irritated or broken skin and pimples, and never share strips, to prevent infection.

questions.q: Which is the strongest reason for cotton underwear?
options: It breathes and reduces moisture that bacteria and yeast like
questions.why: Cotton underwear breathes and absorbs moisture, which bacteria and yeast like. Dry skin lowers the risk of infection; fashion, law or cost are not the reason.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Puberty & growing up
courses.summary: Quick revision of every puberty unit with a facts sheet, myth-buster drill, 'what would you do' cases and a 20-question mock test.
outcomes: Learners can recall key facts about puberty for all genders
Learners can correct common myths
Learners can choose safe actions in everyday puberty situations
courses.guardianNote: Revision of the puberty units: body changes, periods, wet dreams, body image and hygiene, in calm, non-explicit language consistent with UNESCO ITGSE 2018.

lessons.title: Facts sheet: puberty in one page

scenes.text: At a sleepover, cousins quiz each other with cards about puberty.
Lots of giggles, then real questions.
They're surprised how much they each didn't know.

steps.title: Everyone
steps.body: Starts ~8–13 (girls) / 9–14 (boys); lasts 3–5 years; hypothalamus → pituitary (FSH, LH) → ovaries (oestrogen, progesterone) / testes (testosterone). Growth spurt; body odour; acne; hair; mood changes; need for privacy.

steps.title: Girls
steps.body: Breast buds first → periods ~2–3 years later (10–15). Cycle counted from day 1 of bleeding; 21–45 days common early; period 2–7 days; ~30–40 ml blood. Pads 4–6 h; tampons ≤8 h; cups per maker; cloth pads dried in sun. Doctor: no period by 15, very heavy bleeding, severe pain, 3+ months missed.

steps.title: Boys
steps.body: Testicles enlarge first → penis growth, voice deepens, facial hair. Random erections and wet dreams are normal; semen loss doesn't cause weakness. Chest swelling often temporary. Sudden severe testicle pain = emergency.

steps.title: Body image & hygiene
steps.body: Bodies vary; filters distort. Eating disorders are treatable — tell an adult; 14416. Daily bath, clean underwear and socks, deodorant on clean skin, brush twice, never share razors, no douching, wipe front to back.

cards.front: First sign of puberty in girls

quiz.why: By rule, cycle day 1 is the first day of bleeding, since the period starts the new cycle. Ovulation is in the middle of the cycle.
Wet dreams do not cause weakness; that is a myth. They are a normal part of puberty.
FSH and LH are made by the pituitary gland at the base of the brain. They tell the ovaries or testes to work. The ovary makes oestrogen and progesterone instead.
Cloth pads should be dried in sunlight, which helps kill germs. Damp or dark drying lets germs grow.
Childline's helpline number is 1098, for children in need of help. 14416 is Tele-MANAS, 100 is police and 108 is ambulance.

lessons.title: Myth-buster drill

scenes.text: Dadi has many sayings about periods and 'weakness' from nightfall.
Her grandson and granddaughter read the science together with her.
Dadi laughs: 'In my time no one explained anything. I'm glad you know.'

steps.title: How to bust a myth respectfully
steps.body:
1. Listen and thank — elders often mean well.
2. Share the fact simply.
3. Mention a source (doctor, WHO, school health lessons).
4. Don't mock anyone's beliefs; you can respect family traditions and still know the science.

steps.title: Worked myths
steps.body:
- 'Don't bathe on your period' → bathing is hygienic and can ease cramps.
- 'Nightfall makes you weak' → no evidence; it's normal.
- 'Shaving thickens hair' → no.
- 'Tampons take away virginity' → virginity is a social idea, not a medical state; tampons are safe.
- 'Only girls need to learn about periods' → everyone benefits.
- 'Pimples mean you're dirty' → hormones.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Arguing angrily, or assuming every tradition is harmful. Focus on health and safety facts.

statements.s: Bathing during a period is unhealthy.
Semen loss causes memory loss.
Boys benefit from learning about periods.
Acne means poor hygiene.
Shaving doesn't change hair thickness.

quiz.q: Best way to correct an elder's myth:
quiz.why: Correct an elder's myth by listening first, then kindly sharing the facts. Shouting or mocking makes people defensive and they stop listening.

options: Tampons don't affect a medical 'virginity' — it's a social idea
quiz.why: Tampons do not affect a medical 'virginity'; virginity is a social idea, not a medical state. Tampons can be used safely by anyone who has periods.
Everyone should learn about periods, as it is normal human biology. Knowing helps people support each other and reduces shame and myths.
Pimples come mainly from hormones, which make skin glands produce extra oil that blocks pores. Dirt, cold or sin do not cause them.

lessons.title: What would you do? Puberty cases

scenes.text: Drama club acts out tricky puberty moments.
The audience votes on the best response.
The kindest, safest choices win every time.

steps.title: Case 1
steps.body: Your period starts at school and you have no pad. → Ask a female teacher, nurse or friend; many schools keep supplies; tie a sweater; message a parent.

steps.title: Case 2
steps.body: A classmate's voice cracks and others laugh. → Don't join in; change the subject or say 'Happens to everyone.'

steps.title: Case 3
steps.body: Someone online asks for a photo of your changing body. → Refuse, block, tell a trusted adult; report — it's never your fault. (Details in the Safety pack.)

steps.title: Case 4
steps.body: Your friend hasn't eaten lunch for two weeks and talks about being 'disgusting'. → Talk privately, kindly; tell a trusted adult.

a.text: In class, a girl's skirt has a period stain. Two boys start giggling.

choices.label: Quietly tell her and offer your sweater
Laugh along
choices.feedback: That deepens embarrassment and is a form of bullying.

x.text: She looks close to tears. Try again?

choices.label: Stop laughing, tell her quietly, offer help

b.text: She's relieved. The boys keep giggling.

choices.label: Say 'It's just a period, it's normal — grow up' and carry on
Tell the teacher if it continues

end1.text: The moment passes. You helped make the class kinder.

quiz.q: No pad at school — best first step?
quiz.why: Ask a teacher, school nurse or trusted friend for a pad. Asking solves the problem; hiding all day or using paper is unsafe and unhygienic.

quiz.q: Online request for a body photo:
quiz.why: Refuse, block the person and tell a trusted adult. Sharing body photos is unsafe and can be misused; keeping chatting lets the pressure continue.
A cracking voice is a normal part of puberty, so support your friend. Mocking, recording or telling everyone is unkind.

options: Talk privately and involve an adult
quiz.why: Talk to your friend privately and involve a trusted adult, because skipping meals and self-criticism can be early signs of an eating problem. Dieting with them or joking makes things worse.

questions.q: Puberty is controlled by…
questions.why: Puberty is controlled by hormones released by the brain's pituitary gland and the ovaries or testes. Food or school affect health but do not control it.

questions.q: Period usually lasts…
questions.why: A period usually lasts 2–7 days. One day always, 2 weeks or a month are outside the typical range.

questions.q: Wet dreams are…
questions.why: Wet dreams are a normal part of puberty in boys. They are not dangerous or an illness.

questions.q: Never share…
questions.why: Never share razors, as they can carry blood and spread infections. Books and songs are safe to share.

questions.q: Girls start puberty usually…
questions.why: Girls usually start puberty earlier than boys, on average about a year or two earlier.

questions.q: Breast-tissue swelling in teen boys…
questions.why: Breast-tissue swelling in teen boys (gynaecomastia) often resolves by itself as hormones settle. It is not cancer, and surgery is rarely needed.

questions.q: Healthy body image includes…
options: respecting and caring for your body
questions.why: A healthy body image means respecting and caring for your body. Crash diets, filters and constant comparison harm it.

questions.q: Deodorant goes on…
questions.why: Deodorant is applied to clean, dry skin so it works well. On sweaty skin or clothes it is far less effective.

questions.q: Assertion: The testes are in the scrotum. Reason: Sperm need a slightly cooler temperature.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Sperm need a temperature slightly cooler than the body's, so the testes sit in the scrotum.

questions.q: Which needs a doctor?
questions.why: Having no period by age 15 is delayed and should be checked by a doctor. Mild cramps, pimples and a first period at 12 are normal.

questions.q: LH surge causes…
questions.why: A surge of LH (luteinising hormone) triggers ovulation, the release of an egg from the ovary. It does not cause acne, growth or the period directly.

questions.q: Case: Boy hit by cricket ball, pain eases in 20 minutes. Best?
options: Rest, ice; doctor if not better
questions.why: A minor knock that eases in 20 minutes can be managed with rest and ice, and see a doctor if it doesn't get better. Surgery is not needed, but swelling for days must not be ignored.

questions.q: Last period 1 May; cycle 31 days. Next expected:
questions.why: Next period = 1 May + 31 days. May has 31 days, so 31 days after 1 May is 1 June.

questions.q: Cycle 26 days: ovulation about day…
questions.why: Ovulation is about 14 days before the next period. So 26 − 14 = day 12, not day 14, which fits only a 28-day cycle.

questions.q: Pads ₹7 each, 4/day, 5 days, 12 months:
questions.why: Pads per year = 4 × 5 × 12 = 240 pads. Then 240 × ₹7 = ₹1,680.

questions.q: A 'stop nightfall' clinic ad: best judgement?
questions.why: Ads to 'stop nightfall' exploit a myth, because nightfall is normal and needs no treatment. They profit from fear.

questions.q: Case: Fever, rash, vomiting with tampon in 9 h →
questions.why: Fever, rash and vomiting with a tampon in for 9 hours can be toxic shock syndrome. Remove the tampon and get urgent care; a new tampon or sleeping is dangerous.

questions.q: Case: Sudden severe testicle pain at night + vomiting →
questions.why: Sudden severe testicle pain with vomiting at night suggests torsion, an emergency where the testicle twists. Go to hospital now, since delay can lose the testicle.

questions.q: Which is MOST accurate?
options: Normal puberty timing has a wide range
questions.why: The age when puberty starts has a wide normal range. Starting earlier or later than friends is usually normal, and not everyone starts at 12.

questions.q: Friend with signs of an eating disorder asks for secrecy. Best?
options: Express care; involve a trusted adult
questions.why: Show you care and involve a trusted adult, because eating disorders are serious and treatable. Keeping the secret leaves your friend at risk, and telling the class would hurt them.
